κατὰ τούτους οὖν οὐδὲν μὲν τῶν συνθέτων τούτων σωμάτων ἐστὶν ἡ στοιχειώδης γῆ, πλεῖστον μέντοι τῆς γῆς ἔχειν αὐτά φασιν, οἷον τόν τε ἀδάμαντα καὶ τὰς πέτρας, καὶ ὅσῳ γ’ ἂν ὦσι σκληρότερα τὸ σῶμα, τοσούτῳ μᾶλλον αὐτὰ εἶναί φασι γεωδέστερα ἔμπαλιν τοῖς γεωργοῖς.
οὐ γὰρ τὴν σκληροτέραν σύστασιν τῶν σωμάτων ὀνομάζουσιν οὗτοι γεωδεστέραν, ἀλλὰ λίθους μὲν καὶ πέτρας τὰ τοιαῦτα καλοῦσιν ἀνεπιτηδειότατα πρὸς γεωργίαν.
ἀκριβεστάτην δὲ γῆν εἶναί φασι τὴν ποῤῥωτάτην τῇ συ στάσει τῆς πέτρας, ὅπου γε καὶ τὴν ἀργιλώδη τε καὶ τὴν ψαμμώδη μέμφονται πρὸς τὰ πλεῖστα.
κατὰ μὲν οὖν τὸ παρὰ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις σημαινόμενον αἱ τῆς γῆς διαφοραὶ τρισὶν ὁρισθήσονται γένεσιν.

ἔστι γὰρ τὸ μέν τι λίθος αὐτῆς, τὸ δὲ μεταλλευτόν τι σῶμα, τὸ δὲ τρίτον ἡ γεωργουμένη γῆ, διαφωνίας γεγονυίας παρ’ αὐτοῖς περὶ τῶν χεομένων μεταλλευτῶν σωμάτων, οἷον χαλκοῦ καὶ κασσιτέρου καὶ μολύβδου.
ταῦτα γὰρ ἔνιοί φασιν οὐ γῆς, ἀλλ’ ὕδατος ἔχειν τὸ πλέον.
οἵ γε μὴν ἄλλοι πάντες ἄνθρωποι γῆν ὀνομάζουσιν ἐκείνην μόνην τὴν οὐσίαν, ἥτις ὑγρῷ φυραθεῖσα πηλὸς γίνεται.

περὶ ἧς κᾀγὼ νῦν ἔγνωκα τὰς διαφορὰς εἰπεῖν, ἐκεῖνο μόνον ἔτι προσθεὶς, ὡς ἡ προειρημένη τομὴ τῶν γεωδῶν σωμάτων εἴς τε λίθους καὶ τὰ μεταλλευόμενα καὶ τὴν γεωργουμένην γῆν ἄνευ τῶν φυσικῶν ἰδίως ὀνομαζομένων σωμάτων εἴρηται.
τούτων δὲ προσιόντων καὶ τὰ ξύλα πάντα καὶ καρπῶν μόρια πολλὰ, καθάπερ καὶ ζώων, ὀνομασθήσεται γεώδη τὴν οὐσίαν εἶναι.
καρπῶν μὲν μόρια, πυρῆνες ἐλαιῶν καὶ γίγαρτα σταφυλῶν καὶ καρύων λέμματα καὶ κώνων, ἕτερά τε πολλὰ τοιαῦτα, τῶν ζώων δὲ τά τ’ ὀστέα καὶ τὰ κέρατα καὶ οἱ ὀδόντες.

ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τῶν ἐν τοῖς φυτοῖς μορίων ὅσα γεώδη καὶ σκληρὰ, τὸ μέν πού τι καὶ πρόσθεν εἴρηται, τὸ δ’ ἂν καὶ νῦν ῥηθείη· περὶ δὲ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις ἐφεξῆς εἰρήσεται, πρότερον διελθόντος μου τὰ κατὰ τὴν γῆν εἴδη.
καλεῖν μὲν γὰρ ἔξεστί σοι καὶ διαφορὰς αὐτὰ καὶ εἴδη καὶ γένη.

λέγω δὴ ταῦτα λίθους τε καὶ τὰ μεταλλευτὰ σώματα, καὶ τὴν εἰς πηλὸν λυομένην γῆν, καὶ πρῶτόν γε τὰς διαφορὰς ἐρῶ τῆς ὑπὸ πάντων Ἑλλήνων ὀνομαζομένης γῆς, ἥτις ἔχει κοινὸν ὕδατι πλησιάσασα, διαλύεσθαι παραχρῆμα καὶ πηλὸν γίνεσθαι.
τὸ γὰρ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις οὕτω καλούμενον οὐ κοινὸν ἅπασιν, ἀλλ’ ἐκείνοις μόνοις σύνηθες ἔχει τοὶ σημαινόμενον.
english_sentences: [9.1.1] On earths.
On the differences of earth.] Since two things are signified by the name 'earth', it is necessary first to distinguish them for the sake of clarity in what is to be said.
One of them is familiar to all the Greeks.

For both when they sow wheat or barley or any of the other seeds which are called Demetrian, they say the earth must be moderately moist; and when they plant vines or fig-trees or olives or any of the other trees, they bid one guard against both the earth that is extremely devoid of moisture and dry, and that which is moist and muddy.
For indeed they call earth that has been kneaded with liquid 'mud', and those who have written on agriculture, in the differences of lands, speak of black-soiled, clayey and sandy as distinguished.
They also call 'oily' the earth from which the mud becomes viscous, and another, disposed in the opposite way to this, non-oily and producing, as one might say, a crumbly mud.
This, then, is one signification of the name 'earth', familiar to all.
The other belongs to the philosophers alone, since they say that the elements of bodies are earth and water and air and fire.
For they call the body that is extremely dry and cold 'earth'.

According to them, then, none of these composite bodies is the elemental earth, yet they say that they have the greatest share of earth, such as adamant and rocks, and the harder they are in body, the more earthy they say they are — the reverse of the farmers.

For the latter do not call the harder consistency of bodies more earthy, but call such things stones and rocks, most unsuitable for farming; and they say that the most exact earth is that which is furthest in consistency from rock, seeing that they even find fault with the clayey and the sandy for most purposes.

According to the signification among the philosophers, then, the differences of earth will be defined by three genera: for one part of it is stone, another a mined body, and the third the cultivated earth — a disagreement having arisen among them concerning the mined bodies that are poured (fusible), such as copper and tin and lead; for some people say that these have the greater share not of earth but of water.
All other men, however, call 'earth' only that substance which, when kneaded with liquid, becomes mud.

It is about this that I too have now resolved to state the differences, adding only this further, that the aforesaid division of earthy bodies into stones, mined things and cultivated earth has been stated apart from the bodies that are properly called 'natural'.

If these are added, all woods too, and many parts of fruits, as also of animals, will be named earthy in substance: parts of fruits — the stones of olives and the pips of grapes and the shells of nuts and of pine-cones, and many others of this kind; of animals, the bones and the horns and the teeth.

But concerning the parts in plants that are earthy and hard, something has been said before, and something may be said now as well; concerning those in animals it will be said next in order, after I have first gone through the kinds of earth.
For you may call them both differences and kinds and genera.

I mean by these stones and the mined bodies and the earth that dissolves into mud; and first I shall state the differences of the earth so named by all the Greeks, which has in common that, on coming near water, it dissolves immediately and becomes mud.
For that which is so called among the philosophers has its signification not common to all, but familiar to those alone.

beads.greek: Περὶ τῶν διαφορῶν τῆς συνήθως ὀνομαζομένης γῆς.] Γῆν ἔφην ὀνομάζεσθαι σύνηθες ἅπασιν Ἕλλησιν, ἥτις ἂν εἰς τὸ ὑγρὸν ἐμβληθεῖσα παραχρῆμα διαλύεταί τε καὶ πηλὸς γίνεται.
beads.english: On the differences of the earth that is customarily so named.] I said that all Greeks customarily give the name "earth" to that which, when it is thrown into liquid, is at once dissolved and becomes mud.

beads.greek: ταύτης οὖν ἡ μέν τίς ἐστιν ἣν γεωργοῦσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, διαφορὰς ἔχουσά τινας μὲν κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον ἐν τῷ λιπαρά τε εἶναι καὶ γλίσχρος, ἥτις πάντως ἐστὶ καὶ μέλαινα τὴν χρόαν. ἡ δὲ ψαθυρωτέρα τε καὶ ἀλιπὴς, ἣν καλοῦσιν ἄργιλον, οὖσα καὶ ἥδε λευκοτέρα πως.
beads.english: Of this, then, one kind is that which men cultivate, having certain differences in its own right (κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον), in being oily and viscous—a kind which is in every case also black in colour—while the other is more crumbly and non-oily, which they call argil, this too being in some degree whiter.

beads.greek: ἐναντιώταται μὲν αὗται διαφοραί· αἱ δ’ ἄλλαι μεταξὺ τούτων, ἤτοι τῇ ἑτέρᾳ πλησιάζουσαι μᾶλλον ἢ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ, τινὲς δὲ κᾀν τῷ ﻿ μέσῳ δοκεῖν ἀκριβῶς εἶναι, τὴν ἴσην ἀμφοῖν ἀφεστηκυῖαι διάστασιν.
beads.english: These differences are the most opposed; the others lie between these, either approaching more nearly to the one or to the other, and some seem to be exactly in the middle, standing at an equal distance from both.

beads.greek: αἱ δ’ ἐξ ἐπιμιξίας ἑτερογενῶν σωμάτων διαφοραὶ τῆς γῆς εἰσι, καθὸ λιθώδεις τε καὶ ψαμμώδεις ὑπάρχουσιν, καὶ χωρίζουσί γε τῶν τοιούτων τὴν μεμιγμένην οὐσίαν, ἀναδεύσαντες καὶ ἀναφυράσαντες ὕδατι πολλῷ, μέχρι τοῦ πᾶν ὑγρὸν ἐργάσασθαι.
beads.english: There are also differences of earth that arise from admixture of bodies of a different kind, insofar as they are stony and sandy; and they separate the mixed-in substance from such earths by soaking and kneading them with much water, until they make the whole liquid.

beads.greek: καθισταμένου γὰρ τούτου τὸ μὲν τῆς λιθώδους τε καὶ ψαμμώδους ἐμφερόμενον ὑφιζάνει πᾶν, ἐποχεῖται δὲ ἡ ἀκριβὴς γῆ.
beads.english: For when this settles, all the stony and sandy matter carried in it sinks to the bottom, while the exact earth floats above.

beads.greek: τοιοῦτον γάρ τι καὶ κατὰ τὴν Λημνίαν γίνεται γῆν, ἣν μίλτον ὀνομάζουσιν ἔνιοι Λημνίαν καί τινες ἄλλοι σφραγῖδα Λημνίαν, διὰ τὴν ἐπιβαλλομένην αὐτῇ σφραγῖδα τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος ἱεράν.
beads.english: For something of this sort happens also in the case of the Lemnian earth, which some call Lemnian miltos and certain others Lemnian seal, because of the seal sacred to Artemis which is impressed upon it.

beads.greek: ταύτην γάρ τοι τὴν γῆν ἡ ἱέρεια λαμβάνουσα μετά τινος ἐπιχωρίου τιμῆς, οὐ ζώων θυομένων, ἀλλὰ πυρῶν καὶ κριθῶν ἀντιδιδομένων τῷ χωρίῳ, κομίζει μὲν εἰς τὴν πόλιν ἀναφυράσασα ὕδατι καὶ πηλὸν ὑγρὸν ἐργασαμένη καὶ τοῦτον ταράξασα σφοδρῶς, εἶτ’ ἐάσασα καταστῆναι, πρῶτον μὲν ἀφαιρεῖ τὸ ἐπιπολῆς ὕδωρ, εἶθ’ ὑπ’ αὐτῷ τὸ λιπαρὸν τῆς γῆς λαβοῦσα καὶ μόνον ἀπολιποῦσα τὸ ὑφιζηκὸς λιθῶδές τε καὶ ψαμμῶδες, ὅπερ καὶ ἄχρηστόν ἐστιν, ἄχρι τοσούτου ξηραίνει τὸν λιπαρὸν πηλὸν, ἄχρις ἂν εἰς σύστασιν ἀφίκηται μαλακοῦ κηροῦ, καὶ τούτου λαμβάνουσα μόρια σμικρὰ τὴν ἱερὰν τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος ἐπιβάλλει σφραγῖδα, κἄπειτα πάλιν ἐν σκιᾷ ξηραίνει, μέχρις ἂν ἀκριβῶς ἄνικμος ἀποτελεσθῇ, καὶ γένηται τοῦτο δὴ τὸ γινωσκόμενον ἰατροῖς ἅπασι φάρμακον ἡ Λημνία σφραγίς.
beads.english: For the priestess, taking this earth with a certain local honour—not with animals being sacrificed, but with wheat and barley given in return to the place—conveys it to the city, and having kneaded it with water and made a liquid mud and stirred this violently, then having let it settle, she first removes the water on the surface, then, taking the oily part of the earth beneath it and leaving behind only the stony and sandy matter that has settled, which is indeed useless, she dries the oily mud to such a degree until it comes to the consistency of soft wax, and taking small portions of this she impresses upon them the sacred seal of Artemis, and then again dries them in the shade until it is rendered exactly free of moisture, and this becomes the drug known to all physicians, the Lemnian seal.

beads.greek: οὕτω γὰρ αὐτὴν ὀνομάζουσιν, ὡς ἔφην, ἔνιοι διὰ τὴν ἐπιβαλλομένην αὐτῇ σφραγῖδα, καθάπερ γε καὶ διὰ τὴν χρόαν ἔνιοι Λημνίαν μίλτον.
beads.english: For so some name it, as I said, because of the seal impressed upon it, just as some also, because of its colour, call it Lemnian miltos.

beads.greek: ἔχει μὲν οὖν τὴν χρόαν τὴν αὐτὴν τῇ μίλτῳ, διαφέρει δ’ αὐτῆς τῷ μὴ μολύνειν ἁπτομένην, καθάπερ ἐκείνην, καὶ κατά γε τὸν λόφον ἐν τῇ Λήμνῳ τὸν ὅλον ὄντα κιῤῥὸν τῇ χρόᾳ, καθ’ ὃν οὔτε δένδρον ἐστὶν οὔτε πέτρα οὔτε φυτὸν, μόνη δ’ ἡ τοιαύτη γῆ.
beads.english: It has, then, the same colour as miltos, but differs from it in not staining when it is touched, as that one does, and also in respect of the hill in Lemnos, which is wholly tawny in colour, on which there is neither tree nor rock nor plant, but only earth of this sort.

beads.greek: τρεῖς δ’ αὐτῆς εὑρίσκονται διαφοραί· μία μὲν ἡ προειρημένη τῆς ἱερᾶς γῆς, ἧς οὐδεὶς ἄλλος ἅπτεται πλὴν τῆς ἱερείας. δευτέρα δ’ ἑτέρα τῆς ὄντως μίλτου, χρῶνται δ’ οἱ τέκτονες αὐτῇ μάλιστα.
beads.english: Three differences of it are found: one, the aforesaid, of the sacred earth, which no one else touches except the priestess; a second, different one, of the true miltos, which the carpenters especially use; and a third, of the cleansing (ῥυπούσης) kind, which those of the washers of linens and garments who so wish use.

beads.greek: τρίτη δ’ ἡ τῆς ῥυπούσης, ᾗ χρῶνται τῶν πλυνόντων ὀθόνας τε καὶ ἐσθῆτας οἱ βουληθέντες. ἀνεγνωκὼς δὲ ἐγὼ παρά τε Διοσκορίδῃ καὶ ἄλλοις τισὶ μίγνυσθαι τράγειον αἷμα τῇ Λημνίᾳ γῇ, κᾀκ τοῦ διὰ μίξεως ταύτης γενομένου πηλοῦ τὴν ἱέρειαν ἀναπλάττειν τε καὶ σφραγίζειν ἃς ὀνομάζουσι Λημνίας σφραγῖδας, ὠρέχθην αὐτὸς ἱστορῆσαι τὴν συμμετρίαν τῆς μίξεως.
beads.english: Having read in Dioscorides and certain others that goat's blood is mixed with the Lemnian earth, and that from the mud produced by this mixture the priestess moulds and seals what they call Lemnian seals, I desired myself to investigate the proportion of the mixture.

beads.greek: ὥσπερ οὖν εἰς Κύπρον ἕνεκα τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ μετάλλων, εἴς τε τὴν κοίλην Συρίαν, μόριον οὖσαν τῆς Παλαιστίνης, ἕνεκεν ἀσφάλτου καί τινων ἄλλων κατ’ αὐτὴν ἀξίων ἱστορίας ἐπορεύθην, οὕτως καὶ εἰς Λῆμνον οὐκ ὤκνησα πλεῦσαι, θεασόμενος ὁπόσον μίγνυται τοῦ αἵματος τῇ γῇ.
beads.english: Just as, then, I travelled to Cyprus for the sake of the mines in it, and to Coele Syria, which is a part of Palestine, for the sake of asphalt and certain other things in it worth investigating, so too I did not hesitate to sail to Lemnos, intending to see how much of the blood is mixed with the earth.

beads.greek: καὶ τό γε δεύτερον ἐξ Ἀσίας εἰς Ῥώμην ἀφικέσθαι πεζῇ πορευόμενος διὰ Θρᾴκης τε καὶ Μακεδονίας, ἔπλευσα πρότερον ἀπὸ Τρῳάδος Ἀλεξανδρείας εἰς Λῆμνον, ἐπιτυχὼν εἰς Θεσσαλονίκην ἀναγομένου πλοίου, συνθεμένῳ τῷ ναυκλήρῳ παραβάλλειν πρότερον τῇ Λήμνῳ· ὁ δὲ προσέσχε μὲν, οὐ μὴν ᾗ γ’ ἐχρῆν πόλει.
beads.english: And on the second occasion of coming from Asia to Rome, travelling on foot through Thrace and Macedonia, I sailed first from Alexandria Troas to Lemnos, having found a ship putting out for Thessalonica, the ship-master having agreed to put in first at Lemnos; and he did put in, but not at the city where he should have.

beads.greek: τὴν ἀρχὴν γὰρ οὐδ’ ἠπιστάμην δύο πόλεις εἶναι κατὰ τὴν νῆσον, ἀλλὰ ᾤμην, ὡς Σάμον καὶ Χίον καὶ Κῶ Ἄνδρον τε καὶ Τῆνον καὶ πάσας τὰς κατὰ τὸ Αἰγαῖον, οὕτω καὶ τὴν Λῆμνον ὁμώνυμον ἔχειν πόλιν ὅλῃ τῇ νήσῳ μίαν.
beads.english: For at the start I did not even know that there were two cities on the island, but supposed that, like Samos and Chios and Cos and Andros and Tenos and all the islands in the Aegean, so too Lemnos had a single city bearing the same name as the whole island.

beads.greek: ὡς δὲ ἀποβὰς τῆς νεὼς, ἔγνων Μυρίναν μὲν ὀνομάζεσθαι τὴν πόλιν, εἶναι δ’ οὔτε κατὰ Φιλοκτήτην οὔτε κατὰ τὸ ἱερὸν τοῦ Ἡφαίστου λόφον ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ τῆς πόλεως ἐκείνης, ἀλλ’ ἐν ἑτέρᾳ τῇ Ἡφαιστιάδι καλουμένῃ, καὶ οὐδ’ ἐγγὺς εἶναι τὴν πόλιν ἐκείνην τῆς Μυρίνης, ὅ τε ναύκληρος οὐκ ἠδύνατό με περιμένειν, ἀνεβαλλόμην εἰσαῦθις, ὅταν ἀπὸ Ῥώμης εἰς Ἀσίαν ἀφίκωμαι, θεάσασθαι τὴν Ἡφαιστιάδα.
beads.english: But when I disembarked from the ship, I learned that the city was called Myrina, and that the hill was neither in connection with Philoctetes nor in connection with the temple of Hephaestus in the territory of that city, but in the other, called Hephaestias, and that that city was not even near Myrina; and since the ship-master could not wait for me, I deferred to a later time, when I should come from Rome to Asia, the viewing of Hephaestias.

beads.greek: καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἐπράχθη, καθάπερ ἤλπισά τε καὶ προὐθέμην.
beads.english: And this was accomplished for me, just as I hoped and proposed.

beads.greek: ὡς γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας διαβαλὼν εἰς τὴν Μακεδονίαν καὶ σχεδὸν ὅλην αὐτὴν ὁδοιπορήσας ἐν Φιλίπποις ἐγενόμην, ἥπερ ἐστὶν ὅμορος τῇ Θρᾴκῃ πόλις, ἐντεῦθεν ἐπὶ τὴν πλησίον θάλατταν εἴκοσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἑκατὸν ἀπέχουσαν στάδια κατελθὼν, ἔπλευσα πρότερον μὲν εἰς Θάσον ἐγγύς που διακοσίους σταδίους, ἐκεῖθεν δὲ εἰς Λῆμνον ἑπτακοσίους, εἶτ’ αὖθις ἀπὸ Λήμνου τοὺς ἴσους ἑπτακοσίους εἰς Ἀλεξανδρείαν Τρῳάδα.
beads.english: For when, having crossed from Italy to Macedonia and having travelled through almost the whole of it, I arrived at Philippi, which is a city bordering on Thrace, going down from there to the nearby sea, which is a hundred and twenty stades distant, I sailed first to Thasos, somewhere near two hundred stades, from there to Lemnos seven hundred, then again from Lemnos the same seven hundred to Alexandria Troas.

beads.greek: καὶ διὰ τοῦτ’ ἐξεπίτηδες ἔγραψα περί τε τοῦ πλοῦ καὶ τῶν σταδίων, ὅπως εἴ τις ἐθέλῃ θεάσασθαι καὶ αὐτὸς ὁμοίως ἐμοὶ τὴν Ἡφαιστιάδα διαγινώσκων τὴν θέσιν αὐτῆς, οὕτως παρασκευάζοιτο πρὸς τὸν πλοῦν.
beads.english: And for this reason I have deliberately written about the voyage and the stades, so that if anyone wishes to see Hephaestias himself just as I did, knowing its position, he may thus prepare for the voyage.

beads.greek: ἐν γάρ τοι τῇ ὅλῃ νήσῳ τῇ Λήμνῳ, κατὰ μὲν τὸ πρὸς ταῖς ἀνατολαῖς μέρος αὐτῆς ἐστιν Ἡφαιστιὰς, κατὰ δὲ τὸ πρὸς ταῖς δυσμαῖς ἡ Μυρίνα.
beads.english: For in the whole island of Lemnos, Hephaestias lies in the part toward the east and Myrina in the part toward the west.

beads.greek: καὶ τό γε ὑπὸ τοῦ ποιητοῦ λεγόμενον ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἡφαίστου, κάππεσεν ἐν Λήμνῳ, διὰ τὴν φύσιν τοῦ λόφου δοκεῖ μοι τὸν μῦθον ἐπίστασθαι.
beads.english: And what is said by the poet about Hephaestus, "he fell in Lemnos," seems to me to have set up (ἐπίστασθαι) the myth because of the nature of the hill.

beads.greek: φαίνεται γὰρ ὁμοιότατος κεκαυμένῳ κατά γε τὴν χρόαν καὶ διὰ τὸ μηδὲν ἐν αὐτῷ φύεσθαι.
beads.english: For it appears most like something burnt, both in colour and because nothing grows on it.

beads.greek: εἰς τοῦτον οὖν τὸν λόφον ἥ τε ἱέρεια παραγενομένη, καθ’ ὃν ἐγὼ καιρὸν ἐπέβην τῆς νήσου, καί τινα πυρῶν τε καὶ κριθῶν ἀριθμὸν ἐμβάλλουσα τῇ γῇ καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ ποιήσασα κατὰ τὸν ἐπιχώριον σεβασμὸν, ἐπλήρωσεν μὲν ὅλην ἅμαξαν τῆς γῆς.
beads.english: To this hill, then, the priestess came, at the time when I set foot on the island, and casting a certain number of grains of wheat and barley onto the earth and performing certain other acts in accordance with the local reverence, she filled a whole wagon with the earth.

beads.greek: κομίσασα δ’ εἰς τὴν πόλιν, ὡς εἶπον ἀρτίως, ἐσκεύασε τὰς πολυθρυλήτους Λημνίας σφραγῖδας.
beads.english: And having conveyed it to the city, as I said just now, she prepared the much-talked-of Lemnian seals.

beads.greek: ἔδοξεν οὖν μοι πυθέσθαι μή τι πρότερόν ποτε τράγειον ἢ αἴγειον αἷμα τῇ γῇ ταύτῃ μιγνύμενον ἐν ἱστορίᾳ παρειλήφασιν.
beads.english: It seemed good to me, then, to inquire whether they had ever before received in their tradition any account of goat's or she-goat's blood being mixed with this earth.

beads.greek: ἐφ’ ᾗ ﻿ πεύσει πάντες οἱ ἀκούσαντες ἐγέλασαν, οὐχ οἱ τυχόντες ἄνδρες ὄντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάνυ πεπαιδευμένοι τά τ’ ἄλλα καὶ τὴν ἐπιχώριον ἱστορίαν ἅπασαν.
beads.english: At this inquiry all who heard laughed, being not ordinary men but very well educated both in other matters and in the whole local history.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ βιβλίον ἔλαβον. παρά τινος αὐτῶν, γεγραμμένον ὑπό τινος τῶν ἐπιχωρίων ἀνδρῶν ἔμπροσθεν, ἐν ᾧ τὴν χρῆσιν ἅπασαν ἐδίδασκε τῆς Λημνίας γῆς, ὅθεν οὐκ ὤκνησα κᾀγὼ πειραθῆναι τοῦ φαρμάκου, δισμυρίας λαβὼν σφραγῖδας.
beads.english: But I also received a book from one of them, written earlier by one of the local men, in which he taught the whole use of the Lemnian earth, whence I too did not hesitate to make trial of the drug, taking twenty thousand seals.

beads.greek: ἐχρῆτο δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ δοὺς τὸ βιβλίον, ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις ἀριθμούμενος τῆς Ἡφαιστιάδος, εἰς πολλὰ τῷ φαρμάκῳ.
beads.english: And the man himself who gave the book, being counted among the first men of Hephaestias, used the drug for many purposes.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ τραυμάτων καὶ παλαιῶν καὶ δυσεπουλώτων ἐχεοδήκτων τε καὶ ὅλως θηριοδήκτων, ἐπί τε τῶν θανασίμων φαρμάκων, οὐ προδιδοὺς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπιδιδοὺς, ἐχρῆτο τῇ σφραγῖδι.
beads.english: For both on wounds, old ones and those hard to cicatrize, and on viper-bites and in general bites of venomous animals, and in cases of deadly drugs, giving it not only beforehand but also afterwards, he used the seal.

beads.greek: ἔφασκε δὲ καὶ τοῦ διὰ τῶν ἀρκευθίδων φαρμάκου πεῖραν ἔχειν, εἰς ὃ καὶ τῆς Λημνίας ἐμβάλλεται κινοῦντος ἔμετον, εἴ τις ἔτι κατὰ τὴν κοιλίαν ὄντος τοῦ θανασίμου φαρμάκου πίοι τὸ ἀλεξητήριον.
beads.english: He said also that he had experience of the drug made with juniper berries, into which Lemnian earth also is put, which provokes vomiting, if someone drinks the protective remedy while the deadly drug is still in the belly.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ τούτου μὲν καὶ ἡμεῖς ἔχομεν πεῖραν ἐπί τε λαγωοῦ θαλαττίου καὶ κανθαρίδων, ὑποπτευσάντων μὲν εἰληφέναι τι τοιοῦτον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἐμεσάντων δ’ αὐτίκα πᾶν ἐπὶ τῷ διὰ τῆς Λημνίας σφραγῖδος φαρμάκῳ, καὶ μηδὲν μετὰ ταῦτα παθόντων σύμπτωμα τῶν ἑπομένων λαγωῷ τε καὶ κανθαρίσι, καίτοι τῆς δόσεως τῶν ὀλεθρίων φαρμάκων ἐλεγχθείσης.
beads.english: But of this we too have experience in the case of the sea-hare and cantharides, when people suspected that they had taken something of this sort, and immediately vomited everything upon the drug made with the Lemnian seal, and afterwards suffered none of the symptoms that follow sea-hare and cantharides, even though the administration of the deadly drugs was proved.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τἄλλα θανάσιμα φάρμακα, ταῦτα δὴ τὰ δηλητήρια καλούμενα, τὴν αὐτὴν δύναμιν ἔχει τὸ διὰ τῶν ἀρκευθίδων καὶ τῆς Λημνίας φάρμακον, ἐμοὶ μὲν ἄδηλον.
beads.english: But whether against the other deadly drugs, those called deleterious, the drug made with juniper berries and Lemnian earth has the same power, is unclear to me.

beads.greek: ὁ δ’ ἐκ τῆς Ἡφαιστιάδος ἐπηγγείλατο μέχρι τοῦ καὶ λυττῶντος κυνὸς ἰᾶσθαι δῆγμα φάσκειν αὐτὴν, πινομένην δι’ οἴνου κεκραμένου, κατὰ δὲ τοῦ ἕλκους ἐπιτιθεμένην δι’ ὄξους πάνυ δριμέος.
beads.english: The man from Hephaestias went so far as to declare that it even cures the bite of a mad dog, when drunk in diluted wine and applied to the ulcer in very pungent vinegar.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ δι’ ὄξους μὲν καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων θηρίων ἔλεγεν αὐτὴν ἰᾶσθαι δήγματα, φύλλων βοτανῶν ἔξωθεν ἐπιτιθεμένων, ἃς ἐμάθομεν ἀντιπεπονθέναι σηπεδόσιν.
beads.english: But with vinegar he said it cures also the bites of the other venomous creatures, with leaves of herbs applied externally, which we have learned to be opposed to putrefactions.

beads.greek: μάλιστα δ’ ἐπῄνει σκόρδιον, εἶτα κενταύριον τὸ λεπτὸν, εἶτα πράσιον.
beads.english: He praised most of all scordium, then the slender centaury, then horehound.

beads.greek: ἐπί γε μὴν κακοήθων καὶ σηπεδονωδῶν ἑλκῶν εἴ ποτ’ ἐχρησάμην τῇ Λημνίᾳ, μεγάλως ὠφέλησε.
beads.english: On malignant and putrefactive ulcers at any rate, whenever I used the Lemnian earth, it helped greatly.

beads.greek: ἡ δὲ χρῆσις γίνεται κατὰ τὸ μέγεθος τῆς τοῦ ἕλκους κακίας.
beads.english: The use is in accordance with the magnitude of the badness of the ulcer.

beads.greek: τὸ μὲν γὰρ δυσῶδες καὶ λίαν πλαδαρόν τε καὶ ῥυπαρὸν, ἀνέχεται δι’ ὄξους δριμυτάτου τῆς Λημνίας λελυμένης εἰς πηλώδη σύστασιν ὁμοίως τοῖς τροχίσκοις, ὧν ἄλλος ἄλλῳ χρῆται, Πολυείδου λέγω καὶ Πασίωνος καὶ Ἄνδρωνος, καὶ τούτῳ τῷ νῦν εἰρημένῳ, προσαγορευομένῳ δὲ Βητινῷ.
beads.english: For the foul-smelling and very flabby and dirty ulcer admits the Lemnian earth dissolved in very pungent vinegar to a muddy consistency, in the same way as the troches, of which different people use different ones—I mean those of Polyeides and Pasion and Andron, and this one now mentioned, called Betinos.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ οὗτοι πάντες ἰσχυρῶς ξηραίνοντες ὠφελοῦσι τὰ κακοήθη τῶν ἑλκῶν, ἀνιέμενοι ποτὲ μὲν οἴνῳ γλυκεῖ, ποτὲ δὲ σιραίῳ, ποτὲ δ’ οἰνομέλιτι, ποτὲ δὲ τῶν λευκῶν οἴνων ἐνίοις ἢ τῶν κιῤῥῶν ἢ ξανθῶν, ὡς ἂν ἡ χρεία κελεύῃ.
beads.english: For all these, drying strongly, benefit the malignant ulcers, being diluted sometimes with sweet wine, sometimes with boiled-down must, sometimes with honeyed wine, sometimes with some of the white wines or the tawny or the yellow, as the need may command.

beads.greek: διορισθήσεται γὰρ ὑπὲρ τούτων ἐν ἑτέροις.
beads.english: For these matters will be distinguished elsewhere.

beads.greek: ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ δι’ ὄξους ἀνίενταί ποτε, καὶ δι’ οἴνου ἢ ὕδατος ἢ ὀξυμέλιτος, ἢ ὀξυκράτου τε καὶ μελικράτου.
beads.english: Likewise they are also sometimes diluted with vinegar, and with wine or water or oxymel, or with vinegar-and-water and honey-and-water.

beads.greek: καὶ ἡ Λημνία δὲ γῆ δι’ ἑκάστου τῶν εἰρημένων ἀνιεμένη φάρμακον ἐπιτήδειόν ἐστιν εἴς τε τὴν τῶν προσφάτων τραυμάτων κόλλησιν εἴς τε τὴν τῶν χρονίων ἢ δυσεπουλώτων ἢ κακοήθων ἴασιν.
beads.english: And the Lemnian earth, diluted with each of the things mentioned, is a suitable drug both for the agglutination of fresh wounds and for the cure of chronic or hard-to-cicatrize or malignant ulcers.

beads.greek: ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ ἡ ἄλλη πᾶσα φαρμακώδης γῆ.
beads.english: And likewise all the other medicinal earth.

beads.greek: διελέσθαι γὰρ δεήσει, καθάπερ ἔμπροσθεν ἀπὸ τῆς στοιχειώδους γῆς, ἐν ᾗ καὶ οἱ λίθοι περιείχοντο τὴν εἰς πηλὸν λυομένην, οὕτω νῦν ἀπὸ τῆς γεωργουμένης τὴν φαρμακώδη.
beads.english: For it will be necessary to distinguish, just as earlier we distinguished from the elemental earth—in which stones too were included—the earth that is dissolved into mud, so now from the cultivated earth the medicinal.

beads.greek: καλέσαι γὰρ οὐδὲν χεῖρον οὕτως ᾗ πρὸς τὰς θεραπείας χρώμεθα, καίτοι καὶ τῆς γεωργουμένης ἡ λιπαρὰ χρήσιμος εἰς θεραπείαν ἐστὶν ἁπάντων τῶν ξηρανθῆναι δεομένων μορίων, ὅθεν αὐτῇ κατὰ Ἀλεξάνδρειάν τε καὶ Αἴγυπτον χρῶνται πολλοὶ μὲν ἰδίᾳ προαιρέσει, πολλοὶ δ’ ἐξ ὀνειράτων.
beads.english: For it is no worse to name thus that which we use for treatments, although even of the cultivated earth the oily kind is useful for the treatment of all parts that need to be dried; whence in Alexandria and Egypt many use it by their own choice, many as a result of dreams.

beads.greek: εἶδον γοῦν ἐπὶ τῆς Ἀλεξανδρείας ὑδερώδεις τε καὶ σπληνώδεις ἐνίους χρωμένους τῷ πηλῷ τῆς Αἰγυπτίας γῆς.
beads.english: At any rate I saw at Alexandria some dropsical and splenetic people using the mud of Egyptian earth.

beads.greek: πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ κνήμας καὶ μηροὺς καὶ πήχεις καὶ βραχίονας καὶ νῶτα καὶ πλευρὰς καὶ στέρνα τῷ πηλῷ τῆς γῆς ταύτης χριόμενοι σαφῶς ὠφε λοῦντο.
beads.english: And many, anointing their shins and thighs and forearms and upper arms and backs and sides and chests with the mud of this earth, were clearly benefited.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον τάς τε παλαιὰς φλεγμονὰς καὶ τὰ χαῦνα τῶν οἰδημάτων ὀνίνησιν ὁ πηλὸς οὗτος, ὥστ’ ἐνίους οἶδα καὶ ὅλην τὴν ἕξιν οἰδαλέους ἐξ αἱμοῤῥοΐδων ἀμέτρου κενώσεως γενομένους, ὠφεληθέντας ἐναργῶς.
beads.english: In the same way this mud benefits old inflammations and the loose kinds of oedema, so that I know some who had become swollen in their whole habit as a result of immoderate evacuation from haemorrhoids who were manifestly benefited.

beads.greek: καί τινες ἀλγήματα χρόνια κατά τι μόριον ἐστηριγμένα τῷ πηλῷ τούτῳ τελέως ἐξιάσαντο, ξηραντικὴν γὰρ ἔχει πᾶσα γῆ δύναμιν. ἐπεὶ καὶ φύσει ξηρὸν αὐτῆς ἐστι τὸ σῶμα, καὶ ὅτε γε ἀκριβῶς ᾖ πυρώδους ἄμικτος οὐσίας, ἀδηκτότατα ξηραίνει, συντελεῖ δὲ εἰς τοῦτο αὐτῇ τὸ πεπλύσθαι.
beads.english: And some completely cured chronic pains fixed in some part with this mud; for all earth has a drying power, since by nature its body is dry, and when it is exactly unmixed with fiery substance, it dries without the least biting; and its having been washed contributes to this.

greek_sentences: Περὶ τῶν διαφορῶν τῆς συνήθως ὀνομαζομένης γῆς.] Γῆν ἔφην ὀνομάζεσθαι σύνηθες ἅπασιν Ἕλλησιν, ἥτις ἂν εἰς τὸ ὑγρὸν ἐμβληθεῖσα παραχρῆμα διαλύεταί τε καὶ πηλὸς γίνεται.
ταύτης οὖν ἡ μέν τίς ἐστιν ἣν γεωργοῦσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, διαφορὰς ἔχουσά τινας μὲν κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον ἐν τῷ λιπαρά τε εἶναι καὶ γλίσχρος, ἥτις πάντως ἐστὶ καὶ μέλαινα τὴν χρόαν.
ἡ δὲ ψαθυρωτέρα τε καὶ ἀλιπὴς, ἣν καλοῦσιν ἄργιλον, οὖσα καὶ ἥδε λευκοτέρα πως.
ἐναντιώταται μὲν αὗται διαφοραί· αἱ δ’ ἄλλαι μεταξὺ τούτων, ἤτοι τῇ ἑτέρᾳ πλησιάζουσαι μᾶλλον ἢ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ, τινὲς δὲ κᾀν τῷ ﻿ μέσῳ δοκεῖν ἀκριβῶς εἶναι, τὴν ἴσην ἀμφοῖν ἀφεστηκυῖαι διάστασιν.

αἱ δ’ ἐξ ἐπιμιξίας ἑτερογενῶν σωμάτων διαφοραὶ τῆς γῆς εἰσι, καθὸ λιθώδεις τε καὶ ψαμμώδεις ὑπάρχουσιν, καὶ χωρίζουσί γε τῶν τοιούτων τὴν μεμιγμένην οὐσίαν, ἀναδεύσαντες καὶ ἀναφυράσαντες ὕδατι πολλῷ, μέχρι τοῦ πᾶν ὑγρὸν ἐργάσασθαι.
καθισταμένου γὰρ τούτου τὸ μὲν τῆς λιθώδους τε καὶ ψαμμώδους ἐμφερόμενον ὑφιζάνει πᾶν, ἐποχεῖται δὲ ἡ ἀκριβὴς γῆ.
τοιοῦτον γάρ τι καὶ κατὰ τὴν Λημνίαν γίνεται γῆν, ἣν μίλτον ὀνομάζουσιν ἔνιοι Λημνίαν καί τινες ἄλλοι σφραγῖδα Λημνίαν, διὰ τὴν ἐπιβαλλομένην αὐτῇ σφραγῖδα τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος ἱεράν.

ταύτην γάρ τοι τὴν γῆν ἡ ἱέρεια λαμβάνουσα μετά τινος ἐπιχωρίου τιμῆς, οὐ ζώων θυομένων, ἀλλὰ πυρῶν καὶ κριθῶν ἀντιδιδομένων τῷ χωρίῳ, κομίζει μὲν εἰς τὴν πόλιν ἀναφυράσασα ὕδατι καὶ πηλὸν ὑγρὸν ἐργασαμένη καὶ τοῦτον ταράξασα σφοδρῶς, εἶτ’ ἐάσασα καταστῆναι, πρῶτον μὲν ἀφαιρεῖ τὸ ἐπιπολῆς ὕδωρ, εἶθ’ ὑπ’ αὐτῷ τὸ λιπαρὸν τῆς γῆς λαβοῦσα καὶ μόνον ἀπολιποῦσα τὸ ὑφιζηκὸς λιθῶδές τε καὶ ψαμμῶδες, ὅπερ καὶ ἄχρηστόν ἐστιν, ἄχρι τοσούτου ξηραίνει τὸν λιπαρὸν πηλὸν, ἄχρις ἂν εἰς σύστασιν ἀφίκηται μαλακοῦ κηροῦ, καὶ τούτου λαμβάνουσα μόρια σμικρὰ τὴν ἱερὰν τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος ἐπιβάλλει σφραγῖδα, κἄπειτα πάλιν ἐν σκιᾷ ξηραίνει, μέχρις ἂν ἀκριβῶς ἄνικμος ἀποτελεσθῇ, καὶ γένηται τοῦτο δὴ τὸ γινωσκόμενον ἰατροῖς ἅπασι φάρμακον ἡ Λημνία σφραγίς.
οὕτω γὰρ αὐτὴν ὀνομάζουσιν, ὡς ἔφην, ἔνιοι διὰ τὴν ἐπιβαλλομένην αὐτῇ σφραγῖδα, καθάπερ γε καὶ διὰ τὴν χρόαν ἔνιοι Λημνίαν μίλτον.

ἔχει μὲν οὖν τὴν χρόαν τὴν αὐτὴν τῇ μίλτῳ, διαφέρει δ’ αὐτῆς τῷ μὴ μολύνειν ἁπτομένην, καθάπερ ἐκείνην, καὶ κατά γε τὸν λόφον ἐν τῇ Λήμνῳ τὸν ὅλον ὄντα κιῤῥὸν τῇ χρόᾳ, καθ’ ὃν οὔτε δένδρον ἐστὶν οὔτε πέτρα οὔτε φυτὸν, μόνη δ’ ἡ τοιαύτη γῆ.
τρεῖς δ’ αὐτῆς εὑρίσκονται διαφοραί· μία μὲν ἡ προειρημένη τῆς ἱερᾶς γῆς, ἧς οὐδεὶς ἄλλος ἅπτεται πλὴν τῆς ἱερείας.
δευτέρα δ’ ἑτέρα τῆς ὄντως μίλτου, χρῶνται δ’ οἱ τέκτονες αὐτῇ μάλιστα.
τρίτη δ’ ἡ τῆς ῥυπούσης, ᾗ χρῶνται τῶν πλυνόντων ὀθόνας τε καὶ ἐσθῆτας οἱ βουληθέντες.

ἀνεγνωκὼς δὲ ἐγὼ παρά τε Διοσκορίδῃ καὶ ἄλλοις τισὶ μίγνυσθαι τράγειον αἷμα τῇ Λημνίᾳ γῇ, κᾀκ τοῦ διὰ μίξεως ταύτης γενομένου πηλοῦ τὴν ἱέρειαν ἀναπλάττειν τε καὶ σφραγίζειν ἃς ὀνομάζουσι Λημνίας σφραγῖδας, ὠρέχθην αὐτὸς ἱστορῆσαι τὴν συμμετρίαν τῆς μίξεως.

ὥσπερ οὖν εἰς Κύπρον ἕνεκα τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ μετάλλων, εἴς τε τὴν κοίλην Συρίαν, μόριον οὖσαν τῆς Παλαιστίνης, ἕνεκεν ἀσφάλτου καί τινων ἄλλων κατ’ αὐτὴν ἀξίων ἱστορίας ἐπορεύθην, οὕτως καὶ εἰς Λῆμνον οὐκ ὤκνησα πλεῦσαι, θεασόμενος ὁπόσον μίγνυται τοῦ αἵματος τῇ γῇ.

καὶ τό γε δεύτερον ἐξ Ἀσίας εἰς Ῥώμην ἀφικέσθαι πεζῇ πορευόμενος διὰ Θρᾴκης τε καὶ Μακεδονίας, ἔπλευσα πρότερον ἀπὸ Τρῳάδος Ἀλεξανδρείας εἰς Λῆμνον, ἐπιτυχὼν εἰς Θεσσαλονίκην ἀναγομένου πλοίου, συνθεμένῳ τῷ ναυκλήρῳ παραβάλλειν πρότερον τῇ Λήμνῳ· ὁ δὲ προσέσχε μὲν, οὐ μὴν ᾗ γ’ ἐχρῆν πόλει.

τὴν ἀρχὴν γὰρ οὐδ’ ἠπιστάμην δύο πόλεις εἶναι κατὰ τὴν νῆσον, ἀλλὰ ᾤμην, ὡς Σάμον καὶ Χίον καὶ Κῶ Ἄνδρον τε καὶ Τῆνον καὶ πάσας τὰς κατὰ τὸ Αἰγαῖον, οὕτω καὶ τὴν Λῆμνον ὁμώνυμον ἔχειν πόλιν ὅλῃ τῇ νήσῳ μίαν.

ὡς δὲ ἀποβὰς τῆς νεὼς, ἔγνων Μυρίναν μὲν ὀνομάζεσθαι τὴν πόλιν, εἶναι δ’ οὔτε κατὰ Φιλοκτήτην οὔτε κατὰ τὸ ἱερὸν τοῦ Ἡφαίστου λόφον ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ τῆς πόλεως ἐκείνης, ἀλλ’ ἐν ἑτέρᾳ τῇ Ἡφαιστιάδι καλουμένῃ, καὶ οὐδ’ ἐγγὺς εἶναι τὴν πόλιν ἐκείνην τῆς Μυρίνης, ὅ τε ναύκληρος οὐκ ἠδύνατό με περιμένειν, ἀνεβαλλόμην εἰσαῦθις, ὅταν ἀπὸ Ῥώμης εἰς Ἀσίαν ἀφίκωμαι, θεάσασθαι τὴν Ἡφαιστιάδα.
καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἐπράχθη, καθάπερ ἤλπισά τε καὶ προὐθέμην.

ὡς γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας διαβαλὼν εἰς τὴν Μακεδονίαν καὶ σχεδὸν ὅλην αὐτὴν ὁδοιπορήσας ἐν Φιλίπποις ἐγενόμην, ἥπερ ἐστὶν ὅμορος τῇ Θρᾴκῃ πόλις, ἐντεῦθεν ἐπὶ τὴν πλησίον θάλατταν εἴκοσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἑκατὸν ἀπέχουσαν στάδια κατελθὼν, ἔπλευσα πρότερον μὲν εἰς Θάσον ἐγγύς που διακοσίους σταδίους, ἐκεῖθεν δὲ εἰς Λῆμνον ἑπτακοσίους, εἶτ’ αὖθις ἀπὸ Λήμνου τοὺς ἴσους ἑπτακοσίους εἰς Ἀλεξανδρείαν Τρῳάδα.
καὶ διὰ τοῦτ’ ἐξεπίτηδες ἔγραψα περί τε τοῦ πλοῦ καὶ τῶν σταδίων, ὅπως εἴ τις ἐθέλῃ θεάσασθαι καὶ αὐτὸς ὁμοίως ἐμοὶ τὴν Ἡφαιστιάδα διαγινώσκων τὴν θέσιν αὐτῆς, οὕτως παρασκευάζοιτο πρὸς τὸν πλοῦν.
ἐν γάρ τοι τῇ ὅλῃ νήσῳ τῇ Λήμνῳ, κατὰ μὲν τὸ πρὸς ταῖς ἀνατολαῖς μέρος αὐτῆς ἐστιν Ἡφαιστιὰς, κατὰ δὲ τὸ πρὸς ταῖς δυσμαῖς ἡ Μυρίνα.
καὶ τό γε ὑπὸ τοῦ ποιητοῦ λεγόμενον ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἡφαίστου, κάππεσεν ἐν Λήμνῳ, διὰ τὴν φύσιν τοῦ λόφου δοκεῖ μοι τὸν μῦθον ἐπίστασθαι.
φαίνεται γὰρ ὁμοιότατος κεκαυμένῳ κατά γε τὴν χρόαν καὶ διὰ τὸ μηδὲν ἐν αὐτῷ φύεσθαι.

εἰς τοῦτον οὖν τὸν λόφον ἥ τε ἱέρεια παραγενομένη, καθ’ ὃν ἐγὼ καιρὸν ἐπέβην τῆς νήσου, καί τινα πυρῶν τε καὶ κριθῶν ἀριθμὸν ἐμβάλλουσα τῇ γῇ καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ ποιήσασα κατὰ τὸν ἐπιχώριον σεβασμὸν, ἐπλήρωσεν μὲν ὅλην ἅμαξαν τῆς γῆς.
κομίσασα δ’ εἰς τὴν πόλιν, ὡς εἶπον ἀρτίως, ἐσκεύασε τὰς πολυθρυλήτους Λημνίας σφραγῖδας.
ἔδοξεν οὖν μοι πυθέσθαι μή τι πρότερόν ποτε τράγειον ἢ αἴγειον αἷμα τῇ γῇ ταύτῃ μιγνύμενον ἐν ἱστορίᾳ παρειλήφασιν.
ἐφ’ ᾗ ﻿ πεύσει πάντες οἱ ἀκούσαντες ἐγέλασαν, οὐχ οἱ τυχόντες ἄνδρες ὄντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάνυ πεπαιδευμένοι τά τ’ ἄλλα καὶ τὴν ἐπιχώριον ἱστορίαν ἅπασαν.
ἀλλὰ καὶ βιβλίον ἔλαβον.
παρά τινος αὐτῶν, γεγραμμένον ὑπό τινος τῶν ἐπιχωρίων ἀνδρῶν ἔμπροσθεν, ἐν ᾧ τὴν χρῆσιν ἅπασαν ἐδίδασκε τῆς Λημνίας γῆς, ὅθεν οὐκ ὤκνησα κᾀγὼ πειραθῆναι τοῦ φαρμάκου, δισμυρίας λαβὼν σφραγῖδας.
ἐχρῆτο δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ δοὺς τὸ βιβλίον, ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις ἀριθμούμενος τῆς Ἡφαιστιάδος, εἰς πολλὰ τῷ φαρμάκῳ.
καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ τραυμάτων καὶ παλαιῶν καὶ δυσεπουλώτων ἐχεοδήκτων τε καὶ ὅλως θηριοδήκτων, ἐπί τε τῶν θανασίμων φαρμάκων, οὐ προδιδοὺς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπιδιδοὺς, ἐχρῆτο τῇ σφραγῖδι.
ἔφασκε δὲ καὶ τοῦ διὰ τῶν ἀρκευθίδων φαρμάκου πεῖραν ἔχειν, εἰς ὃ καὶ τῆς Λημνίας ἐμβάλλεται κινοῦντος ἔμετον, εἴ τις ἔτι κατὰ τὴν κοιλίαν ὄντος τοῦ θανασίμου φαρμάκου πίοι τὸ ἀλεξητήριον.

ἀλλὰ τούτου μὲν καὶ ἡμεῖς ἔχομεν πεῖραν ἐπί τε λαγωοῦ θαλαττίου καὶ κανθαρίδων, ὑποπτευσάντων μὲν εἰληφέναι τι τοιοῦτον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἐμεσάντων δ’ αὐτίκα πᾶν ἐπὶ τῷ διὰ τῆς Λημνίας σφραγῖδος φαρμάκῳ, καὶ μηδὲν μετὰ ταῦτα παθόντων σύμπτωμα τῶν ἑπομένων λαγωῷ τε καὶ κανθαρίσι, καίτοι τῆς δόσεως τῶν ὀλεθρίων φαρμάκων ἐλεγχθείσης.
εἰ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τἄλλα θανάσιμα φάρμακα, ταῦτα δὴ τὰ δηλητήρια καλούμενα, τὴν αὐτὴν δύναμιν ἔχει τὸ διὰ τῶν ἀρκευθίδων καὶ τῆς Λημνίας φάρμακον, ἐμοὶ μὲν ἄδηλον.
ὁ δ’ ἐκ τῆς Ἡφαιστιάδος ἐπηγγείλατο μέχρι τοῦ καὶ λυττῶντος κυνὸς ἰᾶσθαι δῆγμα φάσκειν αὐτὴν, πινομένην δι’ οἴνου κεκραμένου, κατὰ δὲ τοῦ ἕλκους ἐπιτιθεμένην δι’ ὄξους πάνυ δριμέος.
ἀλλὰ δι’ ὄξους μὲν καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων θηρίων ἔλεγεν αὐτὴν ἰᾶσθαι δήγματα, φύλλων βοτανῶν ἔξωθεν ἐπιτιθεμένων, ἃς ἐμάθομεν ἀντιπεπονθέναι σηπεδόσιν.
μάλιστα δ’ ἐπῄνει σκόρδιον, εἶτα κενταύριον τὸ λεπτὸν, εἶτα πράσιον.
ἐπί γε μὴν κακοήθων καὶ σηπεδονωδῶν ἑλκῶν εἴ ποτ’ ἐχρησάμην τῇ Λημνίᾳ, μεγάλως ὠφέλησε.
ἡ δὲ χρῆσις γίνεται κατὰ τὸ μέγεθος τῆς τοῦ ἕλκους κακίας.

τὸ μὲν γὰρ δυσῶδες καὶ λίαν πλαδαρόν τε καὶ ῥυπαρὸν, ἀνέχεται δι’ ὄξους δριμυτάτου τῆς Λημνίας λελυμένης εἰς πηλώδη σύστασιν ὁμοίως τοῖς τροχίσκοις, ὧν ἄλλος ἄλλῳ χρῆται, Πολυείδου λέγω καὶ Πασίωνος καὶ Ἄνδρωνος, καὶ τούτῳ τῷ νῦν εἰρημένῳ, προσαγορευομένῳ δὲ Βητινῷ.

καὶ γὰρ οὗτοι πάντες ἰσχυρῶς ξηραίνοντες ὠφελοῦσι τὰ κακοήθη τῶν ἑλκῶν, ἀνιέμενοι ποτὲ μὲν οἴνῳ γλυκεῖ, ποτὲ δὲ σιραίῳ, ποτὲ δ’ οἰνομέλιτι, ποτὲ δὲ τῶν λευκῶν οἴνων ἐνίοις ἢ τῶν κιῤῥῶν ἢ ξανθῶν, ὡς ἂν ἡ χρεία κελεύῃ.
διορισθήσεται γὰρ ὑπὲρ τούτων ἐν ἑτέροις.
ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ δι’ ὄξους ἀνίενταί ποτε, καὶ δι’ οἴνου ἢ ὕδατος ἢ ὀξυμέλιτος, ἢ ὀξυκράτου τε καὶ μελικράτου.
καὶ ἡ Λημνία δὲ γῆ δι’ ἑκάστου τῶν εἰρημένων ἀνιεμένη φάρμακον ἐπιτήδειόν ἐστιν εἴς τε τὴν τῶν προσφάτων τραυμάτων κόλλησιν εἴς τε τὴν τῶν χρονίων ἢ δυσεπουλώτων ἢ κακοήθων ἴασιν.
ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ ἡ ἄλλη πᾶσα φαρμακώδης γῆ.
διελέσθαι γὰρ δεήσει, καθάπερ ἔμπροσθεν ἀπὸ τῆς στοιχειώδους γῆς, ἐν ᾗ καὶ οἱ λίθοι περιείχοντο τὴν εἰς πηλὸν λυομένην, οὕτω νῦν ἀπὸ τῆς γεωργουμένης τὴν φαρμακώδη.

καλέσαι γὰρ οὐδὲν χεῖρον οὕτως ᾗ πρὸς τὰς θεραπείας χρώμεθα, καίτοι καὶ τῆς γεωργουμένης ἡ λιπαρὰ χρήσιμος εἰς θεραπείαν ἐστὶν ἁπάντων τῶν ξηρανθῆναι δεομένων μορίων, ὅθεν αὐτῇ κατὰ Ἀλεξάνδρειάν τε καὶ Αἴγυπτον χρῶνται πολλοὶ μὲν ἰδίᾳ προαιρέσει, πολλοὶ δ’ ἐξ ὀνειράτων.
εἶδον γοῦν ἐπὶ τῆς Ἀλεξανδρείας ὑδερώδεις τε καὶ σπληνώδεις ἐνίους χρωμένους τῷ πηλῷ τῆς Αἰγυπτίας γῆς.
πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ κνήμας καὶ μηροὺς καὶ πήχεις καὶ βραχίονας καὶ νῶτα καὶ πλευρὰς καὶ στέρνα τῷ πηλῷ τῆς γῆς ταύτης χριόμενοι σαφῶς ὠφε λοῦντο.

κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον τάς τε παλαιὰς φλεγμονὰς καὶ τὰ χαῦνα τῶν οἰδημάτων ὀνίνησιν ὁ πηλὸς οὗτος, ὥστ’ ἐνίους οἶδα καὶ ὅλην τὴν ἕξιν οἰδαλέους ἐξ αἱμοῤῥοΐδων ἀμέτρου κενώσεως γενομένους, ὠφεληθέντας ἐναργῶς.
καί τινες ἀλγήματα χρόνια κατά τι μόριον ἐστηριγμένα τῷ πηλῷ τούτῳ τελέως ἐξιάσαντο, ξηραντικὴν γὰρ ἔχει πᾶσα γῆ δύναμιν.
ἐπεὶ καὶ φύσει ξηρὸν αὐτῆς ἐστι τὸ σῶμα, καὶ ὅτε γε ἀκριβῶς ᾖ πυρώδους ἄμικτος οὐσίας, ἀδηκτότατα ξηραίνει, συντελεῖ δὲ εἰς τοῦτο αὐτῇ τὸ πεπλύσθαι.
english_sentences: On the differences of the earth that is customarily so named.] I said that all Greeks customarily give the name "earth" to that which, when it is thrown into liquid, is at once dissolved and becomes mud.

Of this, then, one kind is that which men cultivate, having certain differences in its own right (κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον), in being oily and viscous—a kind which is in every case also black in colour—while the other is more crumbly and non-oily, which they call argil, this too being in some degree whiter.

These differences are the most opposed; the others lie between these, either approaching more nearly to the one or to the other, and some seem to be exactly in the middle, standing at an equal distance from both.

There are also differences of earth that arise from admixture of bodies of a different kind, insofar as they are stony and sandy; and they separate the mixed-in substance from such earths by soaking and kneading them with much water, until they make the whole liquid.
For when this settles, all the stony and sandy matter carried in it sinks to the bottom, while the exact earth floats above.

For something of this sort happens also in the case of the Lemnian earth, which some call Lemnian miltos and certain others Lemnian seal, because of the seal sacred to Artemis which is impressed upon it.

For the priestess, taking this earth with a certain local honour—not with animals being sacrificed, but with wheat and barley given in return to the place—conveys it to the city, and having kneaded it with water and made a liquid mud and stirred this violently, then having let it settle, she first removes the water on the surface, then, taking the oily part of the earth beneath it and leaving behind only the stony and sandy matter that has settled, which is indeed useless, she dries the oily mud to such a degree until it comes to the consistency of soft wax, and taking small portions of this she impresses upon them the sacred seal of Artemis, and then again dries them in the shade until it is rendered exactly free of moisture, and this becomes the drug known to all physicians, the Lemnian seal.
For so some name it, as I said, because of the seal impressed upon it, just as some also, because of its colour, call it Lemnian miltos.

It has, then, the same colour as miltos, but differs from it in not staining when it is touched, as that one does, and also in respect of the hill in Lemnos, which is wholly tawny in colour, on which there is neither tree nor rock nor plant, but only earth of this sort.

Three differences of it are found: one, the aforesaid, of the sacred earth, which no one else touches except the priestess; a second, different one, of the true miltos, which the carpenters especially use; and a third, of the cleansing (ῥυπούσης) kind, which those of the washers of linens and garments who so wish use.

Having read in Dioscorides and certain others that goat's blood is mixed with the Lemnian earth, and that from the mud produced by this mixture the priestess moulds and seals what they call Lemnian seals, I desired myself to investigate the proportion of the mixture.

Just as, then, I travelled to Cyprus for the sake of the mines in it, and to Coele Syria, which is a part of Palestine, for the sake of asphalt and certain other things in it worth investigating, so too I did not hesitate to sail to Lemnos, intending to see how much of the blood is mixed with the earth.

And on the second occasion of coming from Asia to Rome, travelling on foot through Thrace and Macedonia, I sailed first from Alexandria Troas to Lemnos, having found a ship putting out for Thessalonica, the ship-master having agreed to put in first at Lemnos; and he did put in, but not at the city where he should have.

For at the start I did not even know that there were two cities on the island, but supposed that, like Samos and Chios and Cos and Andros and Tenos and all the islands in the Aegean, so too Lemnos had a single city bearing the same name as the whole island.

But when I disembarked from the ship, I learned that the city was called Myrina, and that the hill was neither in connection with Philoctetes nor in connection with the temple of Hephaestus in the territory of that city, but in the other, called Hephaestias, and that that city was not even near Myrina; and since the ship-master could not wait for me, I deferred to a later time, when I should come from Rome to Asia, the viewing of Hephaestias.
And this was accomplished for me, just as I hoped and proposed.

For when, having crossed from Italy to Macedonia and having travelled through almost the whole of it, I arrived at Philippi, which is a city bordering on Thrace, going down from there to the nearby sea, which is a hundred and twenty stades distant, I sailed first to Thasos, somewhere near two hundred stades, from there to Lemnos seven hundred, then again from Lemnos the same seven hundred to Alexandria Troas.

And for this reason I have deliberately written about the voyage and the stades, so that if anyone wishes to see Hephaestias himself just as I did, knowing its position, he may thus prepare for the voyage.
For in the whole island of Lemnos, Hephaestias lies in the part toward the east and Myrina in the part toward the west.
And what is said by the poet about Hephaestus, "he fell in Lemnos," seems to me to have set up (ἐπίστασθαι) the myth because of the nature of the hill.
For it appears most like something burnt, both in colour and because nothing grows on it.

To this hill, then, the priestess came, at the time when I set foot on the island, and casting a certain number of grains of wheat and barley onto the earth and performing certain other acts in accordance with the local reverence, she filled a whole wagon with the earth.
And having conveyed it to the city, as I said just now, she prepared the much-talked-of Lemnian seals.
It seemed good to me, then, to inquire whether they had ever before received in their tradition any account of goat's or she-goat's blood being mixed with this earth.
At this inquiry all who heard laughed, being not ordinary men but very well educated both in other matters and in the whole local history.

But I also received a book from one of them, written earlier by one of the local men, in which he taught the whole use of the Lemnian earth, whence I too did not hesitate to make trial of the drug, taking twenty thousand seals.
And the man himself who gave the book, being counted among the first men of Hephaestias, used the drug for many purposes.

For both on wounds, old ones and those hard to cicatrize, and on viper-bites and in general bites of venomous animals, and in cases of deadly drugs, giving it not only beforehand but also afterwards, he used the seal.

He said also that he had experience of the drug made with juniper berries, into which Lemnian earth also is put, which provokes vomiting, if someone drinks the protective remedy while the deadly drug is still in the belly.

But of this we too have experience in the case of the sea-hare and cantharides, when people suspected that they had taken something of this sort, and immediately vomited everything upon the drug made with the Lemnian seal, and afterwards suffered none of the symptoms that follow sea-hare and cantharides, even though the administration of the deadly drugs was proved.
But whether against the other deadly drugs, those called deleterious, the drug made with juniper berries and Lemnian earth has the same power, is unclear to me.
The man from Hephaestias went so far as to declare that it even cures the bite of a mad dog, when drunk in diluted wine and applied to the ulcer in very pungent vinegar.
But with vinegar he said it cures also the bites of the other venomous creatures, with leaves of herbs applied externally, which we have learned to be opposed to putrefactions.
He praised most of all scordium, then the slender centaury, then horehound.
On malignant and putrefactive ulcers at any rate, whenever I used the Lemnian earth, it helped greatly.
The use is in accordance with the magnitude of the badness of the ulcer.

For the foul-smelling and very flabby and dirty ulcer admits the Lemnian earth dissolved in very pungent vinegar to a muddy consistency, in the same way as the troches, of which different people use different ones—I mean those of Polyeides and Pasion and Andron, and this one now mentioned, called Betinos.

For all these, drying strongly, benefit the malignant ulcers, being diluted sometimes with sweet wine, sometimes with boiled-down must, sometimes with honeyed wine, sometimes with some of the white wines or the tawny or the yellow, as the need may command.
For these matters will be distinguished elsewhere.
Likewise they are also sometimes diluted with vinegar, and with wine or water or oxymel, or with vinegar-and-water and honey-and-water.
And the Lemnian earth, diluted with each of the things mentioned, is a suitable drug both for the agglutination of fresh wounds and for the cure of chronic or hard-to-cicatrize or malignant ulcers.
And likewise all the other medicinal earth.

For it will be necessary to distinguish, just as earlier we distinguished from the elemental earth—in which stones too were included—the earth that is dissolved into mud, so now from the cultivated earth the medicinal.

For it is no worse to name thus that which we use for treatments, although even of the cultivated earth the oily kind is useful for the treatment of all parts that need to be dried; whence in Alexandria and Egypt many use it by their own choice, many as a result of dreams.
At any rate I saw at Alexandria some dropsical and splenetic people using the mud of Egyptian earth.
And many, anointing their shins and thighs and forearms and upper arms and backs and sides and chests with the mud of this earth, were clearly benefited.

In the same way this mud benefits old inflammations and the loose kinds of oedema, so that I know some who had become swollen in their whole habit as a result of immoderate evacuation from haemorrhoids who were manifestly benefited.

And some completely cured chronic pains fixed in some part with this mud; for all earth has a drying power, since by nature its body is dry, and when it is exactly unmixed with fiery substance, it dries without the least biting; and its having been washed contributes to this.

beads.greek: Περὶ πλύσεως γῆς.] Πλύνεται δὲ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἅπασα γῆ τῷ προειρημένῳ περὶ τῆς Λημνίας, ὕδατι μὲν πρῶτον ἀναφυραθεῖσα μηδεμιᾶς φαρμακώδους ποιότητος ἔμφασιν ἔχοντι. καταστάντος δὲ τοῦ πηλοῦ καὶ περιαιρεθέντος ἄνωθεν τοῦ ὕδατος, εἶτα τοῦ μετ’ αὐτὸ χωρισθέντος ἀπὸ τῶν ὑφισταμένων κάτω λιθωδῶν τε καὶ ψαμμωδῶν.
beads.english: On the washing of earth.] All earth is washed in the same manner as that previously described for the Lemnian: first it is kneaded up with water that has no indication of any medicinal quality; then, when the mud has settled and the water has been removed from above, next that which lies beneath it is separated from the stony and sandy matter settling at the bottom.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ καὶ γεγυμνασμένην ἔχεις τὴν γευστικὴν αἴσθησιν, αὐτὸς ἔσῃ κριτὴς ἀκριβὴς ἧς τε δεῖ πλύνειν γῆς ἧς τε μή.
beads.english: And if you have a trained gustatory sense, you yourself will be an accurate judge of which earth needs to be washed and which does not.

beads.greek: τίνες μὲν γὰρ οὐ δέονται πλύσεως, τινὲς δὲ δὶς ἢ τρὶς δέονται πλυθῆναι.
beads.english: For some do not need washing, while some need to be washed twice or three times.

beads.greek: τὴν μὲν οὖν Λημνίαν ἑτοίμην λαμβάνεις ἅπαξ πεπλυμένην ὑπὸ τῆς ἱερείας, ἐκ δευτέρου δὲ πλυθῆναι μὴ δεομένην.
beads.english: The Lemnian, then, you receive ready, washed once by the priestess, and not needing to be washed a second time.

greek_sentences: Περὶ πλύσεως γῆς.] Πλύνεται δὲ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἅπασα γῆ τῷ προειρημένῳ περὶ τῆς Λημνίας, ὕδατι μὲν πρῶτον ἀναφυραθεῖσα μηδεμιᾶς φαρμακώδους ποιότητος ἔμφασιν ἔχοντι.
καταστάντος δὲ τοῦ πηλοῦ καὶ περιαιρεθέντος ἄνωθεν τοῦ ὕδατος, εἶτα τοῦ μετ’ αὐτὸ χωρισθέντος ἀπὸ τῶν ὑφισταμένων κάτω λιθωδῶν τε καὶ ψαμμωδῶν.
εἰ δὲ καὶ γεγυμνασμένην ἔχεις τὴν γευστικὴν αἴσθησιν, αὐτὸς ἔσῃ κριτὴς ἀκριβὴς ἧς τε δεῖ πλύνειν γῆς ἧς τε μή.
τίνες μὲν γὰρ οὐ δέονται πλύσεως, τινὲς δὲ δὶς ἢ τρὶς δέονται πλυθῆναι.
τὴν μὲν οὖν Λημνίαν ἑτοίμην λαμβάνεις ἅπαξ πεπλυμένην ὑπὸ τῆς ἱερείας, ἐκ δευτέρου δὲ πλυθῆναι μὴ δεομένην.
english_sentences: On the washing of earth.] All earth is washed in the same manner as that previously described for the Lemnian: first it is kneaded up with water that has no indication of any medicinal quality; then, when the mud has settled and the water has been removed from above, next that which lies beneath it is separated from the stony and sandy matter settling at the bottom.
And if you have a trained gustatory sense, you yourself will be an accurate judge of which earth needs to be washed and which does not.
For some do not need washing, while some need to be washed twice or three times.
The Lemnian, then, you receive ready, washed once by the priestess, and not needing to be washed a second time.

beads.greek: Περὶ Σαμίας γῆς.] Ἡ Σαμία δ’ οὐδὲ δεῖται πλυθῆναι.
beads.english: On Samian earth.] Samian earth does not even need to be washed.

beads.greek: χρώμεθα δ’ αὐτῆς θατέρῳ τῶν εἰδῶν μᾶλλον, ὃ δὴ καὶ Σάμιον ἀστέρα καλοῦσιν, εἰς τὰς τοῦ αἵματος πτύσεις, ﻿ ὁπόθεν ἂν γιγνόμεναι τύχωσιν, ὥσπερ καὶ τῇ Λημνίᾳ σφραγῖδι.
beads.english: We use rather the one of its two kinds which they also call the Samian star, for spittings of blood, from whatever source they happen to arise, just as we use the Lemnian seal.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὴν αὐτὴν δύναμιν ὠφελοῦσι καὶ τὰς ἐκ μήτρας αἱμοῤῥαγίας καὶ τὸν ὀνομαζόμενον ῥοῦν γυναικεῖον, καὶ μέντοι καὶ τὰς δυσεντερικὰς ἑλκώσεις πρὸ τοῦ σηπεδονώδη γενέσθαι τὰ ἕλκη, καλεῖν δ’ ἔθος ἐστὶν τοῖς ἰατροῖς τὰς τοιαύτας διαθέσεις νομὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ νέμεσθαι τὴν σηπεδόνα πρὸς τὰ πλησιάσαντα μόρια, συνδιαφθείρουσαν αὐτὰ τῷ πρώτῳ κακωθέντι.
beads.english: By the same power they also help haemorrhages from the womb and the so-called female flux, and indeed also dysenteric ulcerations before the ulcers become putrefactive; it is the custom of physicians to call such conditions nomai, from the putrefaction 'grazing' (nemesthai) upon the neighbouring parts, destroying them along with the part first damaged.

beads.greek: τῇ γε μὴν Λημνίᾳ κᾀπὶ τοιούτων ἐχρησάμην ἐνίοτε καὶ σαφῶς ὤνησεν ἐνεθεῖσά τε δι’ ἕδρας καὶ ποθεῖσα, προαποκλυσθέντων τῶν ἑλκῶν, ὡς εἰώθαμεν πράττειν, μελικράτῳ μὲν ἀκρατεστέρῳ προτέρῳ, δευτέρῳ δ’ ἅλμῃ.
beads.english: I have sometimes used the Lemnian earth too in such cases, and it clearly did good both when injected through the seat and when drunk, the ulcers having first been washed out, as we are accustomed to do, first with a fairly undiluted melikraton, and second with brine.

beads.greek: ἐνέθη μὲν οὖν δι’ ἀρνογλώσσου χυλοῦ, δι’ ὀξυκράτου δ’ ὑδαροῦς ἐπόθη.
beads.english: It was injected, then, in juice of plantain, and it was drunk in watery oxykraton (vinegar-and-water).

beads.greek: φαίνεται δ’ οὐκ ὀλίγῳ τινὶ δραστικωτέραν δύναμιν ἔχειν ἡ Λημνία γῆ τῆς Σαμίας, ὅθεν οὐδὲ τὰ φλεγμῆναι φθάσαντα φέρει τὴν δύναμιν αὐτῆς, ἀλλὰ τραχύνεται σαφῶς καὶ μάλισθ’ ὅταν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ᾖ μαλακόσαρκος.
beads.english: The Lemnian earth appears to have a power not a little more active than the Samian, which is why parts that have already become inflamed do not tolerate its power, but are plainly made rough, and most of all when the person is soft-fleshed.

beads.greek: ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς Σαμίας οὐ μόνον οὐ παροξύνεταί τι τῶν οὕτως ἐχόντων μορίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ παρηγορεῖται, καὶ μάλιστά γε τὰ θερμότερα καὶ χαυνότερα, καθάπερ οἵ τε τιτθοὶ καὶ οἱ ὄρχεις καὶ οἱ ἀδένες.
beads.english: Whereas by the Samian earth not only is none of the parts in such a state exacerbated, but it is actually soothed, and most of all the hotter and more flaccid parts, such as the breasts and the testicles and the glands.

beads.greek: ἐπιτηδείως δ’ ἂν χρῶ τηνικαῦτα τῇ τοιαύτῃ γῇ, μετὰ τὸ λειῶσαι δι’ ὕδατος, ἐπιμιγνὺς ῥοδίνου καλοῦ τοσοῦτον, ὅσον τὸ μιχθὲν οὐκ ἐάσει ξηρανθῆναι τὸ φάρμακον.
beads.english: In such a case you would use this sort of earth suitably if, after grinding it fine in water, you mix in as much good rose oil as will, once mixed in, not allow the drug to dry out.

beads.greek: ἀγαθὸν δὲ τὸ οὕτως σκευασθέν ἐστι καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἄλλας φλεγμονὰς ὅσαι θερμαὶ καὶ βουβῶνας ἀρχομένους καὶ ποδαγρικὰ ῥεύματα καὶ ὅλως ὅπου ψῦξαι βουλόμεθα μετρίως μετὰ τοῦ παρηγορεῖν, ὥστ’ ἐναργῶς φαίνεσθαι τῆς Σαμίας τὴν δύναμιν μετρίως ψυκτικήν.
beads.english: What is prepared in this way is good also for the other inflammations that are hot, and for incipient buboes and gouty fluxes, and in general wherever we wish to cool moderately while soothing, so that the power of the Samian earth is manifestly shown to be moderately cooling.

beads.greek: ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἀερωδεστέρα πως αὐτῆς ἡ οὐσία παραβαλλομένη τῇ Λημνίᾳ, δηλοῖ δ’ ἡ κουφότης.
beads.english: Its substance is also somewhat more airy when compared with the Lemnian, as its lightness shows.

beads.greek: ἐκ τούτων οὖν τῶν γνωρισμάτων καὶ πᾶσαν ἄλλην φαρ μακώδη γῆν δοκίμαζε.
beads.english: By these marks, then, test every other medicinal earth as well.

beads.greek: λέγω δὲ γνωρίσματα τήν τε ἐν τῇ συστάσει κουφότητά τε καὶ βαρύτητα καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ γεύσει τραχύτητα καὶ λειότητα καὶ προσέτι τὸ κολλῶδές τε καὶ ῥυπτικόν.
beads.english: By marks I mean the lightness and heaviness in its consistency, and the roughness and smoothness in its taste, and in addition the glutinous and the cleansing quality.

beads.greek: ἐχέκολλος μὲν γάρ ἐστι καὶ γλίσχρος ὁ Σάμιος ἀστὴρ, ἐχούσης τι καὶ τῆς Λημνίας σφραγῖδος ὀλίγον τοιοῦτον.
beads.english: For the Samian star is glue-holding and viscous, the Lemnian seal also having a little of this sort of quality.

beads.greek: ῥυπτικήν τε δύναμιν ἔχει καὶ μετρίαν Σελινουσία τε γῆ καὶ Χία, διὸ καί τινες τῶν γυναικῶν ἐπὶ τὸ πρόσωπον αὐταῖς χρῶνται.
beads.english: Both Selinusian and Chian earth have a cleansing power, and a moderate one, which is why some women use them on the face.

beads.greek: δέδεικται δὲ ἐν τῷ τρίτῳ τῆς θεραπευτικῆς μεθόδου τὸ βραχέως ῥυπτικὸν ἅπαν εἰς σάρκωσιν ἑλκῶν ἐπιτήδειον, ἐὰν δὲ ξηραίνῃ, καὶ πρὸς ἐπούλωσιν ἀγαθόν· ἐπιτηδειότατα δ’ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐστι τοῖς τε ἐπιπολῆς ἕλκεσι καὶ πυρικαύτοις ὅσα πρὸς τῷ ξηραίνειν ἀδήκτως οὔτε θερμαίνει σαφῶς οὔτε ψύχει.
beads.english: It has been shown in the third book of the Method of Healing that everything that is slightly cleansing is suited to the fleshing-over of ulcers, and if it dries, it is also good for cicatrization; and the most suitable of these for superficial ulcers and burns are those which, in addition to drying without biting, neither heat nor cool perceptibly.

beads.greek: ὅθεν ἥ τε Σελινουσία καὶ ἡ Χία γῆ κάλλιστα φάρμακα πρὸς τὰ πυρίκαυτα τῶν ἑλκῶν ἐστι· δεῖται γὰρ ταῦτα μετριώτατα ῥυπτόντων φαρμάκων ἄνευ θάλψεως ἢ ψύξεως ἐπιφανοῦς, ὅπερ ὑπάρχει καὶ τῇ Σελινουσίᾳ καὶ τῇ Χίᾳ καὶ τῇ Σαμίᾳ γῇ.
beads.english: Hence Selinusian and Chian earth are the finest drugs for burn ulcers; for these require drugs that cleanse most moderately without conspicuous warming or cooling, which is the case with Selinusian and Chian and Samian earth.

beads.greek: λέλεκται δὲ ὅτι καὶ ταύτης εἶδός ἐστιν ὁ ἀστὴρ ὀνομαζόμενος, ὑπερέχων τῆς ἄλλης γῆς τῷ γλίσχρον τι καὶ κολλῶδες ἔχειν, ὅθεν οὔτε πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα τῶν ἑλκῶν οὔτε πρὸς τὰ πυρίκαυτα ταῖς ἄλλαις ἐνάμιλλός ἐστιν, ὅσαι τε κολλῶδες οὐκ ἔχουσιν.
beads.english: It has been said that the so-called star is also a kind of the latter, surpassing the other earth in having something viscous and glutinous, which is why neither for other ulcers nor for burns is it a match for the others, those at least which do not have the glutinous quality.

beads.greek: ἐμπλαστικωτέραν γὰρ ἐργάζεται τὴν οὐσίαν τὸ κολλῶδες, ὡς μὴ ῥύπτειν, ὅταν γε δηλονότι μηδεμία δριμύτης ἄλλη προσῇ τῷ γλίσχρῳ τε καὶ κολλώδει σώματι, καθάπερ ἐν τοῖς ἰξοῖς ἐστιν.
beads.english: For the glutinous quality makes the substance more clogging, so that it does not cleanse, at least whenever no other pungency is present in addition to the viscous and glutinous body, as there is in bird-lime.

beads.greek: ἥ γε μὴν Χία καὶ ἡ Σελινουσία γῆ τῆς μὲν Σαμίας λείπονται πρὸς τὰς περὶ τιτθοὺς καὶ ὄρχεις καὶ βουβῶνας ἀρχομένας φλεγμονάς.
beads.english: Chian and Selinusian earth, however, fall short of the Samian for incipient inflammations about the breasts and testicles and groins.

beads.greek: ὅμως δ’ οὐκ ἀνάρμοστοι τυγχάνουσιν οὖσαι, μηδενὸς ἄλλου τῶν ἄκρως ποιούντων παρόντος.
beads.english: Nevertheless they are not unsuitable, when nothing else of those that act perfectly is at hand.

beads.greek: ἡ δὲ Κιμωλία μικτῆς οὖσα δυνάμεως, ἔχει μέν τι καὶ ψυκτικὸν, ἔχει δέ τι καὶ διαφορητικὸν βραχὺ, διό πλυθεῖσα μὲν ἀποτίθεται τοῦτο, χωρὶς δὲ τοῦ πλυθῆναι κατ’ ἀμφοτέρας ἐνεργεῖ τὰς δυνάμεις, καθάπερ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων διαφοροῦντά τε καὶ ἀποκρουόμενα.
beads.english: Cimolian earth, being of mixed power, has something cooling, but also something slightly dispersing; hence when washed it lays this aside, while without being washed it acts by both powers, just as many other compound drugs do which both disperse and repel.

beads.greek: παρὰ δὲ τὴν τῶν μιγνυμένων ὑγρῶν αὐτῇ φύσιν ἐναργῶς ἐπιδείκνυται τῶν δυνάμεων ἑκατέραν.
beads.english: And according to the nature of the liquids mixed with it, it manifestly displays each of its two powers.

beads.greek: τοῖς μὲν γὰρ ἀποκρουομένοις καὶ ψύχουσι μιχθεῖσα τὸν γενόμενον ἐξ αὐτῆς τε κᾀκείνων πηλὸν ἐργάζεται ψύχοντά τε καὶ ἀποκρουόμενον, τοῖς δὲ διαφορητικοῖς διαφοροῦντα καὶ αὐτόν.
beads.english: For mixed with repellent and cooling liquids it renders the mud produced from itself and them cooling and repellent, and with dispersing ones it renders it dispersing as well.

beads.greek: οὕτω γοῦν καὶ τοῖς πυρικαύτοις ἁρμόττει, καί τινες τῶν ἰδιωτῶν ἐπιχρίουσιν αὐτὴν, παραχρῆμα φυράσαντες ὄξει.
beads.english: In this way, at any rate, it also suits burns, and some laymen smear it on, having kneaded it on the spot with vinegar.

beads.greek: χρὴ δ’ ἐν τῇ τοιαύτῃ χρήσει μὴ λίαν εἶναι δριμὺ τὸ ὄξος. εἰ δὲ τοιοῦτον εἴη, βέλτιον ὕδατος αὐτῷ μιγνύναι.
beads.english: In such use the vinegar should not be too pungent; and if it should be so, it is better to mix water with it.

beads.greek: μέμνησό γε μὴν τοῦτο κοινὸν ἐπὶ πάσης γῆς εἶναι τῆς κούφης. ἅπασαι γὰρ ὀνίνασι τὰ πυρίκαυτα παραχρῆμα παραχριόμεναι δι’ ὄξους, ἢ ὀξυκράτου, κωλύουσαι φλυκταινοῦσθαι.
beads.english: Remember, however, that this is common to every light earth: for all of them benefit burns when smeared on at once with vinegar or oxykraton, preventing them from blistering.

beads.greek: προσεπιβλέπειν δ’ ἐν τούτῳ καὶ τὴν φύσιν τοῦ θεραπευομένου σώματος, εἰ μαλακὸν ἢ σκληρὸν, εἰδὼς ἀεὶ καθόλου τοῦτο, τὰ μὲν μαλακὰ σώματα μὴ φέρειν τὴν δύναμιν τῶν ἰσχυρῶν φαρμάκων, τὰ δὲ σκληρὰ φέρειν.
beads.english: In this one must look also to the nature of the body being treated, whether it is soft or hard, always knowing this as a general principle, that soft bodies do not tolerate the power of strong drugs, whereas hard bodies tolerate it.

beads.greek: οὐ μὴν τῆς γ’ ἐνεστώσης πραγματείας ἴδια ταῦτα. ῥηθήσεται γὰρ ἐπιπλέον ἔν τε τοῖς περὶ συνθέσεως φαρμάκων κᾀν τοῖς περὶ τῶν εὐπορίστων.
beads.english: These matters, however, are not proper to the present treatise; for they will be spoken of at greater length both in the books on the composition of drugs and in those on readily available remedies.

beads.greek: ἡ δὲ παροῦσα διέξοδος ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἐσπούδακε τὰς καθόλου δυνάμεις τῶν φαρμάκων εὑρεῖν, αἷς προσέχων τις τὸν νοῦν εἰς τὴν τῶν κατὰ μέρος χρῆσιν εὐπορίαν ἕξει παμπόλλην ἐπιμαθὼν δηλονότι τὴν μέθοδον τῆς χρήσεως αὐτῶν, ὥστ’ οὐκέτι προσήκει μηκύνειν, ἀλλ’ ὅπερ εἴρηται καὶ πρόσθεν ἀναμνῆσαι καὶ νῦν αὐτὴν μὲν τὴν ἄμικτον γῆν ἄλλῃ τινὶ τῶν ἑτερογενῶν οὐσιῶν ξηραντικῆς ἀδήκτως εἶναι δυνάμεως.
beads.english: The present exposition has from the beginning striven to discover the general powers of drugs, attending to which a person will have very ample resources for their particular use, provided of course he has learnt in addition the method of using them; so that it is no longer fitting to prolong matters, but, as was said before, to recall now too that earth itself, unmixed with any other substance of a different kind, is of a drying power without biting.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ δ’ ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν ἄμικτον εὑρεῖν ἀκριβῶς τι σῶμα, προσεπισκέπτεσθαι προσήκει τὴν μίξιν τῶν συμβεβηκότων ﻿ αὐτῇ κατά τε τὰς ἐν κουφότητι καὶ βαρύτητι διαφορὰς καὶ τὰς ἐν τῇ γεύσει.
beads.english: But since it is impossible to find any body that is exactly unmixed, it is fitting to examine in addition the admixture of what has come to be attached to it, according to the differences in lightness and heaviness and those in taste.

beads.greek: στύψεως μὲν γάρ τινος ἔμφασιν ἔχουσα τοσοῦτον προσείληφε ψύξεως, ὅσον καὶ στύψεως. εἰ δὲ δριμύτητος ἐμφαίνοιτό τι, τοσοῦτον ἔχει θερμότητος, ὅσον δριμύτητος.
beads.english: For if it has some suggestion of astringency, it has taken on as much coldness as astringency; and if some pungency should appear, it has as much heat as pungency.

beads.greek: ὡσαύτως δ’ ἐπὶ τῆς κούφης καὶ βαρείας σκοπεῖσθαι. τῆς μὲν κούφης τοιαύτης γινομένης, ὅταν ἀερώδους οὐσίας μετέχῃ δαψιλοῦς ἐν τῇ δι’ ὅλης ἑαυτῆς κράσει, τῆς δὲ βαρείας, ὅσῳ περ ἂν ᾖ μᾶλλον τοιαύτη, τοσούτῳ μᾶλλον εἰλικρινεστέρας γῆς ὑπαρχούσης.
beads.english: One must consider in the same way in the case of light and heavy earth: the light earth becoming such whenever it partakes of abundant airy substance in the mixture throughout its whole self, while the heavy, the more it is such, by so much the more is a purer earth.

beads.greek: ἴδιον δὲ γῆς ἐστι τὸ μὴ χεῖσθαι πυρὶ πλησιάζουσαν, ὅπερ ὅ τε μόλυβδος καὶ καττίτερος, ἄργυρός τε καὶ χρυσὸς ἔχουσιν, ὥσθ’ ὅταν ἀργυρῖτιν ἢ χρυσῖτιν ἢ σιδηρῖτιν ἀκούσῃς γῆν, ὀνομάζουσι γὰρ οὕτως ἔνιοι τὰς ἐκ τῶν μετάλλων λαμβανομένας, μὴ νόμιζε δι’ ὅλου κεκρᾶσθαι τὸν ἄργυρον ἢ τὸν χρυσὸν ἢ τὸν σίδηρον τῇ γῇ· πλησιάζειν δὲ μορίοις μικροῖς τῆς γῆς ἀναμεμιγμένα μόρια μικρὰ, κατὰ μὲν τὴν χρυσῖτιν χρυσοῦ, κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἀργυρῖτι νἀργύρου, κατὰ δὲ τὴν σιδηρῖτιν σιδήρου, καὶ ταῦτ’ ἐν ταῖς καμίνοις ὑπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς χεόμενα συνέρχεσθαι πρὸς ἄλληλα.
beads.english: It is a property of earth not to melt when it comes near fire, which lead and tin, silver and gold do have; so that when you hear of a silver-earth or gold-earth or iron-earth—for some so name those taken from the mines—do not suppose that the silver or the gold or the iron is blended through and through with the earth, but that small particles lie near small particles of the earth, mixed in with them, of gold in the gold-earth, of silver in the silver-earth, of iron in the iron-earth, and that these, being melted by the fire in the furnaces, come together with one another.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἡ τὴν ὕαλον ἔχουσα ψάμμιός ἐστιν, ἐν ψάμμῳ γὰρ μάλιστα τῆς τοιαύτης οὐσίας εὑρίσκεται ψήγματα πολλάκις μικρά.
beads.english: In the same way the earth that contains glass is sandy, for it is in sand especially that small grains of this kind of substance are often found.

beads.greek: καὶ ὅσοι τούτων ἔμπειροι θεασάμενοι τὰς τοιαύτας ψάμμους γνωρίζουσιν ὁπόσον ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀθροῖσαι δύνανται τῆς ὑάλου, καὶ χρυσοῦ δὲ ψήγματα μικρὰ πολλὰ κατά τινας εὑρίσκεται ψάμμους, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐξ ἁπάσης ψάμμου τὸν χρυσὸν ἐξαίρουσι καὶ τὴν ὕαλον οἱ περὶ ταῦτ’ ἔχοντες, ἐκλεγόμενοι δηλονότι τὰς μετ’ ὀλίγης δαπάνης ἀθροι ζούσας πλεῖστον, ὡς τό γ’ ἐν ταῖς καμίνοις ἀναλώσαντας πολλὰ βραχύ τι σχεῖν τῆς διαθροιζομένης οὐσίας ἀκερδὲς αὐτοῖς εἶναι δοκεῖ.
beads.english: And those experienced in these matters, on seeing such sands, recognize how much glass they can gather from them; and many small grains of gold are found in certain sands, but those who occupy themselves with these things do not extract the gold and the glass from every sand, choosing, of course, those which yield the most at little expense, since to spend a great deal in the furnaces and obtain a trifle of the substance collected seems to them unprofitable.

beads.greek: διὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν καίτοι γε πολλαῖς ψάμμοις χρυσοῦ καὶ ὑάλου ψηγμάτων περιεχομένων οὐκ ἐπὶ πάσας οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοὶ παραγίνονται.
beads.english: For this reason, then, although many sands contain grains of gold and glass, those skilled in these matters do not go to all of them.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον οὐδὲ χαλκὸν ἢ ἄργυρον ἢ σίδηρον ἢ κασσίτερον ἢ μόλυβδον ἐκ πάσης γῆς ἐκλέγουσιν.
beads.english: By the same reasoning they do not pick out copper or silver or iron or tin or lead from every earth.

beads.greek: οὐ μὴν οὐδ’ ὅταν χωρίσωσιν ἑκάστην τῶν εἰρημένων ἀπὸ τῆς ἀναμεμιγμένης γῆς, ἡ καταλειπομένη παραπλησία ταῖς ἄλλαις γαῖς ἐστιν, ἃς συνήθως ἔφην ὀνομάζεσθαι πᾶσιν Ἕλλησιν, ἐχούσαις γνώρισμα κοινὸν τὸ τέγγεσθαί τε καὶ διαλύεσθαι ῥᾳδίως εἰς πηλόν.
beads.english: Nor indeed, when they separate each of the things mentioned from the earth mixed with it, is the residue like the other earths, which I said are customarily so named by all Greeks, having as a common mark that they are soaked through and easily dissolve into mud.

beads.greek: τῆς γὰρ ἐν τοῖς μετάλλοις γῆς ὑπόλειμμα λιθῶδες γίγνεται, ἄτηκτόν τε καὶ ἄτεγκτον.
beads.english: For the residue of the earth in the mines becomes stony, unmeltable and not to be soaked through.

beads.greek: λέγω δὲ τέγγεσθαι μὲν τὸ δι’ ὅλης τῆς οὐσίας ὑγραίνεσθαι, βρέχεσθαι δὲ τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἔξωθεν ἐπιφάνειαν μόνην, οὐ διικνουμένης εἰς τὸ βάθος αὐτῆς τῆς ὑγρότητος.
beads.english: By 'being soaked through' I mean being moistened through the whole substance, and by 'being wetted' being moistened on the outer surface alone, the moisture not penetrating to its depth.

beads.greek: οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἡ μεταλλευομένη Καδμεία γεννᾶται, λιθώδης οὖσα καὶ ἄτεγκτος.
beads.english: Thus too the mined cadmia is produced, being stony and not to be soaked through.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τῶν τοιούτων σωμάτων ἐφεξῆς εἰρήσεται· νυνὶ δ’ ἐπανήξω πάλιν ἐπὶ τὴν φαρμακώδη γῆν, ἥτις, ὅτι μὲν εἰς πηλὸν λύεται ῥᾳδίως ἐν ὕδατι τεγγομένη, διὰ τοῦτ’ ὀνομάζεται γῆ, διότι δὲ χρῄζομεν αὐτῆς ὥσπερ καὶ ἄλλων φαρμάκων, διὰ τοῦτο φαρμακῖτις εἰκότως ἂν λέγοιτο.
beads.english: But about such bodies we shall speak in due course; now I shall return again to medicinal earth, which, because it readily dissolves into mud when soaked in water, is for this reason named earth, and because we have need of it as of other drugs, for this reason might reasonably be called pharmakitis.

beads.greek: καίτοι τήν γ’ ἀμπελῖτιν ὀνομαζομένην γῆν ἔνιοι φαρμακῖτιν ὀνομάζουσιν μόνην, ἤτοι γ’ ὡς μόνην τοιαύτην οὖσαν ἢ ὡς ἐνεργεστέραν τὴν φαρμακώδη δύναμιν ἔχουσαν, ὅπερ καὶ ἀληθές ἐστιν.
beads.english: And yet some call only the so-called ampelitis earth pharmakitis, either as being the only one of this kind or as having the medicinal power more effectively, which is indeed true.

beads.greek: ὀνομάζεται δ’ ἀμπελῖτις οὐχ ὅτι φυτεύειν ἀμπέλους ἐν ταύτῃ βέλτιον, ἀλλ’ ὅτι περιχριομένη ταῖς ἀμπέλοις φθείρει τοὺς γεννωμένους ἐπ’ αὐτῶν σκώληκας, οὓς σκνῖπας ὀνομάζουσιν οἱ παρ’ ἡμῖν ἀμπελουργοί.
beads.english: It is named ampelitis not because it is better to plant vines in it, but because, smeared around the vines, it destroys the worms that breed on them, which the vine-dressers in our country call sknipes.

beads.greek: γεννῶνται δὲ οὗτοι τοῦ ἦρος εἰσβάλλοντος, ἡνίκα βλαστάνουσιν οἱ ἄμπελοι καὶ τό γ’ ἐνοιδισκόμενον αὐτῶν μέρος, ὅθεν ὁ βλαστὸς φύεται, ὃ καλοῦσιν ὀφθαλμόν.
beads.english: These are bred when spring sets in, when the vines sprout, and especially the swelling part of them from which the shoot grows, which they call the eye.

beads.greek: τούτους οὖν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς διεσθίοντες οἱ σκνῖπες οὐ μικρὰ βλάπτουσιν τὰς ἀμπέλους, διὸ καὶ τὰς ῥίζας τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν τούτων περιχρίουσιν οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοί.
beads.english: By eating through these eyes, then, the sknipes do no small harm to the vines, which is why those skilled in these matters smear the roots of these eyes.

beads.greek: κατὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν ἀμπελῖτίς τε καὶ φαρμακῖτις ἡ τοιαύτη γῆ προσαγορεύεται, δηλοῦσα κᾀκ τοῦ φθείρειν τοὺς σκνῖπας ὅσον αὐτῇ μέτεστι δυνάμεως φαρμακώδους.
beads.english: On this account, then, such earth is called both ampelitis and pharmakitis, showing from its destruction of the sknipes too how much medicinal power it possesses.

beads.greek: ἀφέστηκεν δὲ πολὺ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων εἰδῶν τῆς γῆς, οἷς χρώμεθα πρὸς τὰς ἰάσεις, ἐγγὺς ἤδη τῆς λιθώδους ἥκουσα.
beads.english: It stands far apart also from the other kinds of earth which we use for cures, coming already near to the stony.

beads.greek: διὸ καὶ μιγνυμένην αὐτὴν ἐν ταῖς τῶν φαρμάκων γραφαῖς εὑρήσεις, ἔνθα ξηρᾶναί τι καὶ διαφορῆσαι προσήκει.
beads.english: Hence you will find it mixed in the prescriptions of drugs where it is fitting to dry and disperse something.

beads.greek: τὸ γὰρ ἄδηκτον καὶ μέτριον καὶ παρηγορικὸν οὐκ ἔχει καθάπερ ἡ Χία τε καὶ Σαμία καὶ Σελινουσία.
beads.english: For it does not have the non-biting, moderate and soothing quality like the Chian and Samian and Selinusian.

beads.greek: καὶ περὶ τῆς Κιμωλίας δὲ προείρηται βραχὺ τούτων οὔσης ἰσχυροτέρας, ἀδήκτου δ’ ἔτι καὶ αὐτῆς, καὶ μάλιστα εἰ πλυθείη.
beads.english: Of the Cimolian also it has been said before that it is slightly stronger than these, but still non-biting itself too, and especially if it has been washed.

beads.greek: καὶ ἡ Κρητικὴ δὲ γῆ παραπλησία πώς ἐστι ταύταις, ἀλλ’ ἱκανῶς ἀσθενὴς ὑπάρχει, πολὺ τὸ ἀερῶδες ἔχουσα, τὸ μέντοι ῥυπτικὸν ἔχει, διὸ καὶ οἱ ἄνθρωποι λαμπρύνουσιν αὐτῇ τὰ ῥυπαρὰ τῶν ἀργυρωμάτων, ὥστ’ ἔχοις ἂν καὶ ταύτην ἐς ὅπερ καὶ τὰς ἄλλας τὰς ἀδήκτως ῥυπτούσας προειρήκαμεν ἐπιτηδείους εἶναι.
beads.english: The Cretan earth too is somewhat like these, but it is quite weak, having much of the airy, yet it has the cleansing quality, which is why people brighten dirty silverware with it; so that you might have this too for the purpose for which we have said before that the others which cleanse without biting are suitable.

beads.greek: τούτων δ’ ἁπασῶν ἡ Λημνία δύναμιν ἰσχυροτέραν ἔχει, πρόσεστι γὰρ αὐτῇ τι καὶ στύψεως, ἡ δ’ Ἐρετριὰς ἔτι καὶ ταύτης ἰσχυροτέραν, οὐ μὴν ὥστ’ ἤδη δάκνειν.
beads.english: Of all these the Lemnian has a stronger power, for there is present in it also something of astringency, and the Eretrian a still stronger one than this, though not so as actually to bite.

beads.greek: ἐὰν δὲ καὶ πλυθῇ, πάνυ μετρία γίνεται παραπλησίως ταῖς προειρημέναις.
beads.english: And if it is washed too, it becomes quite moderate, like those mentioned before.

beads.greek: ἐγχωρεῖ δὲ τὴν γῆν ταύτην οὐχ ἅπαξ, ἀλλὰ καὶ δὶς ἢ τρὶς πλυθῆναι, καθάπερ καὶ τὴν Κιμωλίαν.
beads.english: It is possible for this earth to be washed not once but even two or three times, as also the Cimolian.

beads.greek: καὶ μέντοι καὶ καίουσιν αὐτὴν ἔνιοι ποιοῦντες δηλονότι λεπτομερεστέραν τε καὶ δριμυτέραν, ὥστ’ εἰς τὴν διαφορητικὴν μεταπίπτειν δύναμιν.
beads.english: And indeed some also burn it, making it evidently more fine-particled and more pungent, so that it passes over into the dispersing power.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ πλυθείη καυθεῖσα, τὸ μὲν δριμὺ καταλιποῦσα τῷ ὕδατι, τὸ δ’ ἐκ τῆς ὀπτήσεως λεπτομερὲς ἔχουσα, ξηραντικωτέρα γίνεται.
beads.english: And if, having been burnt, it is washed, leaving the pungency behind in the water but keeping the fine-particled quality from the roasting, it becomes more drying.

beads.greek: διὸ τῆς ἀκαύστου τῷ κοινῷ λόγῳ γῆς ἁπάσης ἐπὶ τῶν ἑλκῶν οὔσης χρησίμης, ἔτι μᾶλλον ἡ μετὰ τὸ καυθῆναι πλυθεῖσα, καὶ πρὸς τὰ δυσσάρκωτά τε καὶ δυσεπούλωτα χρήσιμός ἐστιν.
beads.english: Hence, whereas unburnt earth of every kind is, by the common account, useful for ulcers, that which has been washed after being burnt is even more so, and is useful also for ulcers that are hard to flesh over and hard to cicatrize.

beads.greek: ὄντων δ’ αὐτῆς δυοῖν εἰδῶν ἡ ﻿ τεφρώδης κατὰ τὴν χρόαν ἀμείνων ἐστὶ τῆς πάνυ λευκῆς.
beads.english: There being two kinds of it, the one ash-coloured in hue is better than the very white.

beads.greek: ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλη γῆ πνιγῖτις ὀνομαζομένη, κατὰ μὲν τὴν ὅλην δύναμιν ἐοικυῖα τῇ Κιμωλίᾳ, κατὰ δὲ τὴν χρόαν ἀφεστηκυῖα. μέλαινα γάρ ἐστιν ὁμοίως τῇ ἀμπελίτιδι, τὸ δὲ γλίσχρον καὶ κολλῶδες οὐχ ἧττον ἔχει Σαμίας γῆς, ἀλλ’ ἔστιν ὅτε καὶ μᾶλλον.
beads.english: There is also another earth called pnigitis, resembling the Cimolian in its whole power but differing in colour, for it is black, like the ampelitis, and it has the viscous and glutinous quality no less than Samian earth, but sometimes even more.

beads.greek: ἐδόθη δ’ ἡμῖν ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ τούτῳ λοιμῷ, καὶ ἄλλη τις ἐξ Ἀρμενίας τῆς ὁμόρου Καππαδοκίας γῆ ξηραντικωτέρα, τὴν χρόαν ὠχρά· λίθον δ’ αὐτὴν ὠνόμαζεν, οὐ γῆν, ὁ δοὺς, καὶ ἔστιν εὐλειοτάτη, καθάπερ καὶ ἡ τίτανος. ὀνομάζω δ’ οὕτω δηλονότι τὴν κεκαυμένην πέτραν.
beads.english: There was also given to us, in this great plague, another earth from the part of Armenia bordering on Cappadocia, more drying, yellowish-ochre in colour; the one who gave it called it a stone, not an earth, and it is extremely smooth, like lime too—I so name, obviously, burnt rock.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥσπερ ἐκείνης οὐδὲν ἐμφέρεται ψαμμῶδες, οὕτως οὐδὲ τῆς Ἀρμενίας. μετὰ γὰρ τὸ θραυσθῆναι τῷ δοίδυκι κατὰ τὴν θυίαν, οὕτως ἐστὶ λεία καὶ ἄλιθος ὥσπερ ἡ τίτανος καὶ ὁ Σάμιος ἀστὴρ, οὐ μὴν ὁμοίως γε κούφη τῷ ἀστέρι.
beads.english: But just as nothing sandy is carried along in that, so neither in the Armenian; for after being broken up with the pestle in the mortar it is as smooth and stone-free as lime and the Samian star, though not equally light with the star.

beads.greek: διὸ καὶ πεπύκνωται μᾶλλον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἧττον ἀερώδης ἐστὶν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο φαντασίαν ἀποφαίνει τοῖς ἀμελέστερον ὁρῶσι λίθος εἶναι.
beads.english: Hence it is also more compact than it and less airy, and for this reason gives those who look at it more carelessly the impression of being a stone.

beads.greek: διαφέρει δ’ οὐδὲν ὡς πρὸς τὰ παρόντα λίθον ἢ γῆν αὐτὴν ὀνομάζειν, εἰδότας ἄκρως ξηραίνουσαν.
beads.english: It makes no difference for present purposes whether one calls it a stone or an earth, knowing that it dries in the highest degree.

beads.greek: ἐπί τε γὰρ δυσεντεριῶν καὶ τῶν κατὰ γαστέρα ῥευμάτων, αἵματός τε πτύσεως καὶ κατάῤῥου καὶ προσέτι τῶν κατὰ τὸ στόμα σηπεδονωδῶν ἑλκῶν ἁρμόττει μάλιστα.
beads.english: For in dysenteries and fluxes of the belly, and spitting of blood and catarrh, and in addition putrefactive ulcers in the mouth, it is most suitable.

beads.greek: καὶ μέντοι καὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ κεφαλῆς εἰς θώρακα ῥευματιζομένους ὀνίνησι μεγάλως, ὥστε καὶ τοὺς διὰ τὴν τοιαύτην αἰτίαν συνεχῶς δυσπνοοῦντας ἰσχυρῶς ὠφελεῖ.
beads.english: And indeed it greatly benefits those who suffer fluxes from the head into the chest, so that it also strongly helps those who are continually short of breath for such a cause.

beads.greek: καὶ μέντοι καὶ ὅσοι φθόῃ κάμνουσιν, καὶ τούτους ὀνίνησιν.
beads.english: And indeed those who labour under consumption—these too it benefits.

beads.greek: ξηραίνει γὰρ αὐτῶν τὸ ἕλκος, ὡς μηδὲ βήττειν ἔτι, πλὴν εἰ κατὰ τὴν δίαιταν ἁμαρτάνοιεν ἀξιολόγως ἢ τὸ περιέχον ἐξαιφνίδιον εἰς δυσκρασίαν μεταπέσοι.
beads.english: For it dries their ulcer, so that they no longer even cough, unless they should err considerably in their regimen or the surrounding air should suddenly fall into a bad mixture.

beads.greek: καί μοι δοκεῖ, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν συρίγγων ἐθεασάμεθα πολλάκις, οὐ μόνον ἐν ἄλλοις μορίοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἕδραν ἄνευ τοῦ κολλύριον καθεῖναι τὸν ῥύπον ἢ τὸν τύλον ἐξαιροῦν τῆς σύριγγος, αὐτῷ μόνῳ τῷ ξηραίνοντι φαρμάκῳ προστελλομένας τε καὶ κλειομένας αὐτὰς, οὕτω κᾀπὶ τοῦ κατὰ τὸν πνεύμονα συμβαίνειν ἕλκους.
beads.english: And it seems to me that, just as we have often observed in the case of fistulas, not only in other parts but also at the seat, that without inserting a collyrium that removes the filth or the callus from the fistula, by the drying drug alone they are brought together and closed, so it happens also in the case of the ulcer in the lung.

beads.greek: φαίνεται γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο διὰ τῶν ξηραινόντων φαρμάκων ὁμοίως ὀνινάμενον, ὅταν τε μέτριον ᾖ καὶ μὴ μέγα λίαν, ὥστ’ ἔδοξαν ἔνιοι τῶν ἐχόντων αὐτὰ τελείως ἀπηλλάχθαι, καὶ τῶν γ’ εἰς τὴν Λιβύην ἀπὸ Ῥώμης διὰ τοιαύτην αἰτίαν πορευθέντων ἔνιοι τελείως ἐπείσθησαν ὑγιεῖς εἶναι, καὶ μέχρι γέ τινων ἐτῶν ἀμέμπτως διήγαγον, εἶθ’ ὕστερόν ποτε πάλιν ἀφυλακτότερον αὐτοῖς διαιτηθεῖσιν ὑποστροφὴ τοῦ νοσήματος ἐγένετο.
beads.english: For this too appears to be benefited in like manner by drying drugs, whenever it is moderate and not very large; so that some of those who had them thought they had been completely rid of them, and of those who travelled from Rome to Libya for such a cause some were completely persuaded that they were healthy, and for some years passed their lives without complaint, and then at some later time, when they had lived a less guarded regimen, a relapse of the disease occurred.

beads.greek: τούτους οὖν, ὡς ἔφην, ἡ ἐκ τῆς Ἀρμενίας βῶλος ἐναργῶς ὠφέλησε καίτοι γ’ ἐν Ῥώμῃ διατρίβοντας, ἔτι τε μᾶλλον τοὺς δυσπνοοῦντας συνεχῶς.
beads.english: These, then, as I said, the bole from Armenia manifestly helped, even though they were living in Rome, and still more those continually short of breath.

beads.greek: ἐν δὲ τῷ μεγάλῳ τούτῳ λοιμῷ παραπλησίῳ τὴν ἰδέαν ὄντι τῷ κατὰ Θουκυδίδην γενομένῳ πάντες οἱ πιόντες τούτου τοῦ φαρμάκου διὰ ταχέων ἐθεραπεύθησαν, ὅσους δ’ οὐδὲν ὤνησεν ἀπέ θανον πάντες, οὐδ’ ὑπ’ ἄλλου τινὸς ὠφελήθησαν, ᾧ καὶ δῆλον ὅτι μόνους τοὺς ἀνιάτως ἔχοντας οὐκ ὠφέλησε.
beads.english: And in this great plague, which is similar in form to the one that occurred in Thucydides' time, all who drank this drug were cured quickly, while all those whom it did not benefit died, nor were they helped by anything else; from which it is clear that it failed to help only those who were in an incurable state.

beads.greek: πίνεται δὲ μετ’ οἴνου λεπτοῦ τὴν σύστασιν, κεραμένου μετρίως μὲν, εἰ ἀπύρετος εἴη παντάπασιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἢ βραχὺ πυρεταίνοι, πάνυ δ’ ὑδαροῦς, εἰ πυρέττοι μειζόνως.
beads.english: It is drunk with wine thin in consistency, moderately mixed if the person is entirely free of fever or feverish only slightly, but quite watery if he is more strongly feverish.

beads.greek: οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ σφοδροὶ κατὰ τὴν θερμασίαν εἰσὶν οἱ λοιμώδεις πυρετοί.
beads.english: Nor indeed are the pestilential fevers violent in their heat.

beads.greek: περὶ δὲ τῶν ξηρανθῆναι δεομένων ἑλκῶν τί δεῖ καὶ λέγειν ὁπηλίκην ἔχει δύναμιν ἡ Ἀρμενικὴ βῶλος αὕτη;
beads.english: As for ulcers that need to be dried, what need is there even to say how great a power this Armenian bole has?

beads.greek: καλεῖν δ’ ἔξεστί σοι, καθάπερ ἔφην, καὶ λίθον αὐτὴν, ὡς ὁ δοὺς ὠνόμαζεν, καὶ γῆν, ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ φαίην, ἐπειδὴ καὶ τέγγεται τοῖς ὑγροῖς.
beads.english: You may call it, as I said, both a stone, as the one who gave it named it, and an earth, as I would say, since it is also soaked through by liquids.

greek_sentences: Περὶ Σαμίας γῆς.] Ἡ Σαμία δ’ οὐδὲ δεῖται πλυθῆναι.
χρώμεθα δ’ αὐτῆς θατέρῳ τῶν εἰδῶν μᾶλλον, ὃ δὴ καὶ Σάμιον ἀστέρα καλοῦσιν, εἰς τὰς τοῦ αἵματος πτύσεις, ﻿ ὁπόθεν ἂν γιγνόμεναι τύχωσιν, ὥσπερ καὶ τῇ Λημνίᾳ σφραγῖδι.

κατὰ δὲ τὴν αὐτὴν δύναμιν ὠφελοῦσι καὶ τὰς ἐκ μήτρας αἱμοῤῥαγίας καὶ τὸν ὀνομαζόμενον ῥοῦν γυναικεῖον, καὶ μέντοι καὶ τὰς δυσεντερικὰς ἑλκώσεις πρὸ τοῦ σηπεδονώδη γενέσθαι τὰ ἕλκη, καλεῖν δ’ ἔθος ἐστὶν τοῖς ἰατροῖς τὰς τοιαύτας διαθέσεις νομὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ νέμεσθαι τὴν σηπεδόνα πρὸς τὰ πλησιάσαντα μόρια, συνδιαφθείρουσαν αὐτὰ τῷ πρώτῳ κακωθέντι.

τῇ γε μὴν Λημνίᾳ κᾀπὶ τοιούτων ἐχρησάμην ἐνίοτε καὶ σαφῶς ὤνησεν ἐνεθεῖσά τε δι’ ἕδρας καὶ ποθεῖσα, προαποκλυσθέντων τῶν ἑλκῶν, ὡς εἰώθαμεν πράττειν, μελικράτῳ μὲν ἀκρατεστέρῳ προτέρῳ, δευτέρῳ δ’ ἅλμῃ.
ἐνέθη μὲν οὖν δι’ ἀρνογλώσσου χυλοῦ, δι’ ὀξυκράτου δ’ ὑδαροῦς ἐπόθη.
