english_sentences: On psoricum.] Psoricum.
The drug is made from litharge mixed with twice as much chalcitis.
Both are first ground in the most pungent vinegar and then put into a new pot, which you will bury in dung for forty days in midsummer.
This drug becomes both more drying and at the same time less biting than chalcitis, and evidently also more fine-particled.
GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 10.
None of the things now about to be said will bring great benefit to those who are ignorant of what was said at the beginning of the treatise in the first five books.
Perhaps it will even harm a person who uses the drugs written about in it without having a method.
I shall therefore address you as one who has learned those things, after recalling the main point of the whole treatise.
It was shown that drugs act according to the so-called active qualities, heat and coldness and dryness and moisture.
Through the mixture of these they become acerbic and harsh and briny and salty and bitter and pungent and sweet.
Some become cleansing, others repelling, others drawing, others softening, others caustic, others putrefying, others eschar-forming.
In addition to these, according to other more specific actions, they become flesh-forming and cicatrizing and agglutinating of fistulas or ulcers, or reducing of overgrowing flesh.
It was also shown that the universal power would be discovered indicatively from a single trial.
This is not just any trial, but one carried out with the distinctions that were stated.
Once the universal power has been discovered, there is no longer any need of trial for the particular actions, except solely for confirmation of what reason has discovered.
In this way, then, let us now too make our judgement of the material before us, and this is the material from animals.
For in the three books that follow the fifth in sequence, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material concerning plants.
We did not, evidently, go through all of it throughout the whole inhabited world, but only as much as we have experience of.
In the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, we went through the material concerning earthy and stony bodies.
It remains for us still to go through the material concerning animals.
After that there still remains what is generated in the sea and lakes, or generally in water, things which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal.
Such things are altogether very few, and they will be written of last, after we have gone through what concerns the bodies of animals.
The order of instruction for these too will follow the order of the first letters in their names.
In the material of plants I also gave an account of the juices that come from them.
So now too the instruction about power will concern not only the solid parts in animals but also what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like.
In what was said earlier, not many of the particular items in the materia medica written by the physicians remained unknown to me.
I myself took pains to know their powers through experience.

If there was something I did not know, I did not write about it at all, since I did not think it right to trust others about even one such thing, because I had learned that some people tell many lies.
With the material now before us, however, it is not so.
I confess that there are very many of the parts and fluids contained in the bodies of animals of which I myself have had no such experience as some have written about.
For some of them are licentious and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws.
About these I do not know how Xenocrates came to write.
He was a man who lived not long ago but in the time of our grandfathers, when the Roman empire had forbidden men to eat human beings.
Yet he, at any rate, writes quite credibly, as one who had himself made trial of them.

He records which affections the brain or flesh or liver of a human being naturally cures when eaten, and which the bones of the head or shin or fingers cure when drunk, some burnt and others unburnt, and which blood itself cures.
These things, then, even if contrary to the laws, are at least not licentious.
But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman's menses is licentious and disgusting.
No less so than these is dung.
Xenocrates wrote what it can do when smeared on the parts in the mouth and pharynx and when swallowed into the stomach.
He has also written about ear-wax when swallowed.
I, for my part, would not have consented to swallow even this, even on condition of never falling ill.
And I consider dung far more disgusting than it.
Indeed, it is a greater reproach for a temperate man to be called a dung-eater than a doer of obscene acts or a catamite.
But even among those who do obscene acts we loathe the 'phoenicizers' more than the 'lesbianizers', and the one who drinks menses seems to me to suffer something similar to the former.
No man in his natural condition, then, would consent to make trial of these things.

Nor would he consent to make trial of those that are more moderate than these but still licentious, such as smearing some part of the body with dung for the sake of the affection in it, or with human semen.
Xenocrates is accustomed to call it 'gonos'.

He distinguishes with all care which conditions the gonos itself, by itself, naturally benefits when smeared on, and which it benefits after the intercourse of man and woman, when it falls out of the female bosom.
For there must be some great poverty of remedies for anyone to treat chilblains [ὑπερεχούσας?] with a man's semen that has not stayed inside but has flowed out of the woman after intercourse.
This kind of material too is plentiful in what he has written about the benefit from animals.
For he recounts not only, evidently, for man, what power urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and when smeared on the parts in the mouth.
He recounts this also for each of the other animals, and much else that is hard to procure, as when he mentions the elephant or the Nile horse.
The beast called the basilisk I have never even seen, and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal.
Certain others too wrote things similar to Xenocrates about animals, and from them Xenocrates himself copied out most of what he wrote.
For whence would he have had the means to make trial himself of so many and such things?
Our own former king Attalus, at any rate, appears to write of fewer, although he was most ambitious in the testing of such things.
Someone who praised the treatise of Ateuristus on the same subject also gave it to me to go through.
As it seems to me, it had been composed without any personal autopsy on the part of the man who wrote it.
I, then, shall mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor Nile horses, nor anything else of which I myself have no experience.
As for the so-called philtres, attraction-charms, dream-senders and hate-charms, I deliberately use their own very names for them.
I would not have mentioned these in writing at all, not even if I had sufficient experience of them.
In the same way I do not mention the deadly drugs, or those which they themselves call 'affection-producing'.

Some of these are even ridiculous, such as binding one's legal opponents so that they cannot utter anything in court, or causing a pregnant woman to miscarry, or making her never conceive, and other such things.
Most of these are, even by the test of experience, impossible.
Some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to the life of men, so that I, by the gods, wonder with what intention certain people came to write them.
Things that bring disrepute even to the living once they are known, how did they hope these would bring them good repute after death?
Now if they had been kings and had made trial of these things on men condemned to death, they would have done nothing terrible.
But they were private persons who had no such authority in their whole life, and yet they came to write these things.
So it is one of two things.
Either they write, without having made trial themselves, about what they do not know.
Or, if they did make trial, they are the most impious of all men, having given deadly drugs for the sake of trial to those who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men.
Someone, at any rate, saw two physicians standing by the dealers in petty wares and brought them honey, supposedly to sell it.
They tasted it and discussed the price, and as they offered little, he hurriedly went off [ἐχωρήθη], and neither of the physicians survived.
All such things, then, deserve to be hated in those who wrote them no less than in those who did them, indeed even more.
For it is a lesser wrong to do some evil alone than to do it along with many [ὅσῳ ... μετὰ πολλῶν].
The experience of evil precepts died together with the one who did the deed.
But the experience of all those who wrote is immortal, furnishing the wicked with weapons of malefaction.
Let us, then, now speak about the things useful to men, of which we have experience.

beads.greek: [10.2.1] Περὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις ὑγρῶν.
beads.english: [10.2.1] On the fluids in animals.

beads.greek: Περὶ αἵματος.] Αἷμα, προσυπακούειν δηλονότι χρὴ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ἔχοντος ζώου, τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ ὄντως ἐστὶν αἷμα.
beads.english: On blood.] Blood: one must of course understand in addition 'of an animal in its natural state', for this is what is truly blood.

beads.greek: τὸ δὲ μελαγχολικὸν ἢ πικρόχολον ἢ φλεγματῶδες ἢ ὀῤῥῶδες ἢ σηπεδονῶδες αἷμα μικτόν ἐστιν ἔκ τε τοῦ κατ’ ἀλήθειαν αἵματος καὶ τοῦ μεμιγμένου χυμοῦ τε καὶ ἰχῶρος αὐτῷ.
beads.english: Melancholic, bitter-bilious, phlegmatic, serous or putrefactive blood is mixed, composed of blood in the true sense and of the humour and ichor that have been mixed with it.

beads.greek: καὶ αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν αἵματος ἐν ἑκάστῳ ζώῳ τὸ μὲν ὑγρότερόν ἐστι, τὸ δὲ ξηρότερον, καὶ τὸ μὲν μᾶλλον, τὸ δὲ ἧττον θερμὸν, ψυχρὸν γὰρ οὐδέν ἐστιν αἷμα.
beads.english: And of natural blood itself, in each animal some is moister and some drier, and some more and some less hot; for no blood is cold.

greek_sentences: [10.2.1] Περὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις ὑγρῶν.
Περὶ αἵματος.] Αἷμα, προσυπακούειν δηλονότι χρὴ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ἔχοντος ζώου, τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ ὄντως ἐστὶν αἷμα.
τὸ δὲ μελαγχολικὸν ἢ πικρόχολον ἢ φλεγματῶδες ἢ ὀῤῥῶδες ἢ σηπεδονῶδες αἷμα μικτόν ἐστιν ἔκ τε τοῦ κατ’ ἀλήθειαν αἵματος καὶ τοῦ μεμιγμένου χυμοῦ τε καὶ ἰχῶρος αὐτῷ.
καὶ αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν αἵματος ἐν ἑκάστῳ ζώῳ τὸ μὲν ὑγρότερόν ἐστι, τὸ δὲ ξηρότερον, καὶ τὸ μὲν μᾶλλον, τὸ δὲ ἧττον θερμὸν, ψυχρὸν γὰρ οὐδέν ἐστιν αἷμα.
english_sentences: [10.2.1] On the fluids in animals.
On blood.] Blood: one must of course understand in addition 'of an animal in its natural state', for this is what is truly blood.
Melancholic, bitter-bilious, phlegmatic, serous or putrefactive blood is mixed, composed of blood in the true sense and of the humour and ichor that have been mixed with it.
And of natural blood itself, in each animal some is moister and some drier, and some more and some less hot; for no blood is cold.

beads.greek: Περὶ ὑείου αἵματος.] Ὕειον μὲν οὖν ὑγρόν ἐστιν καὶ ἧττον θερμὸν, ἀνθρωπείῳ μάλιστα κατὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν ἐοικὸς, εἵπερ γε καὶ σάρκες τῶν ὑῶν ἐοίκασι ταῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
beads.english: On pig's blood.] Pig's blood, then, is moist and less hot, and most closely resembles human blood in its mixture, since the flesh of pigs too resembles that of humans.

beads.greek: ἴσμεν γοῦν ἤδη πολλοὺς ἁλόντας πανδοκέας τε καὶ μαγείρους ἐν τῷ πιπράσκειν ὡς ὕεια τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων κρέα, καίτοι τῶν ἐσθιόντων αὐτὰ διαφορᾶς οὐδεμιᾶς οὐδεὶς ᾐσθάνετο.
beads.english: Indeed, we already know of many innkeepers and cooks who were caught selling human flesh as pork, and yet none of those who ate it perceived any difference.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ διηγουμένων τινῶν ἤκουσα πιστῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐδηδοκέναι μὲν ἔν τινι πανδοχείῳ ζωμὸν δαψιλῆ μετὰ κρεῶν ἡδίστων, ἤδη δὲ ἐμπεπλησμένων, εὑρεῖν ἐν αὐτῷ δακτύλου μέρος τὸ πρόσω κατ’ αὐτὸν τὸν ὄνυχα, φοβηθέντες δὲ τοὺς ἐν τῷ πανδοχείῳ μὴ καὶ αὐτοὺς φάγωσιν ὡς εἰθισμένοι τοῦ πράγματος, αὐτίκα μὲν ἐξελθεῖν, ἐμέσαντες δὲ τὰ ἐδηδεσμένα τῆς ὁδοιπορίας ἔχεσθαι.
beads.english: Moreover, I heard trustworthy people relate that in a certain inn they had eaten abundant broth with most delicious meat, and when they had already eaten their fill, they found in it the front part of a finger, at the nail itself. Fearing that the people in the inn might eat them too, as being accustomed to the practice, they left at once, vomited up what they had eaten, and continued their journey.

beads.greek: καὶ μέντοι καὶ φωραθῆναι τοὺς κατὰ τὸ πανδοχεῖον οὐ μετὰ πολὺν χρόνον ἔφασαν ἐφ’ οἷς ἔσφαττον ἀνθρώπους, ὥστ’ εἰκότως ἄν τις ὑπολάβοι καὶ τὸ αἷμα τῶν ὑῶν ὁμοιότατον εἶναι τῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
beads.english: They also said that not long afterwards the people at the inn were caught for the human beings they used to slaughter. So one might reasonably suppose that the blood of pigs too is most similar to that of humans.

beads.greek: ἐκ γὰρ τοιούτου αἵματος ἥ τε πρώτη γένεσίς ἐστι καἰ ἡ μετὰ ταῦτα τροφὴ ταῖς σαρξὶν, ὥστε καὶ ﻿ ὅστις ἀνθρώπειον αἷμά φησιν εἶναι πρός τι νόσημα χρήσιμον, ἐν ὑείῳ πρότερον ἐπιδειξάσθω, καὶ εἰ μὴ τὴν αὐτὴν, ἀλλ’ ὁμοίαν ἐνέργειαν.
beads.english: For it is from such blood that the flesh has both its first generation and its nourishment thereafter. Hence whoever says that human blood is useful against some disease, let him first demonstrate in pig's blood, if not the same action, at least a similar one.

beads.greek: εἰ γὰρ καὶ κατά τι τῆς δυνάμεως ἀπολείποιτο ἀνθρωπείου αἵματος, παραπλήσιον γοῦν τι δράσει, δι’ οὗ γνωσθέντος ἐλπίσομεν ὑπ’ ἀνθρωπείου τελεώτερον ἔσεσθαι τὴν ὠφέλειαν.
beads.english: For even if it should fall short of human blood in some respect of its power, it will at any rate do something comparable, and once this is known we shall expect the benefit from human blood to be more complete.

beads.greek: ὡς ἐάν γε μηδὲ μικρόν τι φαίνηται τῆς ἐπαγγελίας διασῶζον, οὐδ’ ἐπ’ ἀνθρωπείου λόγον ἔχει πειρᾶσθαι.
beads.english: But if it appears to preserve not even a little of what is promised, there is no reason to make trial of human blood either.

beads.greek: τὰ μὲν γὰρ ὅμοια τῶν ὁμοίων εἶναι ποιητικὰ πεπειράμεθα.
beads.english: For we have found by experience that similar things are productive of similar effects.

beads.greek: περιστερᾶς γοῦν αἷμα παρ’ ἡμῖν ἐν Περγάμῳ, σχεδὸν δὲ καὶ καθ’ ὅλην τὴν Ἀσίαν, εἰώθασιν οἱ ἀνατρήσαντες ὀστᾶ κεφαλῆς κατεαγότα κατασχεῖν τῆς παχείας μήνιγγος.
beads.english: At any rate, among us in Pergamum, and indeed throughout almost the whole of Asia, those who have trepanned fractured bones of the head are accustomed to pour dove's blood onto the thick membrane [κατασχεῖν, probably to be read καταχεῖν].

beads.greek: εἶτά τις ἔχων μὲν κατὰ τύχην φάτταν, οὐκ ἔχων δὲ περιστερὰν, ἐχρήσατο τῷ τῆς φάττης αἵματι καὶ ὅμως ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐσώθη.
beads.english: Then someone who happened to have a wood-pigeon but not a dove used the wood-pigeon's blood, and the man was nevertheless saved.

beads.greek: καὶ ἄλλος δὲ τρυγόνος ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ χρησάμενος, οὐδὲν ἔβλαψε τὸν ἄνθρωπον.
beads.english: And another, using the blood of a turtle-dove on another patient, did the man no harm.

beads.greek: τοῖς γὰρ ὁμοίοις ἐπὶ τῶν αὐτῶν χρῆσθαι παθῶν μὴ παρόντων τῶν προπεπειρασμένων ἕν τι τῶν ὁμολογουμένων ἐστὶ καὶ μαρτυρουμένων ὑπὸ τῆς ἐμπειρίας.
beads.english: For to use similar things for the same affections when those tested beforehand are not available is one of the things agreed upon and attested by experience.

beads.greek: καὶ τά γε πλεῖστα τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίου κατὰ τοῦτον περαίνεται τὸν τρόπον.
beads.english: And indeed most of human life is carried on in this way.

greek_sentences: Περὶ ὑείου αἵματος.] Ὕειον μὲν οὖν ὑγρόν ἐστιν καὶ ἧττον θερμὸν, ἀνθρωπείῳ μάλιστα κατὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν ἐοικὸς, εἵπερ γε καὶ σάρκες τῶν ὑῶν ἐοίκασι ταῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
