beads.greek: δείσαντες οὖν οἱ θερισταὶ μή τι πάθοιεν ἐκ τοῦ πόματος, αὐτοὶ μὲν ὕδατος ἔπιον, ὡς δ’ ἀπηλλάττοντο, χαρίζονται δῆθεν ὑπὸ φιλανθρωπίας τῷ τὸν ἐλέφαντα νοσοῦντι τὸν ὅλον οἶνον, ἄμεινον αὐτῷ κρίναντες εἶναι τεθνάναι μᾶλλον ἢ ζῇν τοιούτῳ.
beads.english: The reapers, fearing that they might suffer some harm from the drink, drank water themselves. As they were leaving, they made a present of the whole wine, ostensibly out of humanity, to the man ill with elephas, judging that it was better for him to be dead than to live in such a state.

beads.greek: ὁ δ’ ἐκ τούτου πίνων ὑγιὴς ἐγένετο θαυμαστόν τινα τρόπον.
beads.english: He, drinking from it, became healthy in a wonderful manner.

beads.greek: ὅλον γὰρ αὐτοῦ τὸ τοῦ δέρματος ὀχθῶδες ἀπέπεσεν ὡς τῶν μαλακοστράκων ζώων τὸ σκέπασμα.
beads.english: For the whole lumpy part of his skin fell off like the covering of the soft-shelled animals, and what remained appeared quite soft, like that of crayfish and crabs when the shell around them has fallen off.

beads.greek: ὅσον δ’ ὑπόλοιπον ἦν ἔτι μαλακὸν ἱκανῶς ἐφαίνετο καθάπερ τὸ τῶν καράβων τε καὶ καρκίνων, ὅταν ἀποπέσῃ τὸ πέριξ ὄστρακον.
beads.english: Another such case arose from a similar chance occurrence in Asian Mysia, not far from our city.

beads.greek: ἕτερον τοιοῦτον ἐξ ὁμοίας περιπτώσεως ἐγένετο κατὰ τὴν ἐν Ἀσίᾳ Μυσίαν, οὐ πόῤῥω τῆς ἡμετέρας πόλεως.
beads.english: A man suffering from elephas set out to use naturally hot waters in the hope of benefit.

beads.greek: ἄνθρωπος ἐλέφαντι κάμνων ἐπὶ χρῆσιν ὥρμησεν ὑδάτων θερμῶν αὐτοφυῶν ὠφελείας ἐλπίδι.
beads.english: He had a concubine, a slave, young and beautiful and with many lovers.

beads.greek: παλλακὶς δ’ ἦν αὐτῷ δούλη νέα τε καὶ καλὴ πολλοὺς ἐραστὰς ἔχουσα, ταύτῃ καὶ ἄλλα μέν τινα τῶν κατὰ τὴν οἰκίαν, ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸ ταμεῖον ἐπίστευεν ὁ κάμνων.
beads.english: To her the sick man entrusted various other affairs of the household, and in particular those of the storeroom. While he was using the waters they lodged in a house that had next to it a dry, squalid plot full of vipers.

beads.greek: ὡς δὲ καταχθέντων αὐτῶν, ἡνίκ’ ἐχρῆτο τοῖς ὕδασιν, ἐν οἰκίᾳ παρακείμενον ἐχούσῃ χωρίον αὐχμηρὸν ἐχιδνῶν μεστὸν, ἐμπεσοῦσά τις αὐτῶν εἰς οἴνου κεράμιον ἀμελῶς κείμενον ἐναπέθανεν, ἕρμαιον ἡγησαμένη τὸ κατὰ τύχην ἐκβὰν ἡ παλλακὴ τῷ δεσπότῃ τὸν ποτὸν ἐκ τούτου προσέφερεν.
beads.english: One of the vipers fell into a jar of wine that had been carelessly left lying and died in it. The concubine, considering this chance event a windfall, offered her master his drink from that jar.

beads.greek: ὁ δὲ πίνων αὐτὸ τῷ κατὰ τὴν καλύβην ὡσαύτως ὑγιάσθη.
beads.english: He, drinking it, was healed in the same way as the man in the hut.

beads.greek: δύο μὲν ἤδη σοι ταῦτα διδάγματα τῆς κατὰ τὴν περίπτωσιν πείρας, ἕτερον δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς τρίτον ἐξ ἡμετέρας μιμήσεως.
beads.english: These two lessons you now have from the experience of chance occurrence; and besides them a third, from our imitation.

beads.greek: ἐπειδὴ γάρ τις νοσῶν τοῦτο τὸ νόσημα φιλοσοφώτερος ἢ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς ἐδυσχέραινέ τε δεινῶς καὶ τεθνάναι βέλτιον ἢ ζῇν ἔφασκεν εἶναι, διακειμένῳ οὕτως ἀθλίως ἐδήλωσα τὰς προειρημένας δύο περιπτώσεις αὐτῶν.
beads.english: For a man ill with this disease, more philosophical than the many, was terribly vexed by it and kept saying that it was better to be dead than to live. Since he was in so wretched a condition, I disclosed to him the two chance occurrences just related.

beads.greek: ὁ δ’ , αὐτός τε γὰρ ἦν ἔμπειρος οἰωνῶν ἐχρήσατό τε φίλῳ θαυμαστῶς κατορθοῦντι τὸ μάθημα, καθίσας ἐπ’ ὄρνισιν ἅμ’ ἐκείνῳ προὐτράπη ﻿ τε μιμήσασθαι τὰ διὰ τῆς πείρας ἐγνωσμένα καὶ πίνων οἶνον οὕτω φαρμαχθέντα λεπρώδης ἐγένετο.
beads.english: He was himself experienced in bird-omens and had a friend wonderfully successful in this learning. Taking his seat with that friend to observe the birds, he was urged on to imitate what had been learned through experience, and by drinking wine drugged in this way he became leprous.

beads.greek: χρόνῳ δ’ ὕστερον ἰασάμεθα καὶ τὴν λέπραν αὐτοῦ τοῖς συνήθεσι φαρμάκοις.
beads.english: Some time later we cured his lepra too with the usual drugs.

beads.greek: τέταρτος ἐπὶ τούτῳ τέχνην πεποιημένος ἐχίδνας ζώσας συλλαμβάνειν ἐν ἀρχῇ μὲν ἦν τοῦ πάθους ἐκείνου, προὔκειτο δ’ ἡμῖν ὅπως ἰαθῇ τάχιστα.
beads.english: A fourth man after this, who had made it his craft to catch live vipers, was at the beginning of that affection, and our purpose was that he should be cured as quickly as possible.

beads.greek: φλέβα τε οὖν αὐτοῦ τεμόντες καὶ καθήραντες φαρμάκῳ μέλαιναν κενοῦντι, χρήσασθαι ταῖς ἀγρευομέναις ἐχίδναις συνεβουλεύσαμεν, ἐν λοπάδι σκευάζοντι, καθάπερ τὰς ἐγχέλεις.
beads.english: So, having cut his vein and purged him with a drug that evacuates black bile, we advised him to make use of the vipers he caught, preparing them in a lopas as one does eels.

beads.greek: οὗτος μὲν οὖν οὕτως ἐθεραπεύθη, διαπνεύσαντος αὐτῷ τοῦ πάθους.
beads.english: This man, then, was treated in this way, the affection being breathed out of him through transpiration.

beads.greek: ἄλλος δέ τις ἀνὴρ πλούσιος οὐχ ἡμεδαπὸς οὗτός γε, ἀλλ’ ἐκ μέσης Θρᾴκης ἧκεν, ὀνείρατος προτρέψαντος αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ Πέργαμον, εἶτα τοῦ θεοῦ προστάξαντος ὄναρ αὐτῷ πίνειν τε τοῦ διὰ τῶν ἐχιδνῶν φαρμάκου καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν καὶ χρίειν ἔξωθεν τὸ σῶμα, μετέπεσεν τὸ πάθος οὐ μετὰ πολλὰς ἡμέρας εἰς λέπραν, ἐθεραπεύθη τε πάλιν οἷς ὁ θεὸς ἐκέλευεν φαρμάκοις καὶ τοῦτο τὸ νόσημα.
beads.english: Another man, a rich one, was not of our country but came from the middle of Thrace, a dream having urged him to Pergamum. The god then commanded him in a dream to drink each day of the drug made from vipers and to anoint his body from outside.

beads.greek: ἡ μὲν δὴ τῶν ἐχιδνῶν σὰρξ εἰς τοσοῦτον ἥκει τῆς ξηραντικῆς δυνάμεως· ἐπεὶ δ’ ἔνιοι τῶν φαγόντων αὐτὴν ἑάλωσαν δίψει σφοδροτάτῳ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο προσαγορεύουσι τὰς ἐχίδνας διψάδας.
beads.english: Not many days later the affection changed into lepra, and this disease too was cured in its turn with the drugs the god ordered. So great a degree of drying power, then, does the flesh of vipers attain.

beads.greek: εἰσὶ δ’ οἳ καὶ τοὺς δηχθέντας ὑπ’ αὐτῶν φασιν οὐκ ἐμπίπλασθαι πίνοντας, ἀλλὰ διαῤῥήγνυσθαι πρότερον ἢ παύσασθαι διψῶντας.
beads.english: But some of those who ate it were seized by a most violent thirst, and for this reason they call the vipers dipsades.

beads.greek: διὰ τοῦτο τῶν ἐν Ῥώμῃ τὰς ἐχίδνας θηρευόντων, οὓς ὀνομάζουσι Μαρσοὺς, ἐπυθόμην εἴ τι σημεῖον ἔχοιέν με διδάξαι διακριτικὸν ἑκατέρου τοῦ γένους τῶν ἐχιδνῶν· οἱ δ’ οὐδὲν ὅλως ἔφασαν εἶναι γένος ἐχιδνῶν διψάδων, ἀλλὰ τὰς παρὰ θαλάττῃ καὶ τόποις ἁλμυρίδα πολλὴν ἔχουσι διαιτωμένας ἁλμυρὰν ἴσχειν τὴν σάρκα, διὸ καὶ κατὰ Λιβύην πολλὰς γίγνεσθαι τοιαύτας, ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ δ’ οὐκ εἶναι διὰ τὴν ὑγρότητα τῆς χώρας.
beads.english: There are also some who say that those bitten by them, though they drink, are not filled, but burst before they cease to thirst. For this reason I inquired of those in Rome who hunt vipers, whom they call Marsi, whether they had any sign to teach me that distinguishes the two kinds of vipers.

beads.greek: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἤκουσα τῶν Μαρσῶν λεγόντων, οὐ μὴν ἔχω βεβαίως εἰπεῖν εἴτ’ ἀληθεύσουσι τὸ σύμπαν εἴτε καὶ ψεύδονται κατά τι.
beads.english: They said that there is no kind of dipsas vipers at all. Rather, those that live by the sea and in places with much saline earth (halmyris) have briny flesh, and for this reason many such occur in Libya, but there are none in Italy because of the moistness of the land.

beads.greek: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐν οἷς εἰρήκασι χωρίοις γίνεσθαί τινας ἐχίδνας ἁλυκὴν ἐχούσας τὴν σάρκα πιθανώτατον εἶναί μοι δοκεῖ.
beads.english: These things, then, I heard the Marsi say, but I cannot state with certainty whether they speak the truth in everything or are also lying in some respect.

beads.greek: συμμεταβαλλούσας γὰρ οἶδα ταῖς τροφαῖς τὰς τῶν ζώων σάρκας, οὐ μὴν ὡς οὐδέν ἐστι γένος ἐχιδνῶν διψάδων ἀποφήνασθαι δύναμαι.
beads.english: That in the places they named some vipers occur which have salty flesh seems to me most plausible, for I know that the fleshes of animals change along with their foods.

beads.greek: τὸ δ’ οὖν ἀσφαλέστατόν ἐστι φυλάττεσθαι τὰς ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις χωρίοις ἐχίδνας θηρεύειν εἰς ἐδωδὴν ἢ φαρμάκου κατασκευὴν, ὁποῖόν ἐστι καὶ τουτὶ τὸ ἔνδοξον, ὃ καλοῦσιν ἅπαντες σχεδὸν ἰατροὶ θηριακήν.
beads.english: But I cannot declare that there is no kind of dipsas vipers. The safest course, then, is to take care not to hunt vipers in such places, whether for eating or for the preparation of a drug, such as this celebrated one which nearly all physicians call theriac.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ δ’ ἔθος ἡμῖν ἐστιν, ὅταν τοὺς καλουμένους ἀρτίσκους θηριακοὺς σκευάζωμεν, ἀφαιρεῖν οὐ μόνον τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν οὐρὰν, ἐνενόησα πολλάκις εὐλόγως ἴσως μὲν τὴν κεφαλὴν ὅλην, διὰ τὸν ἐν τῷ στόματι περιεχόμενον ἰὸν, ἀλόγως δὲ τὴν οὐρὰν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι.
beads.english: Now it is our custom, when we prepare the so-called theriac pastilles (artiskoi), to remove not only their head but also the tail. I have often reflected that the whole head is perhaps reasonably removed, on account of the venom contained in the mouth, but the tail unreasonably.

beads.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ τοῦτ’ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, ὅτι διὰ τὰ περιττώματα τῆς τροφῆς τά θ’ ὑγρὰ καὶ τὰ ξηρὰ πρακτέον οὕτως ἐστίν.
beads.english: Nor can one say that it must be done so on account of the residues of the food, both the moist and the dry.

beads.greek: ἀποκτείναντες γὰρ αὐτὰς, εἶτ’ ἐκδείραντές τε καὶ ἀναπτύξαντες, ἐξαιροῦμέν τε καὶ ἀποῤῥίπτομεν ἅπαντα τὰ ἔνδον, ὡς μόνην καταλείπεσθαι τὴν τῶν σαρκῶν οὐσίαν ἅμα ταῖς διαπεφυκυίαις αὐτῶν ἀρτηρίαις τε καὶ φλεψὶν, ἐλάχιστον ἐχούσαις ὄγκον ὡς πρὸς τὴν ὅλην σάρκα, καὶ μηδὲ φαινόμενον, ἐὰν μὴ πάνυ τις ἐπιμελῶς κατασκέψηται.
beads.english: For having killed them, then flayed them and laid them open, we take out and throw away all the inner parts, so that only the substance of the fleshes is left, together with the arteries and veins that grow through it. These have a very small bulk relative to the whole flesh and are not even visible unless one inspects very carefully.

beads.greek: τοὺς μὲν οὖν ἀρτίσκους, οὓς δὴ καὶ θηριακοὺς ὀνομάζουσι, σκευάζομεν οὕτως.
beads.english: The pastilles, then, which they also name theriac pastilles, we prepare thus.

beads.greek: κεκαθαρμένας αὐτὰς λαβόντες, εἶθ’ ἕψοντες ἐν ὕδατι, μέχρις ἂν ἀκριβῶς ἡμῖν εἶναι δόξωσιν ἑφθαί.
beads.english: Taking the vipers cleaned, we boil them in water until they seem to us to be exactly boiled.

beads.greek: συνεμβάλλομεν δ’ εὐθέως ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἀνήθου τῷ ὕδατι καὶ μετὰ τὴν ἕψησιν ἀπὸ τῶν σαρκῶν διακρίνομεν τὰς ἀκάνθας, εἶτα μίγνυμεν ἄρτῳ λελειωμένῳ τὴν σάρκα.
beads.english: We put dill into the water along with them right from the start. After the boiling we separate the spines from the fleshes, and then mix the flesh with ground bread.

beads.greek: τὸν δ’ ἄρτον τοῦτον οὐ τὸν ἐπιτυχόντα λαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἔνι μάλιστα καθαρώτατόν τε καὶ καλῶς ὠπτημένον ἐν κλιβάνῳ, συμμέτρων ἁλῶν ἔχοντα καὶ ζύμης.
beads.english: This bread we do not take at random, but the purest possible, well baked in an oven (klibanos), with a moderate amount of salt and leaven.

beads.greek: προαναξηραίνομεν δὲ αὐτὸν ἐν οἴκῳ ξηρῷ καὶ ἀνίκμῳ, μέχρις ἂν οὕτω γένηται ξηρὸς ὡς ἐν ὅλμῳ κοπῆναι δύνασθαι.
beads.english: We dry it beforehand in a dry room without moisture, until it becomes dry enough to be pounded in a mortar.

beads.greek: οὐ μὴν κόπτοντές γε μίγνυμεν, ἀλλὰ διαβρέχοντες τῷ ὕδατι, καθὸ τὰς ἐχίδνας ἑψήσαμεν.
beads.english: Yet we do not mix it in by pounding it, but by soaking it in the water in which we boiled the vipers.

beads.greek: αὐτὴν δὲ τὴν σάρκα πρὶν μιγνύναι τῷ ἄρτῳ, τρίβομεν ἐν θυίᾳ τῶν μαγείρων, ἄχρις ἂν ἀκριβῶς γένηται λεία.
beads.english: The flesh itself, before mixing it with the bread, we triturate in a cooks' mortar until it becomes exactly smooth.

beads.greek: καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα μικροὺς ἀρτίσκους λεπτοὺς πλάσαντες, εἶτα ξηράναντες ἐν οἴκῳ θερμῷ καὶ ξηρῷ φυλάττομεν ἀποτιθέμενοι πάλιν ἐν οἴκῳ τοιούτῳ.
beads.english: After this, having moulded small thin pastilles, we dry them in a warm and dry room and keep them, storing them again in such a room.

beads.greek: τούτους μὲν οὖν εἰσβάλλοντος τοῦ θέρους σκευάζομεν, ἡνίκα μάλιστα βελτίστη τῶν ἐχιδνῶν ἐστιν ἡ σάρξ.
beads.english: These we prepare at the onset of summer, when the flesh of vipers is at its very best.

beads.greek: χρώμεθα δ’ ὕστερον κόπτοντές τε καὶ διάττοντες, εἶτ’ αὖθις λειοῦντες ἀναμιγνύντες τε τοῖς ἐσκευασμένοις εἰς ἡδονὴν ἁλσὶν, ἐμβάλλομεν δ’ αὐτῶν καὶ τῇ θηριακῇ.
beads.english: Later we use them by pounding and sifting them, then triturating them again and mixing them with salts prepared for pleasantness of taste; we also put them into the theriac.

beads.greek: γίγνονται δὲ καὶ οἱ διὰ τῶν ὀπτηθεισῶν ἐχιδνῶν ἅλες ὑπὸ τὸν αὐτὸν καιρὸν εἶς χύτραν καινὴν ἐμβαλλόντων ἡμῶν τὰς ἐχίδνας ζώσας, ἅμα τοῖς ὑπεστορεσμένοις τε καὶ περικειμένοις αὐταῖς φαρμάκοις, ἃ λέγειν ἅπαντα νῦν οὐκ ἔστι τῆς ἐνεστώσης πραγματείας.
beads.english: At the same season the salts made from roasted vipers are also prepared. We throw the vipers alive into a new pot together with the drugs strewn underneath and laid around them, all of which it is not the business of the present treatise to state now.

beads.greek: ἴσως γάρ τις ἡμῖν εὐλόγως ἐγκαλέσει καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀρτίσκων τῆς κατασκευῆς ὡς οὐκ ἐν καιρῷ διελθοῦσιν.
beads.english: Indeed, someone might perhaps reasonably reproach us even over the preparation of the pastilles, as having gone through it out of place.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ἐπειδὴ φθάνει λελέχθαι, φυλαττέσθω, κᾂν δοκῇ μὴ πάνυ τι τῆς προκειμένης εἶναι πραγματείας ἴδια.
beads.english: But since these things have already been said, let them stand, even if they seem not altogether proper to the present treatise.

beads.greek: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς κατὰ τὸ προσῆκον μέτρον λεγέσθω.
beads.english: What follows, let it be said in fitting measure.

beads.greek: προσῆκον δ’ ἐστὶ περὶ τῆς καθόλου δυνάμεως ἀναμνῆσαι τὴν σάρκα τῶν ἐχιδνῶν, εἰπόντα εἶναι ξηραντικήν τε καὶ διαφορητικὴν ἰσχυρῶς, ἄμα τῷ θερμαίνειν μετρίως.
beads.english: It is fitting to recall, concerning the general power of the flesh of vipers, that it is drying and strongly dispersing, while heating moderately.

beads.greek: ἐπείγεται δ’, ὡς ἔοικεν, ἡ δύναμις αὐτῆς ἐπὶ τὸ δέρμα, διὰ τούτου κινοῦσα τὰ κατὰ τὸ σῶμα περιττώματα.
beads.english: Its power, it seems, presses towards the skin, and through the skin it moves the residues in the body.

beads.greek: φθειρῶν τε οὖν πλῆθος οὐκ ὀλίγον γεννᾶται τοῖς ἔχουσι κακοχυμίαν ἐν τοῖς σώμασι δαψιλῆ καὶ τοῦ δέρματος ἀφίσταταί τε καὶ ἀποπίπτει καθάπερ τι λέπος ἡ ἐπιδερμὶς ὀνομαζομένη, καθ’ ἣν ἴσχονται μᾶλλον τῶν ﻿ εἰς τὸ δέρμα φερομένων χυμῶν οἱ παχεῖς καὶ γεώδεις, ὑφ’ ὧν αἵ τε ψῶραι καὶ αἱ λέπραι καὶ οἱ ἐλέφαντες γίνονται.
beads.english: So a not inconsiderable multitude of lice is generated in those who have abundant kakochymia in their bodies. Also, the so-called epidermis separates from the skin and falls off like a husk; it is in the epidermis that the thick and earthy humours, among those carried to the skin, are more held back, and by these psōrai, leprai and elephantes arise.

beads.greek: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν εἶχόν σοι λέγειν περὶ τῶν τῆς ἐχίδνης σαρκῶν, ἐφεξῆς δὲ πάλιν ἀναλήψομαι τὸν λόγον.
beads.english: This, then, is what I had to tell you about the fleshes of the viper; next I shall take up the account again.

beads.greek: αἱ μὲν τῶν θερμοτέρων φύσει ζώων σάρκες οὐ μόνον τρέφουσιν ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ θερμαίνουσιν, αἱ δὲ τῶν ψυχροτέρων ψύχουσιν.
beads.english: The fleshes of animals that are hotter by nature not only nourish us but also heat, while those of colder animals cool.

beads.greek: οὕτως δὲ καὶ αἱ μὲν τῶν ξηροτέρων ξηραίνουσιν, αἱ δὲ τῶν ὑγροτέρων ὑγραίνουσιν.
beads.english: In the same way, those of drier animals dry, and those of moister animals moisten. Remember, then, what you learned in the work On Mixtures.

beads.greek: μεμνημένος οὖν ὧν ἔμαθες ἐν τοῖς περὶ κράσεων, ὅταν γνωρίσῃς τι τῶν ζώων εἶναι τῇ κράσει ξηρότερον, ὥσπερ εἰ τύχοι τὸν ἄγριον ὗν τοῦ ἡμέρου, γίνωσκε τούτου καὶ τὴν σάρκα ξηραντικωτέραν εἶναι καὶ κατὰ τὰς ἄλλας διαφορὰς τῶν κράσεων ὡσαύτως, οἷον ὅτι συὸς μὲν πρόβατον ξηρότερον, τούτου δ’ αἴξ, τούτου δὲ βοῦς, καὶ τούτου λέων.
beads.english: When you recognise that some animal is drier in mixture, as for instance the wild boar than the domestic pig, know that its flesh too is more drying. The same holds for the other differences of mixtures: for example, the sheep is drier than the pig, the goat than the sheep, the ox than the goat, and the lion than the ox.

beads.greek: οὕτω δὲ καὶ κατὰ θερμότητα λέων μὲν κυνὸς θερμότερος, κύων δὲ ταύρου, ταῦρος δὲ τοῦ τοὺς ὄρχεις ἐκτετμημένου βοός.
beads.english: So too in respect of heat, the lion is hotter than the dog, the dog than the bull, and the bull than the ox whose testicles have been cut out.

beads.greek: ἀνάλογον οὖν τῇ κατὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν ὑπεροχῇ τῶν ἄλλων ζώων καὶ αἱ σάρκες αὐτῶν διοίσουσιν.
beads.english: In proportion, then, to their excess in mixture over the other animals, their fleshes will also differ.

beads.greek: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ξηραίνειν μὲν ἐθέλων τὸ σῶμα τῶν ξηροτέρων τῇ κράσει ζώων δώσεις τὴν σάρκα, θερμαίνειν δὲ βουλόμενος τῶν θερμοτέρων, καὶ ψυχρότερον μὲν ἐπιχειρῶν ἐργάζεσθαι τῶν ψυχροτέρων, ὑγρότερον δὲ τῶν ὑγροτέρων.
beads.english: For this reason, when you wish to dry the body, you will give the flesh of animals drier in mixture; when you want to heat it, that of hotter ones; when you undertake to make it colder, that of colder ones; and when moister, that of moister ones.

beads.greek: οὐ σμικρὰ δὲ διαφορὰ τῶν σαρκῶν ἐστι κᾀν τῷ τεταριχεῦσθαί τινας αὐτῶν.
beads.english: No small difference among the fleshes lies also in some of them having been salted.

beads.greek: ὅλῳ γὰρ παντὶ διαλλάττουσιν, ὡς πολλάκις ὑγροτάτου τῇ κράσει ζώου ταριχευθεῖσαν σάρκα ξηραντικωτέραν εἶναι μακρῷ τῆς φύσεως ξηρᾶς.
beads.english: For they differ altogether, so that often the salted flesh of an animal most moist in mixture is far more drying than the unsalted flesh of one dry by nature.

beads.greek: ἀταριχεύτου καὶ ἡ ὀπτηθεῖσα δὲ ξηροτέρα τῆς ἑψηθείσης ἐστὶν ἐν ὕδατι.
beads.english: And the roasted flesh is drier than that boiled in water.

beads.greek: ἔγραψαν δὲ καὶ ἄλλων ζώων ἔνιοι σάρκας ὠφελεῖν ἐσθιομένας τε καὶ κατὰ πεπονθότων μερῶν ἐπιτιθεμένας, οἷον τὴν τοῦ χερσαίου ἐχίνου σκελετευθεῖσαν, εἰ ποθείη ἐλεφαντιῶσιν καὶ καχέκταις καὶ σπασμώδεσιν καὶ νεφριτικοῖς, ἔτι τε τοῖς τὸν ἀνασάρκα προσαγορευόμενον ὕδερον ἔχουσιν.
beads.english: Some have also written that the fleshes of other animals benefit when eaten and when applied to the affected parts. One example is the flesh of the land hedgehog, dried, if it is drunk by those with elephantiasis, cachectics, those subject to spasms and nephritics, and further by those who have the dropsy called anasarca.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ ταῦτα ποιεῖν πέφυκεν, εἴη ἂν ἡ δύναμις αὐτῆς ἰσχυρῶς διαφορητική τε καὶ ξηραντικὴ, ὥσπερ καὶ ἡ τῆς σκελετευθείσης γαλῆς, ἥπερ οὖν ὀνίνησι τοὺς ἐπιληπτικοὺς πινομένη.
beads.english: If it is of a nature to do these things, its power would be strongly dispersing and drying, as is that of the dried weasel, which indeed benefits epileptics when drunk.

beads.greek: τῶν δὲ ταριχευθέντων αἰλούρων τὴν σάρκα λειωθεῖσαν ἐπιτιθεμένην ἐξάγειν σκόλοπάς φασιν, ὡς ἑλκτικὴν ἔχουσαν δύναμιν δηλονότι, τῶν δὲ μυάκων ἁρμόττειν ἕλκεσιν ὑπὸ κυνὸς δάκνοντος γεγονόσιν.
beads.english: They say that the flesh of salted cats, ground and applied, draws out splinters, evidently as having a drawing power. They also say that the flesh of mussels (myakes) suits ulcers caused by a biting dog.

beads.greek: ἐγὼ δ’ οὐδεμίαν ἐξαίρετον εὑρίσκω δύναμιν, ἧς δεῖται τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ἑλκῶν, ὥσπερ τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ λυττῶντος κυνὸς δακόντος γενόμενα.
beads.english: I, however, find no special power that ulcers of this kind require, as those produced by the bite of a rabid dog do.

beads.greek: καὶ ἡ τῶν κοχλιῶν δὲ σὰρξ κοπεῖσα πρότερον ἐν ὅλμῳ καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα λειωθεῖσα ξηραντικωτάτη γίνεται πάντων τῶν ὑγρότητα περιττὴν ἐχόντων μορίων, ὥστε καὶ τοῖς ὑδερικοῖς ἁρμόττειν.
beads.english: The flesh of snails too, first pounded in a mortar and afterwards triturated, becomes the most drying of all for parts having superfluous moisture, so that it suits the dropsical as well.

beads.greek: ἡ δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν ὑγρότης, μόνη καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ἄνευ τῆς σαρκὸς λαμβανομένη, καλεῖται ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν μύξα κοχλίου, μιγνυμένη δὲ λιβανωτῷ ἢ ἀλόῃ ἢ σμύρνῃ ἤ τισι τούτων ἢ πᾶσιν ἄχρι τοῦ κηρωτῆς πάχος ἔχειν, ἐχέκολλόν τε γίνεται φάρμακον καὶ ξηραίνει καλῶς τοὺς ὑποπύους μύξους τῶν ὤτων.
beads.english: The moisture from them, taken alone by itself without the flesh, is called by most people snail's mucus. Mixed with frankincense or aloe or myrrh, or some or all of these, until it has the thickness of a cerate, it becomes a glue-like drug and dries the purulent mucous discharges of the ears well.

beads.greek: ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἀνακόλλημα ξηραντικὸν τῶν εἰς ὀφθαλμοὺς ῥευμάτων, ἐπιτιθεμένη κατὰ τὸ μέτωπον.
beads.english: Applied on the forehead, it is also a drying adhesive application (anakollēma) against fluxes into the eyes.

beads.greek: ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ πρὸς σκόλοπας χρῶνται, λειοῦντες ὅλους μετὰ τῶν ὀστράκων, εἰσὶ δ’ οἳ καὶ πρὸς καταμηνίων ἐπίσχεσιν.
beads.english: Some also use the snails for splinters, triturating them whole with their shells, and there are some who use them for checking the menses.

beads.greek: αὐτὰς δὲ τὰς σάρκας μόνας κᾀγώ ποτε κατ’ ἀγρὸν ἐπὶ τραύματος ἅμα νεύρου τρώσει τε καὶ θλάσει γεγονότος ἐπέθηκα λειώσας, καὶ τό τε τραῦμα καλῶς ἐκολλήθη καὶ τὸ νεῦρον οὐκ ἐφλέγμηνε.
beads.english: The fleshes alone I myself once triturated and applied, in the country, to a wound that had occurred together with a wounding and crushing of a nerve. The wound was glued together well and the nerve did not become inflamed.

beads.greek: ἦν δὲ σκληρὸς καὶ ἀγροῖκος ἄνθρωπος, ἔμιξά γε μὴν λειουμέναις αὐταῖς ἄχνην ἀλεύ ρου, λαβὼν ἀπὸ τοῦ πλησιάζοντος τῇ μύλῃ τοίχου.
beads.english: The man was tough and rustic; I mixed with the fleshes, as they were being triturated, fine flour-dust, taking it from the wall next to the mill.

beads.greek: γεγράφασι δέ τινες τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν ἰατρῶν σμύρναν ἢ λιβανωτὸν μιγνύειν αὐτοῖς δεῖν ἐπὶ τῆς τοιαύτης χρήσεως, ἀλλ’ οὐδετέραν εἶχον τούτων ἔξωθεν τῆς πόλεως ἐπὶ τῆς ἀγροικίας.
beads.english: Some of the physicians before us have written that one ought to mix myrrh or frankincense with them for such a use, but I had neither of these, being outside the city on the country estate.

beads.greek: δύναιτο δ’ ἄν τις καὶ ῥητίνης φρικτῆς λείας μιγνύειν εἰ παρείη.
beads.english: One could also mix in ground roasted resin, if it is to hand.

beads.greek: ὁπόταν μέντοι πολὺ τῆς μύξης τῶν κοχλιῶν ἐθέλεις λαβεῖν μόνης, κατακέντησον αὐτῶν τὴν σάρκα γραφείῳ.
beads.english: Whenever you wish to obtain much of the snails' mucus by itself, prick their flesh with a stylus.

beads.greek: χρὴ δὲ μὴ πρὸ πολλῶν ἡμερῶν αὐτοὺς θηρεῦσαι, καταξηραίνονται γὰρ ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ.
beads.english: One must not catch them many days beforehand, for they dry out over time.

beads.greek: πρόσφατοι δ’ ὄντες πολὺ τῆς γλίσχρας ὑγρότητος ἔχουσιν, ἣν κατακεντούμενοι τῷ γραφείῳ προϊᾶσιν.
beads.english: When fresh they have much of the viscous moisture, which they emit when pricked with the stylus.

beads.greek: ἡ δ’ ὑγρότης αὕτη καὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς βλεφάροις τριχῶν παρὰ φύσιν ἀνακόλλημα γίνεται.
beads.english: This moisture also serves to glue back the hairs in the eyelids that are contrary to nature.

greek_sentences: Περὶ σαρκὸς ἐχίδνης.] Οὐχ ἅπασαι τῶν ζώων αἱ σάρκες ἄνθρωπον τρέφουσιν, ἀλλ’ ἐνίων εἰσὶ καὶ θανάσιμοι τῶν φαρμακωδῶν οὐδὲν ἧττον, ἃ καλοῦσι δηλητήρια, καὶ τῶν τρεφουσῶν δὲ ἡμᾶς σαρκῶν ἔνιαι μὲν αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον εἰσὶ τροφαὶ, τινὲς δὲ πρὸς τῷ τρέφειν ἔχουσι καὶ τὴν ὡς φαρμάκου δύναμιν, ἐπειδὴ κατὰ τὸ ξηραίνειν ἢ ὑγραίνειν καὶ θερμαίνειν ἢ ψύχειν, ἀλλοιοῦσι τὸ σῶμα.
τὰς γοῦν τῶν ἐχιδνῶν θερμαινούσας τε καὶ ξηραινούσας ἐναργῶς ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἀρτυομένας, ὥσπερ αἱ ἐγχέλεις ἐλαίῳ καὶ ἁλσὶ καὶ ἀνήθῳ καὶ πράσῳ καὶ ὕδατι δηλονότι μετὰ τοῦ συμμέτρου.
ὅτι δὲ καθαίρουσιν διὰ τοῦ δέρματος ἅπαν τὸ σῶμα γνῶναί σοι πάρεστι κᾀξ ὧν ἐπειράθην ἐγὼ ἔτι νέος γενόμενος ἐπὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας Ἀσίας, ὧν ἕκαστον ἐφεξῆς ἤδη δίειμι.

ἄνθρωπος νοσῶν τὸ καλούμενον πάθος ἐλέφαντα μέχρι μέν τινος ὁμοδίαιτος ἦν τοῖς συνήθεσιν, ἐπεὶ δ’ ἐκ τῆς πρὸς αὐτὸν κοινωνίας τε καὶ ὁμιλίας ἐκοινώνησαν μὲν ἔνιοι τοῦ πάθους, αὐτὸς δὲ δυσώδης ἦν ἤδη καὶ εἰδεχθὴς, καλύβην αὐτῷ πηξάμενοι πλησίον τῆς κώμης ἐπὶ χθαμαλοῦ τοῦ λόφου παρά τινι πηγῇ ἱδρύουσιν ἐν αὐτῇ τὸν ἄνθρωπον φέροντες τροφὰς αὐτῷ ἐφ’ ἡμέρας τοσαύτας ὅσον ἀποζῆν ἱκανῶς.
περὶ δὲ κυνὸς ἐπιτολὴν θερισταῖς πλησίον αὐτοῦ θερίζουσιν ἐκομίσθη τις οἶνος ἐν κεραμίῳ μάλ’ εὐώδης.

ὁ μὲν κομίσας ἐγγὺς τῶν θεριζόντων καταθεὶς ἐχωρίσθη· τοῖς δ’ ὡς ἧκεν ὁ καιρὸς τοῦ πίνειν, ἔθος μὲν ἦν αὐτοῖς ἐκχέουσι κρατῆρα μεθ’ ὕδατος συμμέτρου κεραννύναι τὸν οἶνον, ὡς δὲ ἀνελομένου νεανίσκου τὸ κεράμιον, ἐξαιροῦντά τε τὸν οἶνον εἰς τὸν κρατῆρα, συνεξέπεσεν ἔχιδνα νεκρά.

δείσαντες οὖν οἱ θερισταὶ μή τι πάθοιεν ἐκ τοῦ πόματος, αὐτοὶ μὲν ὕδατος ἔπιον, ὡς δ’ ἀπηλλάττοντο, χαρίζονται δῆθεν ὑπὸ φιλανθρωπίας τῷ τὸν ἐλέφαντα νοσοῦντι τὸν ὅλον οἶνον, ἄμεινον αὐτῷ κρίναντες εἶναι τεθνάναι μᾶλλον ἢ ζῇν τοιούτῳ.
ὁ δ’ ἐκ τούτου πίνων ὑγιὴς ἐγένετο θαυμαστόν τινα τρόπον.
ὅλον γὰρ αὐτοῦ τὸ τοῦ δέρματος ὀχθῶδες ἀπέπεσεν ὡς τῶν μαλακοστράκων ζώων τὸ σκέπασμα.
ὅσον δ’ ὑπόλοιπον ἦν ἔτι μαλακὸν ἱκανῶς ἐφαίνετο καθάπερ τὸ τῶν καράβων τε καὶ καρκίνων, ὅταν ἀποπέσῃ τὸ πέριξ ὄστρακον.
ἕτερον τοιοῦτον ἐξ ὁμοίας περιπτώσεως ἐγένετο κατὰ τὴν ἐν Ἀσίᾳ Μυσίαν, οὐ πόῤῥω τῆς ἡμετέρας πόλεως.
ἄνθρωπος ἐλέφαντι κάμνων ἐπὶ χρῆσιν ὥρμησεν ὑδάτων θερμῶν αὐτοφυῶν ὠφελείας ἐλπίδι.
παλλακὶς δ’ ἦν αὐτῷ δούλη νέα τε καὶ καλὴ πολλοὺς ἐραστὰς ἔχουσα, ταύτῃ καὶ ἄλλα μέν τινα τῶν κατὰ τὴν οἰκίαν, ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸ ταμεῖον ἐπίστευεν ὁ κάμνων.

ὡς δὲ καταχθέντων αὐτῶν, ἡνίκ’ ἐχρῆτο τοῖς ὕδασιν, ἐν οἰκίᾳ παρακείμενον ἐχούσῃ χωρίον αὐχμηρὸν ἐχιδνῶν μεστὸν, ἐμπεσοῦσά τις αὐτῶν εἰς οἴνου κεράμιον ἀμελῶς κείμενον ἐναπέθανεν, ἕρμαιον ἡγησαμένη τὸ κατὰ τύχην ἐκβὰν ἡ παλλακὴ τῷ δεσπότῃ τὸν ποτὸν ἐκ τούτου προσέφερεν.
ὁ δὲ πίνων αὐτὸ τῷ κατὰ τὴν καλύβην ὡσαύτως ὑγιάσθη.
δύο μὲν ἤδη σοι ταῦτα διδάγματα τῆς κατὰ τὴν περίπτωσιν πείρας, ἕτερον δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς τρίτον ἐξ ἡμετέρας μιμήσεως.

ἐπειδὴ γάρ τις νοσῶν τοῦτο τὸ νόσημα φιλοσοφώτερος ἢ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς ἐδυσχέραινέ τε δεινῶς καὶ τεθνάναι βέλτιον ἢ ζῇν ἔφασκεν εἶναι, διακειμένῳ οὕτως ἀθλίως ἐδήλωσα τὰς προειρημένας δύο περιπτώσεις αὐτῶν.

ὁ δ’ , αὐτός τε γὰρ ἦν ἔμπειρος οἰωνῶν ἐχρήσατό τε φίλῳ θαυμαστῶς κατορθοῦντι τὸ μάθημα, καθίσας ἐπ’ ὄρνισιν ἅμ’ ἐκείνῳ προὐτράπη ﻿ τε μιμήσασθαι τὰ διὰ τῆς πείρας ἐγνωσμένα καὶ πίνων οἶνον οὕτω φαρμαχθέντα λεπρώδης ἐγένετο.
χρόνῳ δ’ ὕστερον ἰασάμεθα καὶ τὴν λέπραν αὐτοῦ τοῖς συνήθεσι φαρμάκοις.
τέταρτος ἐπὶ τούτῳ τέχνην πεποιημένος ἐχίδνας ζώσας συλλαμβάνειν ἐν ἀρχῇ μὲν ἦν τοῦ πάθους ἐκείνου, προὔκειτο δ’ ἡμῖν ὅπως ἰαθῇ τάχιστα.
φλέβα τε οὖν αὐτοῦ τεμόντες καὶ καθήραντες φαρμάκῳ μέλαιναν κενοῦντι, χρήσασθαι ταῖς ἀγρευομέναις ἐχίδναις συνεβουλεύσαμεν, ἐν λοπάδι σκευάζοντι, καθάπερ τὰς ἐγχέλεις.
οὗτος μὲν οὖν οὕτως ἐθεραπεύθη, διαπνεύσαντος αὐτῷ τοῦ πάθους.

ἄλλος δέ τις ἀνὴρ πλούσιος οὐχ ἡμεδαπὸς οὗτός γε, ἀλλ’ ἐκ μέσης Θρᾴκης ἧκεν, ὀνείρατος προτρέψαντος αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ Πέργαμον, εἶτα τοῦ θεοῦ προστάξαντος ὄναρ αὐτῷ πίνειν τε τοῦ διὰ τῶν ἐχιδνῶν φαρμάκου καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν καὶ χρίειν ἔξωθεν τὸ σῶμα, μετέπεσεν τὸ πάθος οὐ μετὰ πολλὰς ἡμέρας εἰς λέπραν, ἐθεραπεύθη τε πάλιν οἷς ὁ θεὸς ἐκέλευεν φαρμάκοις καὶ τοῦτο τὸ νόσημα.
ἡ μὲν δὴ τῶν ἐχιδνῶν σὰρξ εἰς τοσοῦτον ἥκει τῆς ξηραντικῆς δυνάμεως· ἐπεὶ δ’ ἔνιοι τῶν φαγόντων αὐτὴν ἑάλωσαν δίψει σφοδροτάτῳ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο προσαγορεύουσι τὰς ἐχίδνας διψάδας.
εἰσὶ δ’ οἳ καὶ τοὺς δηχθέντας ὑπ’ αὐτῶν φασιν οὐκ ἐμπίπλασθαι πίνοντας, ἀλλὰ διαῤῥήγνυσθαι πρότερον ἢ παύσασθαι διψῶντας.

διὰ τοῦτο τῶν ἐν Ῥώμῃ τὰς ἐχίδνας θηρευόντων, οὓς ὀνομάζουσι Μαρσοὺς, ἐπυθόμην εἴ τι σημεῖον ἔχοιέν με διδάξαι διακριτικὸν ἑκατέρου τοῦ γένους τῶν ἐχιδνῶν· οἱ δ’ οὐδὲν ὅλως ἔφασαν εἶναι γένος ἐχιδνῶν διψάδων, ἀλλὰ τὰς παρὰ θαλάττῃ καὶ τόποις ἁλμυρίδα πολλὴν ἔχουσι διαιτωμένας ἁλμυρὰν ἴσχειν τὴν σάρκα, διὸ καὶ κατὰ Λιβύην πολλὰς γίγνεσθαι τοιαύτας, ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ δ’ οὐκ εἶναι διὰ τὴν ὑγρότητα τῆς χώρας.
ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἤκουσα τῶν Μαρσῶν λεγόντων, οὐ μὴν ἔχω βεβαίως εἰπεῖν εἴτ’ ἀληθεύσουσι τὸ σύμπαν εἴτε καὶ ψεύδονται κατά τι.
τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐν οἷς εἰρήκασι χωρίοις γίνεσθαί τινας ἐχίδνας ἁλυκὴν ἐχούσας τὴν σάρκα πιθανώτατον εἶναί μοι δοκεῖ.
συμμεταβαλλούσας γὰρ οἶδα ταῖς τροφαῖς τὰς τῶν ζώων σάρκας, οὐ μὴν ὡς οὐδέν ἐστι γένος ἐχιδνῶν διψάδων ἀποφήνασθαι δύναμαι.
τὸ δ’ οὖν ἀσφαλέστατόν ἐστι φυλάττεσθαι τὰς ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις χωρίοις ἐχίδνας θηρεύειν εἰς ἐδωδὴν ἢ φαρμάκου κατασκευὴν, ὁποῖόν ἐστι καὶ τουτὶ τὸ ἔνδοξον, ὃ καλοῦσιν ἅπαντες σχεδὸν ἰατροὶ θηριακήν.

ἐπεὶ δ’ ἔθος ἡμῖν ἐστιν, ὅταν τοὺς καλουμένους ἀρτίσκους θηριακοὺς σκευάζωμεν, ἀφαιρεῖν οὐ μόνον τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν οὐρὰν, ἐνενόησα πολλάκις εὐλόγως ἴσως μὲν τὴν κεφαλὴν ὅλην, διὰ τὸν ἐν τῷ στόματι περιεχόμενον ἰὸν, ἀλόγως δὲ τὴν οὐρὰν ἀφαιρεῖσθαι.
οὐδὲ γὰρ τοῦτ’ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, ὅτι διὰ τὰ περιττώματα τῆς τροφῆς τά θ’ ὑγρὰ καὶ τὰ ξηρὰ πρακτέον οὕτως ἐστίν.

ἀποκτείναντες γὰρ αὐτὰς, εἶτ’ ἐκδείραντές τε καὶ ἀναπτύξαντες, ἐξαιροῦμέν τε καὶ ἀποῤῥίπτομεν ἅπαντα τὰ ἔνδον, ὡς μόνην καταλείπεσθαι τὴν τῶν σαρκῶν οὐσίαν ἅμα ταῖς διαπεφυκυίαις αὐτῶν ἀρτηρίαις τε καὶ φλεψὶν, ἐλάχιστον ἐχούσαις ὄγκον ὡς πρὸς τὴν ὅλην σάρκα, καὶ μηδὲ φαινόμενον, ἐὰν μὴ πάνυ τις ἐπιμελῶς κατασκέψηται.
τοὺς μὲν οὖν ἀρτίσκους, οὓς δὴ καὶ θηριακοὺς ὀνομάζουσι, σκευάζομεν οὕτως.
κεκαθαρμένας αὐτὰς λαβόντες, εἶθ’ ἕψοντες ἐν ὕδατι, μέχρις ἂν ἀκριβῶς ἡμῖν εἶναι δόξωσιν ἑφθαί.
συνεμβάλλομεν δ’ εὐθέως ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἀνήθου τῷ ὕδατι καὶ μετὰ τὴν ἕψησιν ἀπὸ τῶν σαρκῶν διακρίνομεν τὰς ἀκάνθας, εἶτα μίγνυμεν ἄρτῳ λελειωμένῳ τὴν σάρκα.
τὸν δ’ ἄρτον τοῦτον οὐ τὸν ἐπιτυχόντα λαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἔνι μάλιστα καθαρώτατόν τε καὶ καλῶς ὠπτημένον ἐν κλιβάνῳ, συμμέτρων ἁλῶν ἔχοντα καὶ ζύμης.
προαναξηραίνομεν δὲ αὐτὸν ἐν οἴκῳ ξηρῷ καὶ ἀνίκμῳ, μέχρις ἂν οὕτω γένηται ξηρὸς ὡς ἐν ὅλμῳ κοπῆναι δύνασθαι.
οὐ μὴν κόπτοντές γε μίγνυμεν, ἀλλὰ διαβρέχοντες τῷ ὕδατι, καθὸ τὰς ἐχίδνας ἑψήσαμεν.
αὐτὴν δὲ τὴν σάρκα πρὶν μιγνύναι τῷ ἄρτῳ, τρίβομεν ἐν θυίᾳ τῶν μαγείρων, ἄχρις ἂν ἀκριβῶς γένηται λεία.
καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα μικροὺς ἀρτίσκους λεπτοὺς πλάσαντες, εἶτα ξηράναντες ἐν οἴκῳ θερμῷ καὶ ξηρῷ φυλάττομεν ἀποτιθέμενοι πάλιν ἐν οἴκῳ τοιούτῳ.
τούτους μὲν οὖν εἰσβάλλοντος τοῦ θέρους σκευάζομεν, ἡνίκα μάλιστα βελτίστη τῶν ἐχιδνῶν ἐστιν ἡ σάρξ.
χρώμεθα δ’ ὕστερον κόπτοντές τε καὶ διάττοντες, εἶτ’ αὖθις λειοῦντες ἀναμιγνύντες τε τοῖς ἐσκευασμένοις εἰς ἡδονὴν ἁλσὶν, ἐμβάλλομεν δ’ αὐτῶν καὶ τῇ θηριακῇ.

γίγνονται δὲ καὶ οἱ διὰ τῶν ὀπτηθεισῶν ἐχιδνῶν ἅλες ὑπὸ τὸν αὐτὸν καιρὸν εἶς χύτραν καινὴν ἐμβαλλόντων ἡμῶν τὰς ἐχίδνας ζώσας, ἅμα τοῖς ὑπεστορεσμένοις τε καὶ περικειμένοις αὐταῖς φαρμάκοις, ἃ λέγειν ἅπαντα νῦν οὐκ ἔστι τῆς ἐνεστώσης πραγματείας.
ἴσως γάρ τις ἡμῖν εὐλόγως ἐγκαλέσει καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀρτίσκων τῆς κατασκευῆς ὡς οὐκ ἐν καιρῷ διελθοῦσιν.
ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ἐπειδὴ φθάνει λελέχθαι, φυλαττέσθω, κᾂν δοκῇ μὴ πάνυ τι τῆς προκειμένης εἶναι πραγματείας ἴδια.
τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς κατὰ τὸ προσῆκον μέτρον λεγέσθω.
προσῆκον δ’ ἐστὶ περὶ τῆς καθόλου δυνάμεως ἀναμνῆσαι τὴν σάρκα τῶν ἐχιδνῶν, εἰπόντα εἶναι ξηραντικήν τε καὶ διαφορητικὴν ἰσχυρῶς, ἄμα τῷ θερμαίνειν μετρίως.
ἐπείγεται δ’, ὡς ἔοικεν, ἡ δύναμις αὐτῆς ἐπὶ τὸ δέρμα, διὰ τούτου κινοῦσα τὰ κατὰ τὸ σῶμα περιττώματα.

φθειρῶν τε οὖν πλῆθος οὐκ ὀλίγον γεννᾶται τοῖς ἔχουσι κακοχυμίαν ἐν τοῖς σώμασι δαψιλῆ καὶ τοῦ δέρματος ἀφίσταταί τε καὶ ἀποπίπτει καθάπερ τι λέπος ἡ ἐπιδερμὶς ὀνομαζομένη, καθ’ ἣν ἴσχονται μᾶλλον τῶν ﻿ εἰς τὸ δέρμα φερομένων χυμῶν οἱ παχεῖς καὶ γεώδεις, ὑφ’ ὧν αἵ τε ψῶραι καὶ αἱ λέπραι καὶ οἱ ἐλέφαντες γίνονται.
ταῦτα μὲν οὖν εἶχόν σοι λέγειν περὶ τῶν τῆς ἐχίδνης σαρκῶν, ἐφεξῆς δὲ πάλιν ἀναλήψομαι τὸν λόγον.
αἱ μὲν τῶν θερμοτέρων φύσει ζώων σάρκες οὐ μόνον τρέφουσιν ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ θερμαίνουσιν, αἱ δὲ τῶν ψυχροτέρων ψύχουσιν.
οὕτως δὲ καὶ αἱ μὲν τῶν ξηροτέρων ξηραίνουσιν, αἱ δὲ τῶν ὑγροτέρων ὑγραίνουσιν.

μεμνημένος οὖν ὧν ἔμαθες ἐν τοῖς περὶ κράσεων, ὅταν γνωρίσῃς τι τῶν ζώων εἶναι τῇ κράσει ξηρότερον, ὥσπερ εἰ τύχοι τὸν ἄγριον ὗν τοῦ ἡμέρου, γίνωσκε τούτου καὶ τὴν σάρκα ξηραντικωτέραν εἶναι καὶ κατὰ τὰς ἄλλας διαφορὰς τῶν κράσεων ὡσαύτως, οἷον ὅτι συὸς μὲν πρόβατον ξηρότερον, τούτου δ’ αἴξ, τούτου δὲ βοῦς, καὶ τούτου λέων.
οὕτω δὲ καὶ κατὰ θερμότητα λέων μὲν κυνὸς θερμότερος, κύων δὲ ταύρου, ταῦρος δὲ τοῦ τοὺς ὄρχεις ἐκτετμημένου βοός.
ἀνάλογον οὖν τῇ κατὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν ὑπεροχῇ τῶν ἄλλων ζώων καὶ αἱ σάρκες αὐτῶν διοίσουσιν.

καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ξηραίνειν μὲν ἐθέλων τὸ σῶμα τῶν ξηροτέρων τῇ κράσει ζώων δώσεις τὴν σάρκα, θερμαίνειν δὲ βουλόμενος τῶν θερμοτέρων, καὶ ψυχρότερον μὲν ἐπιχειρῶν ἐργάζεσθαι τῶν ψυχροτέρων, ὑγρότερον δὲ τῶν ὑγροτέρων.
οὐ σμικρὰ δὲ διαφορὰ τῶν σαρκῶν ἐστι κᾀν τῷ τεταριχεῦσθαί τινας αὐτῶν.
ὅλῳ γὰρ παντὶ διαλλάττουσιν, ὡς πολλάκις ὑγροτάτου τῇ κράσει ζώου ταριχευθεῖσαν σάρκα ξηραντικωτέραν εἶναι μακρῷ τῆς φύσεως ξηρᾶς.
ἀταριχεύτου καὶ ἡ ὀπτηθεῖσα δὲ ξηροτέρα τῆς ἑψηθείσης ἐστὶν ἐν ὕδατι.

ἔγραψαν δὲ καὶ ἄλλων ζώων ἔνιοι σάρκας ὠφελεῖν ἐσθιομένας τε καὶ κατὰ πεπονθότων μερῶν ἐπιτιθεμένας, οἷον τὴν τοῦ χερσαίου ἐχίνου σκελετευθεῖσαν, εἰ ποθείη ἐλεφαντιῶσιν καὶ καχέκταις καὶ σπασμώδεσιν καὶ νεφριτικοῖς, ἔτι τε τοῖς τὸν ἀνασάρκα προσαγορευόμενον ὕδερον ἔχουσιν.
εἰ δὲ ταῦτα ποιεῖν πέφυκεν, εἴη ἂν ἡ δύναμις αὐτῆς ἰσχυρῶς διαφορητική τε καὶ ξηραντικὴ, ὥσπερ καὶ ἡ τῆς σκελετευθείσης γαλῆς, ἥπερ οὖν ὀνίνησι τοὺς ἐπιληπτικοὺς πινομένη.
τῶν δὲ ταριχευθέντων αἰλούρων τὴν σάρκα λειωθεῖσαν ἐπιτιθεμένην ἐξάγειν σκόλοπάς φασιν, ὡς ἑλκτικὴν ἔχουσαν δύναμιν δηλονότι, τῶν δὲ μυάκων ἁρμόττειν ἕλκεσιν ὑπὸ κυνὸς δάκνοντος γεγονόσιν.
ἐγὼ δ’ οὐδεμίαν ἐξαίρετον εὑρίσκω δύναμιν, ἧς δεῖται τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ἑλκῶν, ὥσπερ τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ λυττῶντος κυνὸς δακόντος γενόμενα.
καὶ ἡ τῶν κοχλιῶν δὲ σὰρξ κοπεῖσα πρότερον ἐν ὅλμῳ καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα λειωθεῖσα ξηραντικωτάτη γίνεται πάντων τῶν ὑγρότητα περιττὴν ἐχόντων μορίων, ὥστε καὶ τοῖς ὑδερικοῖς ἁρμόττειν.

ἡ δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν ὑγρότης, μόνη καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ἄνευ τῆς σαρκὸς λαμβανομένη, καλεῖται ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν μύξα κοχλίου, μιγνυμένη δὲ λιβανωτῷ ἢ ἀλόῃ ἢ σμύρνῃ ἤ τισι τούτων ἢ πᾶσιν ἄχρι τοῦ κηρωτῆς πάχος ἔχειν, ἐχέκολλόν τε γίνεται φάρμακον καὶ ξηραίνει καλῶς τοὺς ὑποπύους μύξους τῶν ὤτων.
ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἀνακόλλημα ξηραντικὸν τῶν εἰς ὀφθαλμοὺς ῥευμάτων, ἐπιτιθεμένη κατὰ τὸ μέτωπον.
ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ πρὸς σκόλοπας χρῶνται, λειοῦντες ὅλους μετὰ τῶν ὀστράκων, εἰσὶ δ’ οἳ καὶ πρὸς καταμηνίων ἐπίσχεσιν.
αὐτὰς δὲ τὰς σάρκας μόνας κᾀγώ ποτε κατ’ ἀγρὸν ἐπὶ τραύματος ἅμα νεύρου τρώσει τε καὶ θλάσει γεγονότος ἐπέθηκα λειώσας, καὶ τό τε τραῦμα καλῶς ἐκολλήθη καὶ τὸ νεῦρον οὐκ ἐφλέγμηνε.
ἦν δὲ σκληρὸς καὶ ἀγροῖκος ἄνθρωπος, ἔμιξά γε μὴν λειουμέναις αὐταῖς ἄχνην ἀλεύ ρου, λαβὼν ἀπὸ τοῦ πλησιάζοντος τῇ μύλῃ τοίχου.
γεγράφασι δέ τινες τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν ἰατρῶν σμύρναν ἢ λιβανωτὸν μιγνύειν αὐτοῖς δεῖν ἐπὶ τῆς τοιαύτης χρήσεως, ἀλλ’ οὐδετέραν εἶχον τούτων ἔξωθεν τῆς πόλεως ἐπὶ τῆς ἀγροικίας.
δύναιτο δ’ ἄν τις καὶ ῥητίνης φρικτῆς λείας μιγνύειν εἰ παρείη.
ὁπόταν μέντοι πολὺ τῆς μύξης τῶν κοχλιῶν ἐθέλεις λαβεῖν μόνης, κατακέντησον αὐτῶν τὴν σάρκα γραφείῳ.
χρὴ δὲ μὴ πρὸ πολλῶν ἡμερῶν αὐτοὺς θηρεῦσαι, καταξηραίνονται γὰρ ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ.
πρόσφατοι δ’ ὄντες πολὺ τῆς γλίσχρας ὑγρότητος ἔχουσιν, ἣν κατακεντούμενοι τῷ γραφείῳ προϊᾶσιν.
ἡ δ’ ὑγρότης αὕτη καὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς βλεφάροις τριχῶν παρὰ φύσιν ἀνακόλλημα γίνεται.
english_sentences: On the flesh of the viper.] Not all the fleshes of animals nourish a human being.
Those of some are even deadly, no less than the drug-like substances which they call dēlētēria.

Of the fleshes that do nourish us, some are foods and only that, while others, besides nourishing, also have the power as of a drug, since they alter the body by drying or moistening and by heating or cooling.
At any rate, one can see plainly that the fleshes of vipers heat and dry when they are dressed as eels are, with oil, salts, dill, leek, and of course water in due measure.
That they cleanse the whole body through the skin you may learn also from what I experienced when I was still young, in our Asia;
I shall now go through each of these cases in order.
A man ill with the affection called elephas for a time shared the same regimen with his household.

But when, from association and intercourse with him, some of them came to share the affection, and he himself was by now foul-smelling and loathsome to look upon, they built a hut for him near the village on a low hill beside a spring and settled the man in it, bringing him each day as much food as was sufficient to live on.
About the rising of the Dog Star, some wine was brought in an earthenware jar to reapers who were reaping near him; it was very fragrant.
The man who brought it set it down near the reapers and went away.
When the time for drinking came, their custom was to pour the wine out into a mixing-bowl and mix it with a moderate amount of water.
But when a young man took up the jar and was drawing the wine out into the mixing-bowl, a dead viper fell out along with it.
The reapers, fearing that they might suffer some harm from the drink, drank water themselves.
As they were leaving, they made a present of the whole wine, ostensibly out of humanity, to the man ill with elephas, judging that it was better for him to be dead than to live in such a state.
He, drinking from it, became healthy in a wonderful manner.

For the whole lumpy part of his skin fell off like the covering of the soft-shelled animals, and what remained appeared quite soft, like that of crayfish and crabs when the shell around them has fallen off.
Another such case arose from a similar chance occurrence in Asian Mysia, not far from our city.
A man suffering from elephas set out to use naturally hot waters in the hope of benefit.
He had a concubine, a slave, young and beautiful and with many lovers.
To her the sick man entrusted various other affairs of the household, and in particular those of the storeroom.
While he was using the waters they lodged in a house that had next to it a dry, squalid plot full of vipers.
One of the vipers fell into a jar of wine that had been carelessly left lying and died in it.
The concubine, considering this chance event a windfall, offered her master his drink from that jar.
He, drinking it, was healed in the same way as the man in the hut.
These two lessons you now have from the experience of chance occurrence; and besides them a third, from our imitation.
For a man ill with this disease, more philosophical than the many, was terribly vexed by it and kept saying that it was better to be dead than to live.
Since he was in so wretched a condition, I disclosed to him the two chance occurrences just related.
He was himself experienced in bird-omens and had a friend wonderfully successful in this learning.
Taking his seat with that friend to observe the birds, he was urged on to imitate what had been learned through experience, and by drinking wine drugged in this way he became leprous.
Some time later we cured his lepra too with the usual drugs.
A fourth man after this, who had made it his craft to catch live vipers, was at the beginning of that affection, and our purpose was that he should be cured as quickly as possible.
So, having cut his vein and purged him with a drug that evacuates black bile, we advised him to make use of the vipers he caught, preparing them in a lopas as one does eels.
This man, then, was treated in this way, the affection being breathed out of him through transpiration.
Another man, a rich one, was not of our country but came from the middle of Thrace, a dream having urged him to Pergamum.
The god then commanded him in a dream to drink each day of the drug made from vipers and to anoint his body from outside.
Not many days later the affection changed into lepra, and this disease too was cured in its turn with the drugs the god ordered.
So great a degree of drying power, then, does the flesh of vipers attain.
But some of those who ate it were seized by a most violent thirst, and for this reason they call the vipers dipsades.
There are also some who say that those bitten by them, though they drink, are not filled, but burst before they cease to thirst.
For this reason I inquired of those in Rome who hunt vipers, whom they call Marsi, whether they had any sign to teach me that distinguishes the two kinds of vipers.
They said that there is no kind of dipsas vipers at all.

Rather, those that live by the sea and in places with much saline earth (halmyris) have briny flesh, and for this reason many such occur in Libya, but there are none in Italy because of the moistness of the land.
These things, then, I heard the Marsi say, but I cannot state with certainty whether they speak the truth in everything or are also lying in some respect.
That in the places they named some vipers occur which have salty flesh seems to me most plausible, for I know that the fleshes of animals change along with their foods.
But I cannot declare that there is no kind of dipsas vipers.
The safest course, then, is to take care not to hunt vipers in such places, whether for eating or for the preparation of a drug, such as this celebrated one which nearly all physicians call theriac.
Now it is our custom, when we prepare the so-called theriac pastilles (artiskoi), to remove not only their head but also the tail.
I have often reflected that the whole head is perhaps reasonably removed, on account of the venom contained in the mouth, but the tail unreasonably.
Nor can one say that it must be done so on account of the residues of the food, both the moist and the dry.

For having killed them, then flayed them and laid them open, we take out and throw away all the inner parts, so that only the substance of the fleshes is left, together with the arteries and veins that grow through it.
These have a very small bulk relative to the whole flesh and are not even visible unless one inspects very carefully.
The pastilles, then, which they also name theriac pastilles, we prepare thus.
Taking the vipers cleaned, we boil them in water until they seem to us to be exactly boiled.
We put dill into the water along with them right from the start.
After the boiling we separate the spines from the fleshes, and then mix the flesh with ground bread.
This bread we do not take at random, but the purest possible, well baked in an oven (klibanos), with a moderate amount of salt and leaven.
We dry it beforehand in a dry room without moisture, until it becomes dry enough to be pounded in a mortar.
Yet we do not mix it in by pounding it, but by soaking it in the water in which we boiled the vipers.
The flesh itself, before mixing it with the bread, we triturate in a cooks' mortar until it becomes exactly smooth.
After this, having moulded small thin pastilles, we dry them in a warm and dry room and keep them, storing them again in such a room.
These we prepare at the onset of summer, when the flesh of vipers is at its very best.
Later we use them by pounding and sifting them, then triturating them again and mixing them with salts prepared for pleasantness of taste; we also put them into the theriac.
At the same season the salts made from roasted vipers are also prepared.
We throw the vipers alive into a new pot together with the drugs strewn underneath and laid around them, all of which it is not the business of the present treatise to state now.
Indeed, someone might perhaps reasonably reproach us even over the preparation of the pastilles, as having gone through it out of place.
But since these things have already been said, let them stand, even if they seem not altogether proper to the present treatise.
What follows, let it be said in fitting measure.
It is fitting to recall, concerning the general power of the flesh of vipers, that it is drying and strongly dispersing, while heating moderately.
Its power, it seems, presses towards the skin, and through the skin it moves the residues in the body.
So a not inconsiderable multitude of lice is generated in those who have abundant kakochymia in their bodies.

Also, the so-called epidermis separates from the skin and falls off like a husk; it is in the epidermis that the thick and earthy humours, among those carried to the skin, are more held back, and by these psōrai, leprai and elephantes arise.
This, then, is what I had to tell you about the fleshes of the viper; next I shall take up the account again.
The fleshes of animals that are hotter by nature not only nourish us but also heat, while those of colder animals cool.
In the same way, those of drier animals dry, and those of moister animals moisten.
Remember, then, what you learned in the work On Mixtures.
When you recognise that some animal is drier in mixture, as for instance the wild boar than the domestic pig, know that its flesh too is more drying.
The same holds for the other differences of mixtures: for example, the sheep is drier than the pig, the goat than the sheep, the ox than the goat, and the lion than the ox.
So too in respect of heat, the lion is hotter than the dog, the dog than the bull, and the bull than the ox whose testicles have been cut out.
In proportion, then, to their excess in mixture over the other animals, their fleshes will also differ.

For this reason, when you wish to dry the body, you will give the flesh of animals drier in mixture; when you want to heat it, that of hotter ones; when you undertake to make it colder, that of colder ones; and when moister, that of moister ones.
No small difference among the fleshes lies also in some of them having been salted.
For they differ altogether, so that often the salted flesh of an animal most moist in mixture is far more drying than the unsalted flesh of one dry by nature.
And the roasted flesh is drier than that boiled in water.
Some have also written that the fleshes of other animals benefit when eaten and when applied to the affected parts.

One example is the flesh of the land hedgehog, dried, if it is drunk by those with elephantiasis, cachectics, those subject to spasms and nephritics, and further by those who have the dropsy called anasarca.
If it is of a nature to do these things, its power would be strongly dispersing and drying, as is that of the dried weasel, which indeed benefits epileptics when drunk.
They say that the flesh of salted cats, ground and applied, draws out splinters, evidently as having a drawing power.
They also say that the flesh of mussels (myakes) suits ulcers caused by a biting dog.
I, however, find no special power that ulcers of this kind require, as those produced by the bite of a rabid dog do.
The flesh of snails too, first pounded in a mortar and afterwards triturated, becomes the most drying of all for parts having superfluous moisture, so that it suits the dropsical as well.
The moisture from them, taken alone by itself without the flesh, is called by most people snail's mucus.
Mixed with frankincense or aloe or myrrh, or some or all of these, until it has the thickness of a cerate, it becomes a glue-like drug and dries the purulent mucous discharges of the ears well.
Applied on the forehead, it is also a drying adhesive application (anakollēma) against fluxes into the eyes.
Some also use the snails for splinters, triturating them whole with their shells, and there are some who use them for checking the menses.
The fleshes alone I myself once triturated and applied, in the country, to a wound that had occurred together with a wounding and crushing of a nerve.
The wound was glued together well and the nerve did not become inflamed.
The man was tough and rustic;
I mixed with the fleshes, as they were being triturated, fine flour-dust, taking it from the wall next to the mill.
Some of the physicians before us have written that one ought to mix myrrh or frankincense with them for such a use, but I had neither of these, being outside the city on the country estate.
One could also mix in ground roasted resin, if it is to hand.
Whenever you wish to obtain much of the snails' mucus by itself, prick their flesh with a stylus.
One must not catch them many days beforehand, for they dry out over time.
When fresh they have much of the viscous moisture, which they emit when pricked with the stylus.
This moisture also serves to glue back the hairs in the eyelids that are contrary to nature.

beads.greek: Περὶ πιμελῆς καὶ στέατος.] Πιμελὴ καὶ στέαρ.
beads.english: On fat and suet.] Fat (pimelē) and suet (stear).

beads.greek: κοινότατα καὶ ταῦτα τῶν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις μορίων ἐστί.
beads.english: These too are among the commonest of the parts in animals.

beads.greek: τὰ γὰρ εὐτροφοῦντα πάντα πιμελὴν ἢ στέαρ ἴσχει, τὰ δὲ ἰσχνὰ καὶ ἄτροφα πολλάκις μὲν οὐδ’ ὅλως ἔχειν φαίνεται, πολλάκις δ’ οὕτως ὀλίγην τε καὶ ξηρὰν, ὡς δύσχρηστον εἶναι.
beads.english: For all well-nourished animals have fat or suet, whereas lean and ill-nourished ones often appear to have none at all, and often have so little, and that so dry, that it is hard to use.

beads.greek: διαφέρει δὲ πιμελῆς στέαρ τῷ πάχει, διὸ καὶ τοῖς γεωδεστέραν ἔχουσιν τὴν ὅλην φύσιν ζώοις τὸ στέαρ γίνεται καθάπερ τοῖς ὑγροτέραν ἡ πιμελή.
beads.english: Suet differs from fat in thickness; for this reason suet arises in animals whose whole nature is more earthy, just as fat does in those whose nature is more moist.

beads.greek: διὰ τοῦτο τοιγαροῦν ἡ μὲν πιμελὴ τήκεται ῥαδίως ὑπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς, οὐ ῥᾳδίως δὲ πήγνυται τακεῖσα. τὸ δὲ στέαρ οὔτε τήκεται ῥᾳδίως, κᾂν τακῇ, πήγνυται τάχιστα καὶ φαίνεται πολὺ σκληρότερον τῆς πιμελῆς.
beads.english: For this very reason, then, fat melts easily under fire, but once melted does not easily congeal; suet, by contrast, does not melt easily, and if it is melted it congeals very quickly and appears much harder than fat.

beads.greek: ὗς μὲν οὖν εὐτροφῶν πιμελὴν πλείστην ἔχει διὰ τὴν φυσικὴν τῆς κράσεως ὑγρότητα, βόες δὲ καὶ αἶγες ὅσα τε ἄλλα κερασφόρα διὰ τὴν ξηρότητα τὸ στέαρ πλεῖστον γεννᾷ.
beads.english: The pig, then, when well nourished, has a very great deal of fat on account of the natural moistness of its mixture, whereas oxen and goats and all other horned animals produce suet in greatest quantity on account of their dryness.

beads.greek: σὺ δ’ εἰ βούλει τὴν ἐλαιώδη καὶ λιπαρὰν οὐσίαν ἅπασαν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις κάλει στέαρ, ὥσπερ οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἰατρῶν. ἔξεστι δέ σοι καὶ πιμελὴν ὀνομάζειν ἅπαν τοῦτο τὸ γένος.
beads.english: You may, if you wish, call the whole oleaginous and oily substance in animals suet, as most physicians do; and you may also name this whole kind fat.

beads.greek: οὐ μὴν ἔξεστί γέ σοι βουλομένῳ μὴ ψεύδεσθαι τὸ στέαρ τῶν αἰγῶν ὑγρότερον εἶναι φάναι τοῦ τῶν ὑῶν.
beads.english: You may not, however, if you wish not to speak falsely, say that the suet of goats is moister than that of pigs.

beads.greek: ὑγρότατον γὰρ τοῦτο σχεδὸν ἁπάντων τῶν ἄλλων ἐστὶ, καὶ ﻿ διὰ τοῦτο κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν ἐγγὺς ἐλαίου τὴν δύναμιν, μαλακτικώτερόν γε μὴν ἐλαίου καὶ πεπτικώτερόν ἐστι.
beads.english: For the latter is the moistest of nearly all the others, and for this reason in its action it is close to oil in power, though it is more softening than oil and more concoctive.

beads.greek: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τοῖς πρὸς φλεγμονὰς ἁρμόττουσιν καταπλάσμασι μίγνυται.
beads.english: And for this reason it is mixed into the poultices suited to inflammations.

beads.greek: τοῖς δὲ δακνομένοις τὰ κατὰ τὸ ἀπευθυσμένον ἢ τὸ κῶλον ἐνίεμεν αἴγειον μᾶλλον ἢ ὕειον στέαρ, οὐχ ὅτι μᾶλλον ἀμβλυτικόν ἐστι δριμύτητος, ὅσον γὰρ ἐπὶ τῇ φύσει μᾶλλον ἀμβλύνει τὸ ὕειον καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μίγνυται καὶ τοῖς ἕλκη θεραπεύουσι φαρμάκοις, οἷόν πέρ ἐστι καὶ τὸ καλούμενον πάρυγρον. ἀλλ’ ὅτι τὸ μὲν αἴγειον πήγνυται ῥᾳδίως διὰ πάχος, ἀποῤῥεῖ δὲ τὸ ὕειον ὁμοίως τῷ ἐλαίῳ διὰ τοῦτ’ ἐνίεμεν αὐτὸ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τῶν δυσεντερικῶν τε καὶ τεινεσμωδῶν, ὅταν παρηγορῆσαι τὴν δῆξιν αὐτῶν βουληθῶμεν.
beads.english: But for those who are bitten in the region of the rectum or the colon we inject goat's rather than pig's suet, not because it is more blunting of pungency (for, so far as its nature goes, pig's suet blunts more, and for this reason it is also mixed into drugs that treat ulcers, such as the one called parygron), but because goat's suet congeals easily on account of its thickness, whereas pig's flows away just like oil; for this reason we inject the former rather in dysenteric and tenesmic patients, when we wish to soothe their biting.

beads.greek: καὶ διὰ λεπτομέρειαν δ’ ἔνια μᾶλλον ἀμβλύνει δριμύτητας, ὅταν ἐν τῷ βάθει τῶν δακνομένων σωμάτων τὸ λυποῦν ᾖ.
beads.english: Some things also blunt pungencies more on account of fineness of particles, when what is giving pain lies in the depth of the bodies that are being bitten.

beads.greek: ἧττον μὲν γὰρ τὸ παχυμερὲς, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸ λεπτομερὲς ὅλα διεξέρχεται τὰ σώματα καὶ πᾶσι κεράννυται τοῖς δάκνουσιν ἰχῶρσιν αὐτό.
beads.english: For the coarse-particled passes less, and the fine-particled more, through whole bodies, and mixes itself with all the biting ichors.

beads.greek: κατὰ τοῦτο γοῦν καὶ τὸ χήνειον στέαρ τὰ κατὰ βάθος τῶν σωμάτων δάκνοντα μᾶλλον ἀμβλύνει.
beads.english: In this respect, at any rate, goose suet blunts more effectively what bites in the depth of bodies.

beads.greek: ἔστι δὲ καὶ θερμότερον τοῦ ὑείου.
beads.english: It is also hotter than pig's.

beads.greek: μεταξύ γε μὴν αὐτῶν ἐστι τὸ τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων, θερμότερον δ’ ἀεὶ καὶ ξηρότερον τὸ τῶν ἀῤῥένων ζώων ἐστίν.
beads.english: Between them lies that of cocks; and that of male animals is always hotter and drier.

beads.greek: αὐτῶν δὲ τούτων τὸ τῶν ἐκτεμνομένων τοὺς ὄρχεις ἧττον θερμόν τε καὶ ξηρόν. ὁμοιοῦται γὰρ ἀεὶ τὸ εὐνουχισθὲν ἄῤῥεν τοῖς ὁμογενέσι θήλεσι.
beads.english: Among these themselves, that of those whose testicles are excised is less hot and dry; for the castrated male always comes to resemble the females of the same kind.

beads.greek: κεφάλαιον δ’ ἐστὶ τοῦ λόγου τόδε κοινὸν, οὗ μεμνῆσθαι χρὴ, τὸ κατὰ τὴν τῶν ζώων κρᾶσιν ἀεὶ τὰς διαφορὰς γίνεσθαι τῆς ἐν αὐτοῖς πιμελῆς ἢ στέατος ἢ ὅπως ἂν ὀνομάζειν ἐθέλῃς ὅλον τὸ γένος τοῦτο τοῦ κατὰ τὰ ζῶα σώματος ἐλαιώδους τε καὶ λιπαροῦ.
beads.english: The general heading of the account, which must be remembered, is this: that the differences of the fat or suet in animals (or however you wish to name this whole kind of oleaginous and oily body in animals) always arise according to the mixture of the animals.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ὗς ἀπολείπεται κατὰ θερμότητά τε καὶ ξηρότητα σχεδὸν ἁπάντων τῶν τετραπόδων ζώων, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ πιμελὴν ἧττόν τε θερμὴν ἔχει καὶ μᾶλλον ὑγράν.
beads.english: Since, then, the pig falls short in heat and dryness of nearly all four-footed animals, for this reason it also has fat that is both less hot and more moist.

beads.greek: ἁπάσης μὲν οὖν πιμελῆς δύναμίς ἐστιν ὑγραντική τε καὶ θερμαντικὴ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων σωμάτων. τούτου γὰρ μεμνῆσθαι χρὴ διὰ παντὸς, εἰρημένου κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆσδε τῆς πραγματείας· αἱ δὲ καθ’ ἕκαστον αὐτῶν διαφοραὶ κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττόν εἰσιν.
beads.english: Now the power of all fat is moistening and heating of human bodies; for this must be remembered throughout, having been stated at the beginning of this treatise; and the differences in each of them are matters of more and less.

beads.greek: τοῦ μὲν γὰρ ὑὸς ὡς πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἡ πιμελὴ τὸ μὲν ὑγραίνειν ἔχει δαψιλῶς, τὸ θερμαίνειν δ’ οὐχ ὁμοίως ὥσπερ τοὔλαιον, ἀλλ’ ἔστι κατὰ τὴν ἐν ἡμῖν θερμότητα καὶ ἡ τοῦ λίπους τῶν ὑῶν.
beads.english: For the fat of the pig, relative to us, has moistening in abundance, but heating not in the same way as oil; rather, the fat (lipos) of pigs is on a level with the heat in us.

beads.greek: ἡ δὲ τῶν ταύρων πολὺ θερμοτέρα καὶ ξηροτέρα τῆς τῶν ὑῶν, μεμνημένων ἡμῶν πάλιν κἀνταῦθα τὸ μὲν ἄῤῥεν τοῦ θήλεος ἀεὶ ξηρότερον εἶναι καὶ θερμότερον, τὸ δ’ εὐνουχισθὲν ἄῤῥεν ὁμοιοῦσθαι τῷ θήλει, καθάπερ γε καὶ τὸ νέον ἅπαν. αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν νέων τὸ θῆλυ τοῦ ἄῤῥενος ὑγρότερόν τε εἶναι καὶ ἧττον θερμόν.
beads.english: That of bulls is much hotter and drier than that of pigs, we again remembering here too that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the castrated male resembles the female, as indeed does everything young; and that among the young themselves the female is moister and less hot than the male.

beads.greek: οὕτως οὖν καὶ τὸ μόσχειον στέαρ ἀπολείπεται τοῦ τῶν ταύρων θερμότητί τε καὶ ξηρότητι καὶ τὸ τῶν ἐρίφων τοῦ τῶν αἰγῶν, ἀπολείπεται δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν αἰγῶν τοῦ τῶν τράγων, αὐτῶν δὴ πάλιν τὸ τῶν ταύρων τοῦ τῶν λεόντων· διαφορητικώτατον γὰρ ἐκεῖνο σχεδὸν ἁπάντων τῶν ἐν τοῖς τετράποσι.
beads.english: Thus calf's suet falls short of that of bulls in heat and dryness, and that of kids of that of goats, and that of goats falls short of that of he-goats, and again that of bulls in turn falls short of that of lions; for that is the most dispersing of nearly all those in quadrupeds.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ καὶ θερμότατον αὐτῶν ἐστι καὶ λεπτομερέστατον, ὥστε εἰ μίξαις αὐτὸ τοῖς πρὸς ἕλκη καὶ φλεγμονὰς ἁρμόττουσι φαρμάκοις, οὐ μόνον οὐδὲν ὀνήσεις, ἀλλὰ καὶ βλάψεις δριμύτερον τοῦ προσήκοντος ἐργασάμενος.
beads.english: For it is also the hottest of them and the most fine-particled, so that if you mix it into the drugs suited to ulcers and inflammations, you will not only do no good but will even do harm, having made the drug more pungent than is fitting.

beads.greek: ὄγκοις δὲ χρονίοις ἐσκληρυσμένοις καὶ νεύρων ἀγκύλαις καὶ ἁπλῶς ὅσα σκιῤῥώδη, προσφορώτατόν ἐστιν ἐφ’ ὧν ἀπρακτότατον φαίνεται τὸ τῶν ὑῶν.
beads.english: But for chronic hardened swellings, contractures (ankylai) of sinews, and in short whatever is scirrhous, it is most suitable, in cases in which that of pigs appears most ineffective.

beads.greek: τὸ δὲ τῶν ταύρων ἶσόν πως ἑκατέρου διέστηκεν, ὅσῳ θερμότερόν τέ ἐστι καὶ ξηρότερον τοῦ τῶν ὑῶν, τοσούτῳ καὶ τοῦ τῶν λεόντων ἀπολειπόμενον.
beads.english: That of bulls stands roughly equally distant from each, being as much hotter and drier than that of pigs as it falls short of that of lions.

beads.greek: ὡς ἂν οὖν ἐν τῷ μέσῳ τεταγμένον, εἰκότως ἑκατέρῳ τῷ γένει μίγνυται τῶν φαρμάκων, τοῖς τε τὰ σκιῤῥώδη θεραπεύουσι. καὶ τοῖς τὰ φλεγμαίνοντα πέπτουσιν, ὁποῖόν ἐστιν τὸ τετραφάρμακον ὀνομαζόμενον ἐκ κηροῦ καὶ ῥητίνης καὶ πίττης καὶ στέατος συγκειμένου.
beads.english: As being placed in the middle, then, it is reasonably mixed into each kind of drug, both those that treat scirrhous conditions and those that concoct inflamed parts, such as the one called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax, resin, pitch and suet.

beads.greek: εἰς γάρ τοι τοῦτο, κᾂν ταύρειον βάλῃς κᾂν μόσχειον κᾂν τράγειον κᾂν αἴγειον κᾂν ὕειον, ἐκπυπτικόν τε καὶ πεπτικὸν ἐργάσῃ φάρμακον.
beads.english: For into this, whether you put bull's or calf's or he-goat's or goat's or pig's, you will make a suppurative and concoctive drug.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν ὕειον ἐμβληθὲν ἐπὶ παίδων ἁρμόζει καὶ γυναικῶν καὶ συνελόντι φάναι τῶν ἁπαλοσάρκων, τὸ δὲ τοῦ ταύρου σκαπανεῦσι καὶ θερισταῖς καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς σκληρὰς ἔχουσι σάρκας ἢ διὰ τὴν φυσικὴν κρᾶσιν ἢ διὰ τὴν ἰδέαν τοῦ βίου χρήσιμον ὑπάρχει.
beads.english: But pig's, when put in, suits children and women and, in a word, the soft-fleshed, while bull's is useful for diggers, reapers and all who have hard flesh, whether through their natural mixture or through the kind of life they lead.

beads.greek: χρονίζον δ’ ἅπαν στέαρ ἑαυτοῦ γίνεται θερμότερόν τε καὶ λεπτομερέστερον, ὥστε καὶ διαφορητικώτερον.
beads.english: All suet, as it ages, becomes hotter and more fine-particled than it was, and so also more dispersing.

beads.greek: ὑπάρχει δὲ τοῦτο σχεδὸν ἅπασι τοῖς χρονίζουσιν, ὅσα γε μὴ φθάνει σαπῆναι.
beads.english: This holds for nearly all things that age, at least those that do not rot first.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ οἶνος καὶ μέλι καὶ ὄξος καὶ τυρὸς καὶ βούτυρον καὶ οἴσυπος ἔλαιόν τε πᾶν, εἴτε σχίνινον εἴτε κίκινον εἴτε ῥαφάνινον εἴτ’ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐλαιῶν εἴη, χρονίζοντα λεπτότερά τε καὶ λεπτομερέστερα γίνεται καὶ διὰ τοῦτο δριμύτερά τε γευομένοις φαίνεται διαφορητικώτερόν τε χρωμένοις, ἐπὶ τῶν σκληρυνομένων τε καὶ δυσλύτων ἁπάντων παθῶν.
beads.english: For wine, honey, vinegar, cheese, butter and oesypum, and every oil, whether mastic oil or castor oil or radish oil or the very oil from olives, become thinner and more fine-particled as they age, and for this reason appear more pungent to those who taste them and more dispersing to those who use them, in all hardened and hard-to-resolve affections.

beads.greek: ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν εἴρηκα δριμύτερον γευομένοις φαίνεσθαι.
beads.english: I, then, have said that they appear more pungent to those who taste them.

beads.greek: τινὲς δὲ τῶν διαφθειρόντων τὰ σημαινόμενα τῶν ὀνομάτων οὐ δριμέα καλοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ στύφοντα τὰ τοιαῦτα πάντα, μέχρι τοῦ πεπέρεως, ὡς οὐδὲν διαφέρον ἢ στῦφον εἰπεῖν ἢ δριμύ.
beads.english: But some of those who corrupt the meanings of words call all such things not pungent but astringent, even down to pepper, as if it made no difference whether one says astringent or pungent.

beads.greek: καὶ εἰ αὖθις αὐτοὺς ἔροιο περί τε κηκίδων καὶ μύρτων καὶ μεσπίλων καὶ σιδίων ῥοιᾶς, ὀμφακίου τε καὶ ῥοῦ, καὶ ταῦτα στύφειν φασὶ, καίτοι γε ἐναντιωτάτην αἴσθησιν ἔχομεν ἐπ’ αὐτῶν τῆς γινομένης ἡμῖν ἀπὸ πεπέρεως καὶ πυρέθρου καὶ νάπυος, εὐφορβίου τε καὶ κρομμύου καὶ σκορόδου καὶ ἀδάρκης.
beads.english: And if you ask them in turn about oak-galls, myrtles, medlars, pomegranate rinds, omphakion and sumach, they say that these too are astringent, although the perception we have from them is the most opposite to that which arises in us from pepper, pyrethron, mustard, euphorbium, onion, garlic and adarce.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν οὖν ὡς τὸ τῆς στύψεως ὄνομα κοινὸν ἐπιφέρουσιν, κατ’ ἀμφοτέρων τῶν γιγνομένων ἡμῖν ἐν τῇ γεύσει παθῶν, οὕτω καὶ αὐτὰ τὰ ﻿ πάθη μίαν ἔχειν οἴονται φύσιν, ἀλλ’ ὅτι μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώπους αὐτοὺς εἶναι νομιστέον ἰδίας αἰσθήσεις ἔχοντας μόνους.
beads.english: If, then, just as they apply the name of astringency in common to both of the affections arising in us in taste, so too they think that the affections themselves have a single nature, they must be considered anything rather than human beings, as alone possessing senses peculiar to themselves.

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ ὄμφακα μὲν καὶ ῥοῦν καὶ κηκῖδα βαλαύστιόν τε καὶ ὑποκυστίδα, συνάγειν τε καὶ σφίγγειν ἡμῶν ὁμολογοῦσι τὴν οὐσίαν, διακρίνειν τε καὶ δάκνειν καὶ διεξέρχεσθαι τὸ πέπερι καὶ νᾶπυ καὶ πύρεθρον, ἀκύρως μὲν ὀνομάζουσι στύφοντα τὰ δάκνοντα καὶ θερμαίνοντα, τῆς γνώσεως μέντοι τῶν φαρμάκων αὐτῶν οὐχ ἡμαρτήκασιν.
beads.english: But if they agree that unripe grape, sumach, oak-gall, balaustion and hypocistis draw together and constrict our substance, while pepper, mustard and pyrethron separate, bite and pass through it, then they improperly name the biting and heating things astringent, but they have not erred in their knowledge of the drugs themselves.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ δεῖ στοχασάμενον εἰπεῖν πότερον ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασιν ἢ ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι σφάλλονται, φαίην ἂν ἔγωγε μᾶλλον ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασιν ἐσφάλθαι τοὺς ἄνδρας, καὶ μάλιστα τοὺς ἀήθεις Ἑλλάδος φωνῆς, οἷός ἐστιν ὁ Ἀναζαρβεὺς Διοσκορίδης, πολλὰ μὲν καλῶς εἴρηκε τῶν περὶ τῆς ἰατρικῆς ὕλης ἱστορουμένων, ἀγνοῶν δὲ τὰ σημαινόμενα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ὀνομάτων.
beads.english: If one must say by conjecture whether they err in the names or in the things, I for my part would say that these men have erred rather in the names, and especially those unaccustomed to the Greek tongue, such as Dioscorides of Anazarbus, who has said many things well among the matters recorded concerning medical material, but is ignorant of the meanings of Greek words.

beads.greek: οὗτος οὖν, ὅταν λέγει στυπτικώτερον στέαρ εἶναι τὸ τῶν αἰγῶν τοῦ τῶν ὑῶν, εἰ μὲν οὖν τὸ δριμύτερον διὰ τοῦ στυπτικωτέρου βούλεται δηλῶσαι, ἐκδεξόμεθα τὸν λόγον ὡς ἀληθῆ· εἰ δὲ τὸ τοιαύτην ἔχον ποιότητά τε καὶ δύναμιν, οἷον ῥοῦς καὶ ῥῆον ὑπόκυστίς τε καὶ βαλαύστιον, οὐκ ἀληθῆ φήσομεν εἶναι τὸν λόγον.
beads.english: When this man, then, says that the suet of goats is more astringent than that of pigs, if by 'more astringent' he wishes to indicate 'more pungent', we shall accept the statement as true; but if he means what has the kind of quality and power that sumach and rhēon, hypocistis and balaustion have, we shall say that the statement is not true.

beads.greek: ἐπειδὴ δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἐχιδνῶν στέαρ, ὅταν ἐκ ῥιζῶν τις ἀνασπάσας τὰς ἐν ταῖς μασχάλαις τρίχας ἐπαλείφῃ, φασὶ μὴ καὶ ταύτας φύεσθαι, κάλλιον ἔδοξέ μοι καὶ τούτου πειραθῆναι, καὶ πράξας ὡς ἐκέλευσαν εὗρον ψευδομένους αὐτοὺς, ὥσπερ καὶ ὅτι τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν ὑποχύσεων ἰᾶται.
beads.english: Since they also say that the suet of vipers, when someone plucks out the hairs in the armpits by the roots and anoints the place, prevents these from growing again, I thought it better to test this too, and having done as they bade I found them to be lying, as also in the claim that it cures the beginnings of hypochyses.

beads.greek: τὸ δὲ τῶν ἄρκτων στέαρ ἀλωπεκίαις ἁρμόττείν ἀληθῶς ἔγραψαν, ἔχομεν δ’ αὐτοῦ δοκιμώτερα φάρμακα πρὸς τὸ πάθος.
beads.english: That the suet of bears suits alopecias they wrote truly, but we have more approved drugs than it for the affection.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ τό γε μὴν τῶν ἀλωπέκων ὅταν ὠταλγίας φῶσι θεραπεύειν, ἄνευ τοῦ διορίσασθαι ποίας λέγουσιν ὠταλγίας, ὡς οὐδὲ γινώσκουσιν διηρθρωμένως αὐτοῖς ἃ λέγουσιν, οὐδ’ ὅλως χρὴ προσέχειν τὸν νοῦν.
beads.english: As for that of foxes, however, when they say that it treats earaches without distinguishing what sort of earaches they mean, as men who do not even know articulately what they are saying, one should not pay any attention to them at all.

beads.greek: ἄλλοι δὲ ἰχθύων ἐπαινοῦσι στέαρ, ὡς πρὸς τὰς ὑποχύσεις ἢ ὅπερ ἂν ἐθέλωσι πάθος ὀνομάζειν.
beads.english: Others praise the suet of fishes, as being for hypochyses or whatever affection they wish to name.

beads.greek: ἕτεροι δ’ οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἰχθύων, ἀλλὰ ποταμίων γράφουσιν, ἄλλοι δὲ μᾶλλον θαλαττίων, ἵνα δοκῶσί τι πλέον ἐπίστασθαι τῶν πολλῶν.
beads.english: Others again write not simply of fishes, but of river fishes, and others rather of sea fishes, so that they may seem to know something more than the many.

greek_sentences: Περὶ πιμελῆς καὶ στέατος.] Πιμελὴ καὶ στέαρ.
κοινότατα καὶ ταῦτα τῶν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις μορίων ἐστί.
τὰ γὰρ εὐτροφοῦντα πάντα πιμελὴν ἢ στέαρ ἴσχει, τὰ δὲ ἰσχνὰ καὶ ἄτροφα πολλάκις μὲν οὐδ’ ὅλως ἔχειν φαίνεται, πολλάκις δ’ οὕτως ὀλίγην τε καὶ ξηρὰν, ὡς δύσχρηστον εἶναι.
διαφέρει δὲ πιμελῆς στέαρ τῷ πάχει, διὸ καὶ τοῖς γεωδεστέραν ἔχουσιν τὴν ὅλην φύσιν ζώοις τὸ στέαρ γίνεται καθάπερ τοῖς ὑγροτέραν ἡ πιμελή.
διὰ τοῦτο τοιγαροῦν ἡ μὲν πιμελὴ τήκεται ῥαδίως ὑπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς, οὐ ῥᾳδίως δὲ πήγνυται τακεῖσα.
τὸ δὲ στέαρ οὔτε τήκεται ῥᾳδίως, κᾂν τακῇ, πήγνυται τάχιστα καὶ φαίνεται πολὺ σκληρότερον τῆς πιμελῆς.
ὗς μὲν οὖν εὐτροφῶν πιμελὴν πλείστην ἔχει διὰ τὴν φυσικὴν τῆς κράσεως ὑγρότητα, βόες δὲ καὶ αἶγες ὅσα τε ἄλλα κερασφόρα διὰ τὴν ξηρότητα τὸ στέαρ πλεῖστον γεννᾷ.
σὺ δ’ εἰ βούλει τὴν ἐλαιώδη καὶ λιπαρὰν οὐσίαν ἅπασαν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις κάλει στέαρ, ὥσπερ οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἰατρῶν.
ἔξεστι δέ σοι καὶ πιμελὴν ὀνομάζειν ἅπαν τοῦτο τὸ γένος.
οὐ μὴν ἔξεστί γέ σοι βουλομένῳ μὴ ψεύδεσθαι τὸ στέαρ τῶν αἰγῶν ὑγρότερον εἶναι φάναι τοῦ τῶν ὑῶν.
ὑγρότατον γὰρ τοῦτο σχεδὸν ἁπάντων τῶν ἄλλων ἐστὶ, καὶ ﻿ διὰ τοῦτο κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν ἐγγὺς ἐλαίου τὴν δύναμιν, μαλακτικώτερόν γε μὴν ἐλαίου καὶ πεπτικώτερόν ἐστι.
καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τοῖς πρὸς φλεγμονὰς ἁρμόττουσιν καταπλάσμασι μίγνυται.

τοῖς δὲ δακνομένοις τὰ κατὰ τὸ ἀπευθυσμένον ἢ τὸ κῶλον ἐνίεμεν αἴγειον μᾶλλον ἢ ὕειον στέαρ, οὐχ ὅτι μᾶλλον ἀμβλυτικόν ἐστι δριμύτητος, ὅσον γὰρ ἐπὶ τῇ φύσει μᾶλλον ἀμβλύνει τὸ ὕειον καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μίγνυται καὶ τοῖς ἕλκη θεραπεύουσι φαρμάκοις, οἷόν πέρ ἐστι καὶ τὸ καλούμενον πάρυγρον.

ἀλλ’ ὅτι τὸ μὲν αἴγειον πήγνυται ῥᾳδίως διὰ πάχος, ἀποῤῥεῖ δὲ τὸ ὕειον ὁμοίως τῷ ἐλαίῳ διὰ τοῦτ’ ἐνίεμεν αὐτὸ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τῶν δυσεντερικῶν τε καὶ τεινεσμωδῶν, ὅταν παρηγορῆσαι τὴν δῆξιν αὐτῶν βουληθῶμεν.
καὶ διὰ λεπτομέρειαν δ’ ἔνια μᾶλλον ἀμβλύνει δριμύτητας, ὅταν ἐν τῷ βάθει τῶν δακνομένων σωμάτων τὸ λυποῦν ᾖ.
ἧττον μὲν γὰρ τὸ παχυμερὲς, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸ λεπτομερὲς ὅλα διεξέρχεται τὰ σώματα καὶ πᾶσι κεράννυται τοῖς δάκνουσιν ἰχῶρσιν αὐτό.
κατὰ τοῦτο γοῦν καὶ τὸ χήνειον στέαρ τὰ κατὰ βάθος τῶν σωμάτων δάκνοντα μᾶλλον ἀμβλύνει.
ἔστι δὲ καὶ θερμότερον τοῦ ὑείου.
μεταξύ γε μὴν αὐτῶν ἐστι τὸ τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων, θερμότερον δ’ ἀεὶ καὶ ξηρότερον τὸ τῶν ἀῤῥένων ζώων ἐστίν.
αὐτῶν δὲ τούτων τὸ τῶν ἐκτεμνομένων τοὺς ὄρχεις ἧττον θερμόν τε καὶ ξηρόν.
ὁμοιοῦται γὰρ ἀεὶ τὸ εὐνουχισθὲν ἄῤῥεν τοῖς ὁμογενέσι θήλεσι.

κεφάλαιον δ’ ἐστὶ τοῦ λόγου τόδε κοινὸν, οὗ μεμνῆσθαι χρὴ, τὸ κατὰ τὴν τῶν ζώων κρᾶσιν ἀεὶ τὰς διαφορὰς γίνεσθαι τῆς ἐν αὐτοῖς πιμελῆς ἢ στέατος ἢ ὅπως ἂν ὀνομάζειν ἐθέλῃς ὅλον τὸ γένος τοῦτο τοῦ κατὰ τὰ ζῶα σώματος ἐλαιώδους τε καὶ λιπαροῦ.
ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ὗς ἀπολείπεται κατὰ θερμότητά τε καὶ ξηρότητα σχεδὸν ἁπάντων τῶν τετραπόδων ζώων, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ πιμελὴν ἧττόν τε θερμὴν ἔχει καὶ μᾶλλον ὑγράν.
ἁπάσης μὲν οὖν πιμελῆς δύναμίς ἐστιν ὑγραντική τε καὶ θερμαντικὴ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων σωμάτων.
τούτου γὰρ μεμνῆσθαι χρὴ διὰ παντὸς, εἰρημένου κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆσδε τῆς πραγματείας· αἱ δὲ καθ’ ἕκαστον αὐτῶν διαφοραὶ κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττόν εἰσιν.
τοῦ μὲν γὰρ ὑὸς ὡς πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἡ πιμελὴ τὸ μὲν ὑγραίνειν ἔχει δαψιλῶς, τὸ θερμαίνειν δ’ οὐχ ὁμοίως ὥσπερ τοὔλαιον, ἀλλ’ ἔστι κατὰ τὴν ἐν ἡμῖν θερμότητα καὶ ἡ τοῦ λίπους τῶν ὑῶν.

ἡ δὲ τῶν ταύρων πολὺ θερμοτέρα καὶ ξηροτέρα τῆς τῶν ὑῶν, μεμνημένων ἡμῶν πάλιν κἀνταῦθα τὸ μὲν ἄῤῥεν τοῦ θήλεος ἀεὶ ξηρότερον εἶναι καὶ θερμότερον, τὸ δ’ εὐνουχισθὲν ἄῤῥεν ὁμοιοῦσθαι τῷ θήλει, καθάπερ γε καὶ τὸ νέον ἅπαν.
αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν νέων τὸ θῆλυ τοῦ ἄῤῥενος ὑγρότερόν τε εἶναι καὶ ἧττον θερμόν.

οὕτως οὖν καὶ τὸ μόσχειον στέαρ ἀπολείπεται τοῦ τῶν ταύρων θερμότητί τε καὶ ξηρότητι καὶ τὸ τῶν ἐρίφων τοῦ τῶν αἰγῶν, ἀπολείπεται δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν αἰγῶν τοῦ τῶν τράγων, αὐτῶν δὴ πάλιν τὸ τῶν ταύρων τοῦ τῶν λεόντων· διαφορητικώτατον γὰρ ἐκεῖνο σχεδὸν ἁπάντων τῶν ἐν τοῖς τετράποσι.

καὶ γὰρ καὶ θερμότατον αὐτῶν ἐστι καὶ λεπτομερέστατον, ὥστε εἰ μίξαις αὐτὸ τοῖς πρὸς ἕλκη καὶ φλεγμονὰς ἁρμόττουσι φαρμάκοις, οὐ μόνον οὐδὲν ὀνήσεις, ἀλλὰ καὶ βλάψεις δριμύτερον τοῦ προσήκοντος ἐργασάμενος.
ὄγκοις δὲ χρονίοις ἐσκληρυσμένοις καὶ νεύρων ἀγκύλαις καὶ ἁπλῶς ὅσα σκιῤῥώδη, προσφορώτατόν ἐστιν ἐφ’ ὧν ἀπρακτότατον φαίνεται τὸ τῶν ὑῶν.
τὸ δὲ τῶν ταύρων ἶσόν πως ἑκατέρου διέστηκεν, ὅσῳ θερμότερόν τέ ἐστι καὶ ξηρότερον τοῦ τῶν ὑῶν, τοσούτῳ καὶ τοῦ τῶν λεόντων ἀπολειπόμενον.
ὡς ἂν οὖν ἐν τῷ μέσῳ τεταγμένον, εἰκότως ἑκατέρῳ τῷ γένει μίγνυται τῶν φαρμάκων, τοῖς τε τὰ σκιῤῥώδη θεραπεύουσι.
καὶ τοῖς τὰ φλεγμαίνοντα πέπτουσιν, ὁποῖόν ἐστιν τὸ τετραφάρμακον ὀνομαζόμενον ἐκ κηροῦ καὶ ῥητίνης καὶ πίττης καὶ στέατος συγκειμένου.
εἰς γάρ τοι τοῦτο, κᾂν ταύρειον βάλῃς κᾂν μόσχειον κᾂν τράγειον κᾂν αἴγειον κᾂν ὕειον, ἐκπυπτικόν τε καὶ πεπτικὸν ἐργάσῃ φάρμακον.

ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν ὕειον ἐμβληθὲν ἐπὶ παίδων ἁρμόζει καὶ γυναικῶν καὶ συνελόντι φάναι τῶν ἁπαλοσάρκων, τὸ δὲ τοῦ ταύρου σκαπανεῦσι καὶ θερισταῖς καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς σκληρὰς ἔχουσι σάρκας ἢ διὰ τὴν φυσικὴν κρᾶσιν ἢ διὰ τὴν ἰδέαν τοῦ βίου χρήσιμον ὑπάρχει.
χρονίζον δ’ ἅπαν στέαρ ἑαυτοῦ γίνεται θερμότερόν τε καὶ λεπτομερέστερον, ὥστε καὶ διαφορητικώτερον.
ὑπάρχει δὲ τοῦτο σχεδὸν ἅπασι τοῖς χρονίζουσιν, ὅσα γε μὴ φθάνει σαπῆναι.

καὶ γὰρ οἶνος καὶ μέλι καὶ ὄξος καὶ τυρὸς καὶ βούτυρον καὶ οἴσυπος ἔλαιόν τε πᾶν, εἴτε σχίνινον εἴτε κίκινον εἴτε ῥαφάνινον εἴτ’ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐλαιῶν εἴη, χρονίζοντα λεπτότερά τε καὶ λεπτομερέστερα γίνεται καὶ διὰ τοῦτο δριμύτερά τε γευομένοις φαίνεται διαφορητικώτερόν τε χρωμένοις, ἐπὶ τῶν σκληρυνομένων τε καὶ δυσλύτων ἁπάντων παθῶν.
ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν εἴρηκα δριμύτερον γευομένοις φαίνεσθαι.
τινὲς δὲ τῶν διαφθειρόντων τὰ σημαινόμενα τῶν ὀνομάτων οὐ δριμέα καλοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ στύφοντα τὰ τοιαῦτα πάντα, μέχρι τοῦ πεπέρεως, ὡς οὐδὲν διαφέρον ἢ στῦφον εἰπεῖν ἢ δριμύ.

καὶ εἰ αὖθις αὐτοὺς ἔροιο περί τε κηκίδων καὶ μύρτων καὶ μεσπίλων καὶ σιδίων ῥοιᾶς, ὀμφακίου τε καὶ ῥοῦ, καὶ ταῦτα στύφειν φασὶ, καίτοι γε ἐναντιωτάτην αἴσθησιν ἔχομεν ἐπ’ αὐτῶν τῆς γινομένης ἡμῖν ἀπὸ πεπέρεως καὶ πυρέθρου καὶ νάπυος, εὐφορβίου τε καὶ κρομμύου καὶ σκορόδου καὶ ἀδάρκης.

εἰ μὲν οὖν ὡς τὸ τῆς στύψεως ὄνομα κοινὸν ἐπιφέρουσιν, κατ’ ἀμφοτέρων τῶν γιγνομένων ἡμῖν ἐν τῇ γεύσει παθῶν, οὕτω καὶ αὐτὰ τὰ ﻿ πάθη μίαν ἔχειν οἴονται φύσιν, ἀλλ’ ὅτι μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώπους αὐτοὺς εἶναι νομιστέον ἰδίας αἰσθήσεις ἔχοντας μόνους.

εἰ δ’ ὄμφακα μὲν καὶ ῥοῦν καὶ κηκῖδα βαλαύστιόν τε καὶ ὑποκυστίδα, συνάγειν τε καὶ σφίγγειν ἡμῶν ὁμολογοῦσι τὴν οὐσίαν, διακρίνειν τε καὶ δάκνειν καὶ διεξέρχεσθαι τὸ πέπερι καὶ νᾶπυ καὶ πύρεθρον, ἀκύρως μὲν ὀνομάζουσι στύφοντα τὰ δάκνοντα καὶ θερμαίνοντα, τῆς γνώσεως μέντοι τῶν φαρμάκων αὐτῶν οὐχ ἡμαρτήκασιν.

εἰ δὲ δεῖ στοχασάμενον εἰπεῖν πότερον ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασιν ἢ ἐν τοῖς πράγμασι σφάλλονται, φαίην ἂν ἔγωγε μᾶλλον ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασιν ἐσφάλθαι τοὺς ἄνδρας, καὶ μάλιστα τοὺς ἀήθεις Ἑλλάδος φωνῆς, οἷός ἐστιν ὁ Ἀναζαρβεὺς Διοσκορίδης, πολλὰ μὲν καλῶς εἴρηκε τῶν περὶ τῆς ἰατρικῆς ὕλης ἱστορουμένων, ἀγνοῶν δὲ τὰ σημαινόμενα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ὀνομάτων.

οὗτος οὖν, ὅταν λέγει στυπτικώτερον στέαρ εἶναι τὸ τῶν αἰγῶν τοῦ τῶν ὑῶν, εἰ μὲν οὖν τὸ δριμύτερον διὰ τοῦ στυπτικωτέρου βούλεται δηλῶσαι, ἐκδεξόμεθα τὸν λόγον ὡς ἀληθῆ· εἰ δὲ τὸ τοιαύτην ἔχον ποιότητά τε καὶ δύναμιν, οἷον ῥοῦς καὶ ῥῆον ὑπόκυστίς τε καὶ βαλαύστιον, οὐκ ἀληθῆ φήσομεν εἶναι τὸν λόγον.

ἐπειδὴ δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἐχιδνῶν στέαρ, ὅταν ἐκ ῥιζῶν τις ἀνασπάσας τὰς ἐν ταῖς μασχάλαις τρίχας ἐπαλείφῃ, φασὶ μὴ καὶ ταύτας φύεσθαι, κάλλιον ἔδοξέ μοι καὶ τούτου πειραθῆναι, καὶ πράξας ὡς ἐκέλευσαν εὗρον ψευδομένους αὐτοὺς, ὥσπερ καὶ ὅτι τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν ὑποχύσεων ἰᾶται.
τὸ δὲ τῶν ἄρκτων στέαρ ἀλωπεκίαις ἁρμόττείν ἀληθῶς ἔγραψαν, ἔχομεν δ’ αὐτοῦ δοκιμώτερα φάρμακα πρὸς τὸ πάθος.
ἀλλὰ τό γε μὴν τῶν ἀλωπέκων ὅταν ὠταλγίας φῶσι θεραπεύειν, ἄνευ τοῦ διορίσασθαι ποίας λέγουσιν ὠταλγίας, ὡς οὐδὲ γινώσκουσιν διηρθρωμένως αὐτοῖς ἃ λέγουσιν, οὐδ’ ὅλως χρὴ προσέχειν τὸν νοῦν.
ἄλλοι δὲ ἰχθύων ἐπαινοῦσι στέαρ, ὡς πρὸς τὰς ὑποχύσεις ἢ ὅπερ ἂν ἐθέλωσι πάθος ὀνομάζειν.
ἕτεροι δ’ οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἰχθύων, ἀλλὰ ποταμίων γράφουσιν, ἄλλοι δὲ μᾶλλον θαλαττίων, ἵνα δοκῶσί τι πλέον ἐπίστασθαι τῶν πολλῶν.
english_sentences: On fat and suet.] Fat (pimelē) and suet (stear).
These too are among the commonest of the parts in animals.
For all well-nourished animals have fat or suet, whereas lean and ill-nourished ones often appear to have none at all, and often have so little, and that so dry, that it is hard to use.
Suet differs from fat in thickness; for this reason suet arises in animals whose whole nature is more earthy, just as fat does in those whose nature is more moist.

For this very reason, then, fat melts easily under fire, but once melted does not easily congeal; suet, by contrast, does not melt easily, and if it is melted it congeals very quickly and appears much harder than fat.

The pig, then, when well nourished, has a very great deal of fat on account of the natural moistness of its mixture, whereas oxen and goats and all other horned animals produce suet in greatest quantity on account of their dryness.
You may, if you wish, call the whole oleaginous and oily substance in animals suet, as most physicians do; and you may also name this whole kind fat.
You may not, however, if you wish not to speak falsely, say that the suet of goats is moister than that of pigs.
For the latter is the moistest of nearly all the others, and for this reason in its action it is close to oil in power, though it is more softening than oil and more concoctive.
And for this reason it is mixed into the poultices suited to inflammations.

But for those who are bitten in the region of the rectum or the colon we inject goat's rather than pig's suet, not because it is more blunting of pungency (for, so far as its nature goes, pig's suet blunts more, and for this reason it is also mixed into drugs that treat ulcers, such as the one called parygron), but because goat's suet congeals easily on account of its thickness, whereas pig's flows away just like oil; for this reason we inject the former rather in dysenteric and tenesmic patients, when we wish to soothe their biting.
Some things also blunt pungencies more on account of fineness of particles, when what is giving pain lies in the depth of the bodies that are being bitten.
For the coarse-particled passes less, and the fine-particled more, through whole bodies, and mixes itself with all the biting ichors.
In this respect, at any rate, goose suet blunts more effectively what bites in the depth of bodies.
It is also hotter than pig's.
Between them lies that of cocks; and that of male animals is always hotter and drier.
Among these themselves, that of those whose testicles are excised is less hot and dry; for the castrated male always comes to resemble the females of the same kind.

The general heading of the account, which must be remembered, is this: that the differences of the fat or suet in animals (or however you wish to name this whole kind of oleaginous and oily body in animals) always arise according to the mixture of the animals.
Since, then, the pig falls short in heat and dryness of nearly all four-footed animals, for this reason it also has fat that is both less hot and more moist.

Now the power of all fat is moistening and heating of human bodies; for this must be remembered throughout, having been stated at the beginning of this treatise; and the differences in each of them are matters of more and less.
For the fat of the pig, relative to us, has moistening in abundance, but heating not in the same way as oil; rather, the fat (lipos) of pigs is on a level with the heat in us.

That of bulls is much hotter and drier than that of pigs, we again remembering here too that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the castrated male resembles the female, as indeed does everything young; and that among the young themselves the female is moister and less hot than the male.

Thus calf's suet falls short of that of bulls in heat and dryness, and that of kids of that of goats, and that of goats falls short of that of he-goats, and again that of bulls in turn falls short of that of lions; for that is the most dispersing of nearly all those in quadrupeds.

For it is also the hottest of them and the most fine-particled, so that if you mix it into the drugs suited to ulcers and inflammations, you will not only do no good but will even do harm, having made the drug more pungent than is fitting.
But for chronic hardened swellings, contractures (ankylai) of sinews, and in short whatever is scirrhous, it is most suitable, in cases in which that of pigs appears most ineffective.
That of bulls stands roughly equally distant from each, being as much hotter and drier than that of pigs as it falls short of that of lions.

As being placed in the middle, then, it is reasonably mixed into each kind of drug, both those that treat scirrhous conditions and those that concoct inflamed parts, such as the one called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax, resin, pitch and suet.
For into this, whether you put bull's or calf's or he-goat's or goat's or pig's, you will make a suppurative and concoctive drug.

But pig's, when put in, suits children and women and, in a word, the soft-fleshed, while bull's is useful for diggers, reapers and all who have hard flesh, whether through their natural mixture or through the kind of life they lead.
All suet, as it ages, becomes hotter and more fine-particled than it was, and so also more dispersing.
This holds for nearly all things that age, at least those that do not rot first.

For wine, honey, vinegar, cheese, butter and oesypum, and every oil, whether mastic oil or castor oil or radish oil or the very oil from olives, become thinner and more fine-particled as they age, and for this reason appear more pungent to those who taste them and more dispersing to those who use them, in all hardened and hard-to-resolve affections.
I, then, have said that they appear more pungent to those who taste them.
